read.text: How to Use This Guide

Throughout this guide, every teaching activity is marked with a coloured box and an icon, so you can see at a glance what you are expected to do. Plain text is content to be taught; the boxes are where you act.
FACILITATOR HINT What you do, say and prepare as facilitator — instructions, scripts, prompts and notes.

EXERCISE / PRACTICE Hands-on work: role play, demonstration, individual and
supervised practice, video sessions.
GROUP DISCUSSION Questions you put to the whole group or to small groups, and the Q&A guides.
CASE-BASED DISCUSSION Clinical cases and scenarios to be read out and worked through by participants.
ANSWER KEY The expected answers — for the facilitator, after the group has tried.
KEY MESSAGE The one sentence participants must leave the session with.
Timing shown in a box heading is the time allocated to that activity. Answer keys are for you only — do not read them out before the group has worked the case.
Introduction & Training Framework

This Facilitator Guide has been developed to support the effective implementation of the Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns (MSSN) – 2026. It provides practical, step-by-step guidance to facilitators on:

• Planning and organizing the training
  • Delivering high-quality, competency-based sessions
  • Facilitating skills practice and clinical learning
  • Assessing participant competence
  • Adapting training to real hospital constraints in Sudan
This guide is intended to be used together with:

• The Sudan Training Manual for Management of Sick and Small Newborn – 2026
  • Participant modules and job aids
  • Skills checklists and assessment tools

Care of sick and small newborns is a strategic priority under the Sudan Newborn Action Plan (2022– 2030) Neonatal mortality remains a major public health challenge in Sudan. Most preventable neonatal deaths are due to:

• Birth asphyxia
  • Prematurity and its complications
  • Neonatal sepsis
  • Delayed recognition and referral of sick newborns
This training course and facilitator guide are designed to:

• Strengthen hospital-based newborn care
  • Improve early recognition and timely management
  • Standardize care across facilities
  • Build practical clinical competence among doctors, nurses, and midwives
This course covers newborn care from:

• Birth and the Golden Minute
  • Emergency and essential newborn care
  • Special care (SCBU / NICU level)
  • Ventilation and advanced care
  • Stabilization, referral, and discharge
This is a hospital-based course only. Training assumes access to:

• Delivery rooms
  • Newborn units (SCBU / NICU)
  • Skills labs or simulation space
Primary Participants

• Medical Officers (General Practitioners)
  • Pediatric residents and pediatricians
  • NICU / SCBU Nurses
Prerequisites Participants should have:

• Basic training in maternal and newborn care
  • Current clinical role in hospital newborn services
  • Commitment to full course attendance.

• Certification authority: Federal Ministry of Health – Sudan
  • Certification is awarded only after:
      • Completion of required sessions
      • Passing knowledge assessments
      • Demonstrated clinical and skills competence
  • No state certification is permitted
Educational Principles This course is based on:

• Adult learning principles
  • Competency-based training
  • Learning by doing
  • Case-based and skills-focused instruction
Emphasis

• Skills over theory
  • Decision-making over memorization
  • Patient safety over speed
  • Team communication
Participants

• Ideal: 16–24
  • Maximum: 24
Facilitators

• Ratio: 1 facilitator: 4–6 participants
  • Minimum facilitators for 24 participants: 4 facilitators + 1 course director
Pre-Course Checklist (Course Director)
item done

• Confirm venue and clinical access
  • Identify facilitators
  • Confirm participant list
  • Arrange equipment and supplies
  • Print materials and assessments
  • Coordinate with hospital management
Facilitators must:
item done

• Read the Sudan Training Manual 2026
  • Review assigned modules
  • Practice demonstrations
  • Prepare scenarios
  • Review assessment tools
A facilitator is not a lecturer. A facilitator:

• Guides learning
  • Coaches skills
  • Observes practice
  • Provides immediate feedback
  • Protects patient safety during training
Facilitators spend most of their time:

• In small groups
  • At skills stations
  • In clinical areas
  • Giving individual feedback
Core Responsibilities of Facilitators Instruct

• Explain how to use modules and job aids
  • Demonstrate clinical skills
  • Clarify difficult concepts
  • Guide case discussions and scenarios
  • Supervise bedside practice
Motivate

• Encourage participation
  • Reinforce correct practice
  • Create a safe learning environment
Manage

• Monitor participant progress
  • Ensure smooth movement between sessions
  • Maintain time discipline
  • Ensure required materials are available
What Facilitators Should NOT Do

• Deliver long lectures
  • Read slides or manuals word-for-word
  • Humiliate or embarrass participants
  • Allow unsafe clinical practice
  • Rush skills training without supervision

read.text: Interactive session: the golden minute of life By the end of this section, participants should be able to:

• Define the Golden Minute
  • Explain why it is critical for neonatal survival
  • Demonstrate readiness for immediate newborn care at birth
Teaching Method: short presentation +Interactive discussion
Facilitator Instructions
Opening Discussion
Ask participants:

• “What happens in the first minute after birth?”
  • “Why do some babies fail to breathe at birth?”
Allow brief responses. Do not correct immediately.
Key Teaching Points
Emphasize:

• The Golden Minute starts when the baby is fully delivered
  • It is the critical window to establish breathing
  • Do NOT wait for APGAR scoring to act
  • Delayed action leads to:
  • Brain injury
  • Long-term disability
  • Death

sections.title: Early essential newborn Care (Birth Up to 90 minutes of age): Role-play (1): delivery of a breathing newborn without coaching

read.text: Role-play (1): delivery of a breathing newborn without coaching

This role play includes scenario of a health-care provider doing their usual practice (to be done in a large group); the facilitators use the Skills checklist to assess every step of the action by the demonstrator including the exact time (to the second) where relevant. This will be used as a baseline performance score of the demonstration.

• Ask for three participants, one participant each to play: (1) the woman delivering the baby; (2) the attending health worker; and (3) the recorder.
  • Ask the “mother” to wear the Mamanatalie™ and sit on the delivery bed. A facilitator will do the set-up of the “baby” to appear to be in the mother’s womb.
  • Explain to the attending health worker: “You will deliver a baby and provide new-born care. The woman is fully dilated. You have already weighed her, taken her blood pressure, and listened for fetal heart tones. There is no more time, she will deliver in about a minute. Please do exactly as you would during and immediately following the delivery from the first step immediately before delivery until the last step in the immediate postpartum care period. Please do not explain what you are doing. However, please do request the mother or other health workers to perform actions as needed.” Ask if there is anything that needs further clarification
  • Explain to the note taker: “You will write down the exact actions/interventions you observe before, during and immediately after delivery. Please record the time of each activity: to the second for events occurring within three minutes of delivery, and to the minute for events occurring thereafter.”
  • Ask the other participants to pay close attention to what the attendant is doing, and take key notes, as they will be asked to comment later. During the demonstration, they should not tell the demonstrator what to do or how to do it.
  • Ask the attendant to start the role-play. When the baby is “born”, a facilitator will make the baby’s crying sound and make the cord pulsate. The facilitator should record – and time – exactly what is happening: to the second for events occurring within the first three minutes after delivery, and to the minute, at other times.
Notes

• Most participants doing the role-play will describe what they do in their practice instead of actually doing it. In this case, ask them to do what they are describing.
  • Many participants will not do exactly what they do in their practice during deli-very (e.g.

wash hands, put on gloves and gowns, and organize delivery space). You can say, “Most people… [Wear gloves, for instance]. Would you like to start over and do it exactly as you would normally do where you work?”
Discussion and simulation based on current practices and sequence of events
FACILITATOR HINT
Facilitators generate participatory agreement or disagreement with every stage of practice and encourage discussion on the evidence base for the correct practice (done in a large group).

• A. Give the attendant a chance to discuss her/his thoughts on the delivery, then ask the participants to give their thoughts. If there are interesting points raised that will be covered during re-enactment, take note of them and state: “We will come back to this point shortly.”
  • B. Ask the note taker to read aloud his record of only the first action that the attendant(s) had performed. Ask the attendant to do the action again; ask the participants if this is correct or needs improvement. Facilitate a discussion around the: (1) order of actions; (2) quality of the action; and (3) the evidence base for the recommendation (see Facilitator’s Notes on page
    • 15) .
  • C. At the appropriate time during step b, have each of the participants demonstrate their proficiency in the following areas:
  • setting up the newborn resuscitation area,
  • checking bag and mask for functionality,
  • immediate, thorough and sequential drying,
  • checking cord pulsations, and
  • Measuring distance for cord clamping.
  • D. Repeat steps b and c until all actions have been practiced.

Group discussion (early essential newborn care)
let us think together about why newborns die, and what we can actually do about it in the first minutes of life.
I will ask you a series of questions. There is no test here. Most of what we need is already in this room, in what you do every day — so please answer from your own practice, not from a textbook.
Let each other finish. I will not correct answers immediately; we will build the picture together and reach the right answer as a group.
By the end you should see how a small number of simple actions — keeping the baby warm, drying well, helping the baby breathe, touching less — prevent most newborn deaths."

• What are the major causes of newborn death?
        • Asphyxia, sepsis and prematurity.
  • What are underlying causes of death?
        • Not breathing, hypothermia, not breastfeeding.
  • Why is hypothermia dangerous to newborns?
        • Hypothermia can cause newborns to have infection, coagulation defects, acidosis, delayed fetal-to-newborn circulatory adjustment, hyaline membrane disease (respiratory distress syndrome) and brain haemorrhage. It is dangerous.
  • What are major causes of hypothermia?
        • Cold room with draft (convection), being wet (evaporation), touching cold surfaces (conduction), being exposed (radiation).
  • What actions can health workers perform to prevent hypothermia?
        • Ensure room temperature of 25–28 °C. Close all windows, turn off fan and air-conditioning to ensure there is no draught (i.e. airflow) in the room. Dry baby thoroughly and then cover; put in skin-to-skin contact with the mother. For the rare resuscitation that would be needed, turn on the radiant warmer (if available) before delivery or cover the resuscitation area surface with a clot
  • Can we predict which babies will not be breathing?
        • Even babies born of mothers with no risk factors may not breathe.
  • Is it important to prepare the newborn resuscitation area?
        • Even though rare, we cannot predict which babies will not breathe at birth. Thus, we need the newborn resuscitation area set up for all deliveries.
  • How do we prepare the delivery space?
        • Ensure that all delivery equipment and supplies are available, clean, and ready for use. Lay out in sequence: gloves*, gauze, povidone-iodine, 2 cloths, oxytocin, needle and syringe, 2 cord clamps** and sterile scissors.
        • Aside from cloth, ventilation bag and mask, ensure that suction device, hat and clock/timer are in easy reach/view of the newborn resuscitation area. All equipment should be tested before the delivery.
        • If only one provider handles the mother’s and the newborn’s cord sections, 2 pairs of gloves should be worn. The outer pair should be removed prior to handling the cord.
  • Why is drying important?
        • It stimulates breathing. Most babies who are not breathing at birth will start to breathe after thorough drying.
        • It prevents hypothermia.
  • How do we dry well?
        • Before delivery, place a clean cloth over the mother’s bare abdomen. Deliver the baby and place on the clean cloth. Drying should be immediate (within a few seconds of delivery), thorough and systematic. Wipe the eyes, mouth/nose, face, head, front, back, arms and legs. Thorough drying takes around 30 seconds. It should be by rubbing, not patting, but should not remove the vernix. Assess the baby for breathing during drying.
  • Why is skin-to-skin contact good?
        • It keeps a baby warm, promotes bonding, contributes to overall success of breastfeeding/ colostrum feeding, stimulates the immune system (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue), protects from hypoglycaemia, and helps colonization with maternal skin flora (friendly family bacteria).
  • How do we maintain direct skin-to-skin contact?
        • You have just finished drying the baby. Remove the wet cloth so that the baby is in direct skin-to-skin contact with the mother’s bare abdomen. Cover, but do not wrap, the baby with another clean dry cloth. This keeps the skin of the baby’s abdomen directly in contact with the skin of the mother’s abdomen. Cover the newborn’s head with a hat.
  • Why should we delay cord clamping until after the cord stops pulsating?
        • Delaying cord-clamping protects against anaemia, intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotizing enterocolitis.
  • How do we know the cord is pulsating?
        • Demonstrate with the manikin. Ask every participant to look and to feel the cord.
  • Why should we stop our usual practice of clamping the cord far from the umbilical base for later trimming?
        • Unnecessary handling of the cord gives opportunity for bacteria to get into the cord.
        • Cutting at 2 cm (between the clamps/ties) eliminates the need to “trim” the cord later.
  • Should we apply disinfectant to the cord?
        • No. If allowed to air dry, the cord will dry more quickly. Remind participants that they need to tell caretakers: “Do not use a binder or apply any substance to the cord.”
  • Why should we call out the time of delivery precise to the second?
        • Actions in the first minute especially need timing to the second. Thorough drying takes around 30 seconds. A baby not breathing after 30 seconds needs to be helped to breathe/ or have lungs aerated within 60 seconds. The cord should be clamped after cord stops pulsating at 1–3 minutes.
  • Why is unnecessary handling bad?
  • Each time a health worker handles a baby, the baby is at risk for infection and cold.
  • When should a health worker handle the baby?
        • Only when there is a medical need.
  • When should a health worker perform hand hygiene (handwashing or alcohol hand rub)?
        • Immediately before and immediately after handling a baby/mother or their surroundings, after exposure to body fluids, and before and after an aseptic procedure.
  • When should a baby be suctioned?
        • Only when the airway is blocked and baby is completely not breathing, for example, a non-vigorous, meconium-stained baby.
  • Does a baby with thick meconium staining but who is breathing well need suctioning?
        • No. The baby is breathing well and suctioning does not prevent meconium aspiration.
  • Why is suctioning a baby dangerous? (Ask for as many answers as possible.)
        • Hold the bulb up. Pretend to suction a participant, then move to the next and ask if it is OK to suction them with this. Ask why. Do the same for five participants. Bulbs are dirty even when cleaning has been attempted. You cannot get rid of all the bacteria. Suction bulbs spread infection. Ask if they would feel comfortable if you suctioned them. Ask why. Gagging a baby is dangerous. It can cause the baby to stop breathing and get sick. It can cause trauma to the mouth and nose.

sections.title: Support breast feeding in the first hour of life

read.text: Facilitator has following objectives to achieve by end of this session:
The participant after completing this module should be able to:

• 1. Enumerate advantages of breastfeeding.
  • 2. Understand and help mother(s) with the correct technique of breastfeeding.
  • 3. Understand the physiology of lactation.
  • 4. Identify factors enhancing lactation.
  • 5. Describe difficulties associated with breast feeding and their solutions.
  • 6. Learn skills related to expression of breast milk.
Demonstration Using the MamaBreast Simulator

MamaBreast is a wearable simulator designed to provide a highly realistic simulation of breastfeeding. It specifically supports training in proper breastfeeding positioning and attachment, making it ideal for this demonstration. To prepare and adjust the MamaBreast simulator for the volunteer, follow these steps:

• Open the cap on the MamaBreast and pour in water until the bag is partially full.
  • Massage the bag from the outside with both hands to separate the foils, which makes filling the bag easier.
  • Pour a total of 500 ml of water into each bag.
  • Avoid using actual milk in the simulator, as this will damage the product.
  • Place the MamaBreast simulator on the volunteer's body.
  • Adjust the waist strap to ensure a comfortable fit around the side of the body.
  • Adjust the overall height of the simulator by pulling the strap located on the neck.
Step 1: Simulator Preparation

• Fill both bags of the MamaBreast simulator with exactly 500 ml of water each, strictly avoiding the use of real milk to prevent damage to the equipment.
  • Assist the volunteer in putting on the MamaBreast simulator.
  • Adjust the waist strap to ensure a secure, comfortable fit around the side, and adjust the neck strap so the breasts sit at a natural height.
Step 2: Demonstrating Good Positioning

• Hand the newborn doll to the volunteer and instruct them to hold the baby close to their body.
  • Demonstrate that the neonate's head and body must be aligned in a straight line, ensuring the neck is neither twisted nor bent.
  • Show participants how to support the baby's entire body rather than just the head and neck, which is particularly vital when handling neonates under 28 days old.
  • Position the baby so they are facing the breast, with their nose directly opposite the nipple, to encourage the rooting reflex.

sections.title: Support breast feeding in the first hour of life: Step 3: Demonstrating Good Attachment

read.text: Step 3: Demonstrating Good Attachment

• Verbally outline the four key clinical signs of a proper latch while the volunteer acts out the motion with the doll.
  • Chin: The baby's chin should firmly touch the breast.
  • Mouth: The baby's mouth must be open wide.
  • Lip: The baby's lower lip should be curled or turned outward.
  • Areola: More of the mother's areola should be visible above the baby's upper lip than below the lower lip.
Instruct the volunteer to bring the baby to the breast (not the breast to the baby) to simulate achieving this attachment on the MamaBreast
Group Discussion:(support breast feeding)
"We have talked about keeping the baby warm and helping the baby breathe. Now we come to feeding — and this is where much of what we do out of habit turns out to work against the baby.

I will ask you questions about breastfeeding. Answer from what you see on your ward, not from what you know is supposed to happen. Some of our routine practices are the problem, so please be honest about them.

Watch for two things as we go. First, the baby sets the timing, not us — we wait for the baby to show readiness. Second, almost every mother can feed her baby; when it seems she cannot, the cause is usually something we have done or something we have given.
I will not correct answers straight away. We will reach them together."
Why is breastfeeding beneficial?

• Breastfeeding is one of the most life-saving interventions we have. Delays in initiation of breastfeeding are associated with dramatic increase in death and illness. Babies who are fed formula have 4–6 times the risk of dying compared with exclusively breastfed babies. Formula is more dangerous to a newborn than is smoking to an adult.
When is a typical baby ready to breastfeed?

• Never immediately after birth. Leave the baby between the mother’s breasts in continuous skin-to-skin contact. The baby may want to rest for 20–30 minutes or even longer before showing signs of readiness to breastfeed (i.e. feeding cues). Just under half of all babies initiate breastfeeding naturally after one hour from birth.
  • Note: Please explain to the participants that babies should not be forced onto the breast or have the nipple forced into the mouth. Wait for the feeding cues.
What are the feeding cues that a baby is ready to breastfeed?

• The earliest sign is drooling, followed by mouth opening, tonguing, licking, rooting and biting of fingers or hand. Eventually, the baby will locate the breast and open his/her mouth widely to attach to the breast.
Do some mothers not have enough milk?

• Studies in very poor countries (Ecuador, Nigeria) showed that all mothers (many of whom were severely malnourished) were able physiologically to breastfeed. A newborn’s stomach is only the size of your thumbnail. It may not be perceived that the baby has gotten enough milk.
  • If the baby appears to be fussy or dissatisfied at the mother’s breast, first ensure that no other liquids are being given, i.e. formula, sugar water or other fluids.
  • Counsel the mother on offering her breasts 8–12 times over the day and night upon her baby’s early feeding cues.
  • Stimulation of the breast by the baby’s sucking results in messages being sent to the mother’s brain and back to the breast to produce more milk. Thus, milk production will increase if the mother’s breast is stimulated more frequently through offering the breast more often.
What are signs of good feeding position?

• The baby’s head and body are in a straight line (neck is not twisted or flexed), the baby is facing the breast, with nose opposite nipple, the mother is holding the baby’s body close to her body and supporting the baby’s whole body (not just neck and shoulders).
  • What are signs of good attachment?
  • More areola is visible above the baby’s mouth than below; the mouth is wide open with the lower lip turned outward, the baby’s chin touching breast; sucking is slow and deep with occasional pauses.
  • Note: Signs of ineffective attachment include in-drawing of newborn’s cheeks, lip-smacking sounds or mother’s nipple pain
How can we improve attachment?

• By touching the baby’s lips with her nipple, waiting until the mouth is opened wide, moving baby quickly onto breast, aiming baby’s lower lip well below nipple; also, by trying different positions, e.g. sitting upright or laying on her side

read.text: Demonstrate correct technique for giving vitamin K injections to newborns
• Have participants practice injection technique (simulation) in pairs.
Site

• Anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis), middle third — the only routine IM site in a newborn.
  • Never the buttock: risk of sciatic nerve injury and unreliable absorption. Never the deltoid.
  • Two injections at the same visit go into different thighs — for example vitamin K 1 mg in one, hepatitis B vaccine 0.5 mL in the other.
  • Maximum 0.5 mL per site.
Technique

• Clean the skin only if visibly soiled; if alcohol is used, let it dry fully.
  • Hold the thigh firmly. Bunch the muscle between thumb and finger.
  • Insert at 90° with a 23–25G needle, about 16 mm, to the correct depth.
  • Do not aspirate — not required, and it increases pain.
  • Inject slowly over 3–5 seconds.
  • Withdraw, press gently with dry gauze. Do not rub.
Demonstration of GIVING EYE CARE

• Wash your hands.
  • Hold one eye open and put a ribbon of Tetracycline 1% eye ointment along the inside of the lower eyelid.
  • Make sure not to let the medicine dropper or tube touch the baby's eye or anything else.
  • Repeat this step to put medication into the other eye.
  • Do not rinse out the eye medication.
Role play: Keeping baby warm in post-natal ward during examination and routine care

• Purpose: The purpose of this role play is to help you practice counseling skills for teaching families to keep their Newborns warm.
  • Scenario The baby has been placed in skin-to-skin contact with Mother. and covered with a blanket. He is not Soiled with blood or meconium. It is now 30 minutes after birth and Mother wants to know why her Baby has not yet been bathed. She says that her other babies were bathed within 10 minutes after birth And that she would like her new baby to be bathed immediately
  • Health worker: The health worker is experienced in the care of newborn babies and has good Interpersonal communication skills.
  • Mother: The mother, 30-year-old, just gave birth to her fifth child, a healthy full-term Boy, at the district health center.
  • During the role play, all particpnat are observers, they should Think about what they see and prepare to participate in the discussion.
  • After the role play, the group will discuss what happened. Think about how you would answer the Discussion questions for this role play.
Discussion Questions "You have just watched the role play. Before we go through what happened, I want you to think about two things: what the health worker said, and how she said it.
Good clinical knowledge is not enough if the mother does not understand or trust what she is being told. So as we discuss, notice both the message and the manner.
Answer from what you observed — not from what should have happened."

• How did the health worker explain to Mother why it is important to wait to bathe her baby?
  • How did the health worker reassure Mr. A that her baby did not need a bath immediately?
  • What key messages did the health worker discuss with Mother?
  • While skin–to-skin is optimal, can we also discuss how to keep the baby warm if Mom doesn’t want to do skin-to-skin – i.e. the baby should be wrapped, not too tight, with the head covered, then placed beside the mother. Advise on keeping the baby warm beyond the immediate period after delivery.
  • How did the health worker show good counseling skills when explaining to mother the importance of waiting to bathe her baby?
      • By speaking in a calm reassuring manner
      • By using words that mother understood
      • By using the same reassuring manner to answer mother’s questions
      • By encouraging mother to ask questions and express her concerns
  • How did the health worker reassure Mother that her baby did not need a bath immediately?
The health worker explained that:

• Bathing her baby so soon may cause dangerous heat loss (i.e., the baby may develop hypothermia or become cold). The new baby needs time to adjust to regulating its own temperature.
      • It is good to wait until at least 24 hours of life for the first bath, but if it is important to her to bathe her baby early, she should wait until the baby is warm and at least 6 hours after birth.
  • What key messages did the health worker discuss with Mother? The key messages stressed by the health worker should include the following:
      • All newborns lose heat quickly after birth, and this can be dangerous.
      • Skin-to-skin contact with the mother is the best way to keep the baby warm.
Skin-to-skin contact helps maternal-infant attachment and early breast-feeding

Case-Based Scenarios: Managing Temperature, Weight, and Feeding Problems in the Newborn

Case 1 — Temperature Problem
Baby Nour — female, born at term, 39 weeks gestation 90 minutes of age Read aloud to the provider:

“Baby Nour is 90 minutes old. She cried at birth and breastfed within the first hour. On examination she is active, breathing 44 breaths per minute with no chest indrawing, and pink. Her weight is 2900 g. Axillary temperature is 36.2°C.”

• 1. Using the Assessment on 90 minutes Quick reference table, which row applies to Baby Nour?
  • 2. What actions does that row list?
  • 3. What should the provider do right now?
Facilitator Answer Key — Part A

• 36.2°C is not in the danger-sign row (Temp <35.5°C or >38°C) and not in the well-baby row (Temp 36.5–37.5°C).
  • It falls in the middle row: Weight 1500–<2500 g / Temp 35.5–38°C / Feeding difficulty / Risk of infection. Her weight (2900 g) is normal, but the temperature finding on its own places her in this row.
  • Apply the row's actions:
  • Maintain skin-to-skin, support breastfeeding, and treat risk of infection.
  • The “low weight or low temperature” sub-action applies: provide continuous skin-to-skin, improve thermal care.
  • Continue skin-to-skin contact; if interrupted, clothe/wrap in a clean, dry blanket and cover the head; avoid drafts and contact with wet or cold surfaces.
  • Reassess by touching the foot or forehead; if it feels too cool or too hot, measure with a thermometer. “if not improved or had danger sign, stabilize for referral” — “if improved, immunize and advise about home care.”
Part B — one hour later
Read aloud to the provider:
“One hour later, Baby Nour's temperature is rechecked: 35.3°C. She is still skin-to-skin and attempting to breastfeed, but her feet feel cool to touch.”

• 1. Which row of the table applies now?
  • 2. What must the provider do, in order?

sections.title: Newborn Examination: Facilitator Answer Key — Part B

read.text: Facilitator Answer Key — Part B

• 35.3°C is below 35.5°C — this now meets the top (danger-sign) row of the table. The action listed is: give antibiotics; stabilize for referral as needed.
  • Improve thermal care immediately: remove any wet clothing, cover the head, add a dry layer/blanket, warm the room, keep continuous, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact.
  • Give antibiotics: give the first dose without delay, per the Sudan neonatal sepsis protocol (Ampicillin 50 mg/kg + Gentamicin 5 mg/kg). Do not delay waiting for investigations.
  • Stabilize for referral as needed: explain to the parents why urgent treatment and referral are needed; keep mother and baby together; maintain warmth and skin-to-skin during transport;
complete a referral note.
• Recheck temperature once thermal care is improved. Do not use uncontrolled heat sources — the manual warns against placing a baby close to heat sources and against over-wrapping.
Debrief questions:

• Who in your facility is authorized to give the first antibiotic dose, and how quickly can this actually happen after a danger sign is identified?
  • What are the risks of overheating a baby while trying to correct hypothermia?
Case 2 — Birth Weight Problem
Baby Yasin — male, born at 32 weeks gestation
Read aloud to the provider:
“Baby Yasin was born at 32 weeks gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery at a health centre.
He cried weakly at birth. At 90 minutes of age he is weighed: 1350 g. Temperature is 36.6°C. He is breathing 48 breaths per minute with no chest indrawing. He has not yet attempted to breastfeed.”

• 1. Which row of the Section 3.2 table applies to Baby Yasin?
  • 2. What does Section 3.4 say for a baby this size?
  • 3. What immediate care is required?
Facilitator Answer Key
• Weight <1500 g is listed on its own in the top row of the table — action: stabilize for referral as needed. This applies even though his temperature and breathing are currently normal.
babies <1500 g “should receive advanced care and prolonged skin-to-skin (kangaroo mother care).”

• Begin prolonged skin-to-skin (Kangaroo Mother) care with the mother or another family member.
  • Complete essential newborn care if not yet done: eye care, cord care, vitamin K.
  • Support attempts at the breast; if he cannot attach, plan for expressed breast milk by cup or tube, per the table's feeding-difficulty sub-action.
  • Prepare for referral if this facility cannot provide the advanced care,Complete the newborn record and fill a referral note; keep mother and baby together.
Case 3 — Feeding Problem
Baby Salma — female, born at 35 weeks gestation
Read aloud to the provider:

“Baby Salma is 4 hours old, born at 35 weeks, weighing 1950 g. Temperature is 36.8°C and breathing is normal. She attempted to breastfeed at 1 hour of age but has not latched. She licks at the nipple but falls asleep after a few minutes without sucking.”

• 1. Which row of the Section 3.2 table applies to Baby Salma, and why?
  • 2. What does that row say to do about her feeding difficulty specifically?
Facilitator Answer Key

• Weight 1950 g (1500–<2500 g) with feeding difficulty places her in the table's middle row.
  • The row's feeding-difficulty sub-action lists:
  • Support attachment keep mother and baby together; encourage breastfeeding whenever she shows signs of readiness; help the mother into a comfortable, semi-reclined position, baby held close, supported along the whole body, head and body in line, facing the breast.
  • Express breast milk and feed with cup or tube, exactly as the table's sub-action states.
  • Reassess using signs of good attachment: more areola seen above the lips than below; mouth wide open; lower lip turned outward; chin touching the breast.
  • If not improved, or a danger sign appears, stabilize for referral

read.text: Introduction This section focuses on time-critical neonatal emergencies that commonly cause preventable death or brain injury in Sudan if recognition or treatment is delayed. Core principle to emphasize: Recognize early → Treat immediately → Reassess → Refer if needed LEARNING OBJECTIVES By the end of this section, participants should be able to: Knowledge

• Identify early and late signs of neonatal shock
  • Define neonatal hypoglycemia and seizure emergencies
  • Describe first-line emergency management
Skills

• Perform rapid emergency assessment
  • Initiate correct immediate treatment
  • Stabilize newborns prior to referral
Attitudes

• Act without delay
  • Prioritize safety and reassessment
  • Communicate clearly with the team and family
teaching Methods: Case-based discussion + algorithm review + simulation
Facilitator Preparation

• Review shock section in Sudan MSSN manual
  • Prepare:
  • Shock recognition chart
  • IV fluids (simulation)
  • Glucose chart
Interactive session: neonatal shock Ask participant to open Chrtbooklet . Interactive Introduction Ask the participants:

• “How does shock present in adults?”
  • “Why is shock difficult to recognize in newborns?”

Guide the discussion toward: subtle signs, and late hypotension in neonates. “In an adult you wait for the blood pressure to tell you. In a newborn, by the time the blood pressure falls, you have lost the argument. The newborn tells you earlier — but quietly. Tachycardia and a slow capillary refill are the whole message.” Key Teaching Points Neonatal shock often presents with:

• Tachycardia
  • Poor perfusion
  • Prolonged capillary refill
  • Lethargy
Blood pressure falls LATE. A normal blood pressure does not exclude shock. Common causes in Sudan:

• Sepsis
  • Hypovolemia
  • Hypoglycaemia
  • Birth asphyxia
Cold Shock vs Warm Shock — Teach the Difference

COLD shockWARM shock
ExtremitiesCold, mottledWarm, flushed
Capillary refillProlonged (> 3 sec)Flash (< 1 sec)
PulsesWeak, threadyBounding
Commonest inHypovolaemia, cardiogenic, late sepsisEarly septic shock
What it meansVasoconstricted — the body is fighting to hold pressureVasodilated — the vessels have given up
Both are shock. Both need fluid. Cold shock is what you will see most often in Sudan.

Case Study: Neonatal Shock Management
A 5-day-old newborn is brought into the emergency unit.
SystemFindings
Weight3 kg
HistoryPoor feeding, vomiting
GeneralLethargic, low temperature
RespiratoryFast breathing, mild grunting
CardiovascularFast heart rate, cold extremities, mottled skin, poor capillary refill
MetabolicPoint-of-care test shows hypoglycaemia

Question 1: What is your primary assessment? Answer: Neonatal shock (cold type), complicated by respiratory distress and hypoglycaemia. Question 2: What is your immediate and targeted management using the ABC approach? Airway (A) & Breathing (B):

• Secure the airway.
  • Administer oxygen to treat the hypoxaemia and respiratory distress.
Circulation (C):

• Establish IV access immediately and draw labs (blood culture, metabolic panel).
  • Fluids: give normal saline or Ringer’s lactate.
    • Calculation: 20 ml/kg × 3 kg = 60 ml. Give over 15 to 30 minutes. (Reduce to 10 ml/kg = 30 ml if cardiogenic shock is suspected.)
  • Antibiotics: give broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics immediately after drawing the cultures.
  • Support: prepare vasopressors (epinephrine or dopamine) if hypotension persists after the 60 ml fluid bolus.
Dextrose / Disability (D):

• Treat the hypoglycaemia immediately to prevent further neurological deterioration.
  • Dextrose: give 10% dextrose (D10W).
    • Calculation: 2 ml/kg × 3 kg = 6 ml IV bolus.
Question 3: What indicators show the baby is improving?

• Normalized heart rate and blood pressure.
  • Stronger pulses, warm extremities, improved skin perfusion.
  • Improved alertness and return of normal reflexes — no longer lethargic.
Follow-up labs showing normal blood glucose, corrected metabolic acidosis, and reduced lactate.

Case 2 — The Preterm with Cold Shock
A preterm baby is lethargic and feeding poorly. On assessment:
ParameterValue
Heart rate180 / min
Capillary refill time5 seconds
Hands and feetCold
Respiratory rate60 / min
Oxygen saturation92% on oxygen
Blood glucose2.1 mmol/L

• What signs suggest poor circulation?
  • Is this baby in shock?
  • What type of shock is most likely?
  • What is the first life-saving action?
  • What investigations should NOT delay treatment?
Expected Participant Responses Signs of shock:

• Tachycardia
  • Prolonged capillary refill
  • Cold extremities
  • Lethargy
Likely causes:

• Sepsis
  • Hypovolaemia
  • Hypoglycaemia contributing
Appropriate Actions

• 1. Immediate stabilization
    • Ensure airway and breathing are supported.
    • Keep the baby warm.
  • 2. Correct hypoglycaemia
    • Give IV 10% dextrose bolus if indicated.
    • Start a glucose infusion.
  • 3. Fluid management
    • Give a careful fluid bolus if there are signs of hypovolaemia: 10 ml/kg normal saline over 30–60 minutes.
    • Avoid rapid or repeated boluses without reassessment.
  • 4. Start empirical antibiotics
    • As per the Sudan neonatal sepsis protocol.
    • Do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for labs.
  • 5. Close monitoring
    • Reassess: heart rate, capillary refill, urine output, respiratory status.
  • 6. Escalation If no improvement: suspect septic shock, prepare for referral, consider inotropes where available.

FACILITATOR HINT notice the two different fluid volumes in these two cases — 20 ml/kg for the 5-day-old in the first case, and 10 ml/kg here for the preterm. That is not an error. Ask the group why. Guide toward: prematurity, the risk of IVH, and a heart that may already be failing. The volume is a decision, not a reflex.
Key Teaching Points

• Shock in newborns is often subtle.
  • Tachycardia + poor perfusion = danger.
  • Treat first, investigate later.
  • Fluids must be careful and controlled.
Common Errors Giving large or repeated fluid boluses rapidly Ignoring glucose Delaying antibiotics Failure to reassess after intervention

The presence of ANY clinical symptom — even jitteriness — immediately confirms the need for clinical intervention, rather than just continued observation.
“A number alone does not decide. A number plus a symptom decides. And a symptom with a borderline number still decides.”
Case Study: Neonatal Shock
Divide into three groups. Each group rotates through all three stations. 20 minutes per station.
Station A — Recognition & Screening
CASE-BASED DISCUSSION
Scenario: an at-risk newborn requires screening. The group must identify who to screen, when, and what the reading means.

sections.title: NEONATAL HYPOGLYCEMIA: Facilitator Q&A — Station A

read.text: Facilitator Q&A — Station A
Debrief: action threshold.

• Discuss with the trainees that the operational threshold for hypoglycaemia is typically < 2.5 mmol/L (45 mg/dL).
  • Emphasize that the presence of any clinical symptom (like jitteriness) immediately confirms the need for clinical intervention, rather than just continued observation.
Who to Screen

• Infants of diabetic mothers (IDM)
  • Large for gestational age (LGA)
  • Small for gestational age (SGA) and IUGR
  • Preterm and low birth weight
  • Any sick, septic, asphyxiated or hypothermic baby
  • Any baby with poor feeding, jitteriness, lethargy, apnoea or seizures Station B — Moderate Hypoglycaemia Management
CASE-BASED DISCUSSION
Scenario: a term infant of a diabetic mother (IDM) is breastfeeding poorly. The current blood glucose reads 2.3 mmol/L (41 mg/dL).
Equipment provided: breastmilk substitute, NG tubes, feeding syringes.
Facilitator Q&A — Station B
Task 1: Identify and classify.
Question: Based on the glucose reading of 2.3 mmol/L and the baby’s current clinical presentation, how do you classify this condition?

Answer: This is moderate hypoglycaemia. The reading is slightly below the target threshold of 2.5 mmol/L (45 mg/dL). Because there are no severe neurological signs (such as seizures or coma), an immediate enteral feeding trial is appropriate rather than jumping straight to IV dextrose.
Task 2: Initiate NG feeding.
Question: What is your immediate intervention using the provided equipment?

Answer: Initiate a nasogastric (NG) tube feed. Since the baby is feeding poorly and expending energy, the NG tube guarantees immediate caloric intake. Administer expressed breastmilk or the provided substitute.
Task 3: Document.
Question: What key details must be recorded in the patient’s chart right now?
Answer: Document the initial blood glucose level (2.3 mmol/L), the clinical presentation (poor feeding), and the exact time, type and volume of the feed given via the NG tube.
Task 4: Plan monitoring.
Question: When is the appropriate time to recheck this baby’s blood glucose?
Answer: Recheck 30 to 60 minutes after the NG feed is completed, to confirm the level has risen to a safe threshold (≥ 2.5 mmol/L).
Teaching point for Station B: not every low glucose needs a needle. A baby who can be fed, should be fed. Reaching for IV dextrose in a feeding baby is over-treatment.
Station C — Severe Hypoglycaemia Emergency
CASE-BASED DISCUSSION
Scenario: a large for gestational age (LGA) newborn, estimated weight 4 kg, presents with clinical seizures. The current blood glucose reads 1.2 mmol/L (21 mg/dL).
Equipment provided: IV arm simulator, infusion pumps, medication labels, 10% dextrose (D10W) syringes and bags.
Facilitator Q&A — Station C
Task 1: Identify and classify.
Question: Given the glucose reading of 1.2 mmol/L and the presentation of seizures, how do you classify and approach this condition?

Answer: This is a severe, symptomatic hypoglycaemic emergency. The presence of acute neurological signs (seizures) combined with profoundly low glucose mandates immediate intravenous intervention. Enteral feeding is contraindicated at this moment.
Task 2: IV access & bolus calculation.
Question: You have established IV access on the simulator. Calculate the exact dose of the immediate rescue medication for this 4 kg baby.
Answer: 10% dextrose at 2.5 ml/kg. Calculation: 4 kg × 2.5 ml/kg = 10 ml of D10W IV bolus.
The medication role must draw up exactly 10 ml.
Task 3: Set up the continuous infusion.
Answer: Program the infusion pump for an initial glucose infusion rate (GIR) of 8 mg/kg/min, or a baseline of 10% dextrose at 60 ml/kg/day.
Task 4: Reassess.
Answer: Recheck the blood glucose exactly 30 minutes after the intervention, then follow the traffic-light pathway below.
Halt the drill at the 5-minute mark. Review team communication, role clarity, and time-to-medication delivery. In a seizing hypoglycaemic baby, the clock is the assessment.
The Traffic-Light Decision Pathway — at 30 Minutes

PathwayBlood glucose at 30 minAction
RED< 1.0 mmol/L OR abnormal clinical signs persistRepeat the entire cycle:
• Give another bolus
• Increase the GIR
• Recheck in 30 minutes
YELLOW1.0 – 2.5 mmol/L AND no abnormal clinical signs• Increase GIR by 2 mg/kg/min
• Continue oral feeds
• Recheck blood glucose in 30 minutes
• An IV bolus is NOT indicated — say this out loud
GREEN> 2.5 mmol/L AND no abnormal clinical signs• Continue enteral feeds
• Begin a slow wean of the IV infusion

Resolution and discharge: continue monitoring blood glucose until the infant is on full enteral feeds AND the blood glucose is > 2.5 mmol/L (> 3.0 in hyperinsulinism) over several feed cycles for at least 24 hours.

4.Disability (D)Correctly identifies clinical emergency criteria: blood glucose < 1.0 mmol/L OR clinical signs consistent with hypoglycaemia
5.Administers an immediate IV bolus of 2.5 ml/kg of 10% dextrose, correctly calculated for the weight
6.Follows the bolus with a continuous infusion of 10% dextrose at 60 ml/kg/day (can increase GIR by 2 mg/kg/min by increasing volume or concentration)
7.Recognises and corrects hypothermia as a driver of hypoglycaemia
8.Reassessment (30 min)Schedules and executes a blood glucose recheck exactly 30 minutes after the intervention
9.If BG < 1.0 mmol/L OR abnormal clinical signs persist:
repeats the entire cycle — another bolus, increases GIR, rechecks in 30 min
10.If BG 1.0–2.5 mmol/L AND no abnormal signs:
increases GIR by 2 mg/kg/min, continues oral feeds, rechecks in 30 min, and explicitly states an IV bolus is NOT indicated
11.If BG > 2.5 mmol/L AND no abnormal signs: continues enteral feeds and initiates a slow wean of the IV infusion
12.Continues monitoring BG until the infant is on full enteral feeds AND BG > 2.5 mmol/L (> 3.0 in hyperinsulinism) over several feed cycles for at least 24 hours
13.DocumentationRecords glucose values, times, doses and clinical signs accurately
Teaching methods: Video examples + case discussion + simulation Objectives

• 1. Differentiate true neonatal seizures from common mimics using the STOP protocol.
  • 2. Initiate appropriate emergency management within 10 minutes of recognition.
  • 3. Administer correct first-line anticonvulsant therapy safely.
  • 4. Document seizure events comprehensively using standardized forms.
  • 5. Determine appropriate referral timing and prepare for safe transport.
Facilitator Preparation

• Review the neonatal seizure guide.
  • Prepare: a case-based interactive presentation; seizure videos or descriptions; medication charts (phenobarbital); documentation forms.
  • Load the videos offline before the session and test the sound.
Interactive session: Neonatal Convulsion Ask participant to open Chrtbooklet Discuss:

• What is a seizure?
  • Common mimics: jitteriness, startle reflex, normal movements.

Introduce and repeat: the importance of a glucose check BEFORE anticonvulsants. The STOP Test — Seizure or Mimic? Use the S-T-O-P mnemonic at the cot side. It takes 20 seconds and it decides whether you give a drug.

AskSeizure if…
SStimulus — did I provoke it?It happens on its own. A mimic is often provoked or made worse by handling.
TTouch — what happens if I hold the limb gently?It carries on; you feel the muscle contracting. A mimic stops immediately with gentle restraint.

AskSeizure if…
OObserve — the pattern and the eyesRhythmic and slow (< 4 jerks/sec), localized; there may be nystagmus or tonic eye deviation. A mimic is fast, tremor-like, oscillatory, generalized, with normal eyes.
PPresence — is the baby there?Consciousness is often altered. In a mimic the baby is awake, or asleep but arousable.
Seizure vs Mimic

FeatureSeizure (e.g. focal clonic)Non-seizure event (jitteriness, benign myoclonus)
Stimulus sensitivityNot provoked by stimulusOften provoked or enhanced by handling / stimulation
Movement patternRhythmic, slow (< 4 jerks/sec), localizedTremor-like, rapid, oscillatory, generalized
Effect of restraintPersists — you can feel the muscle contractingStops immediately with gentle restraint
ConsciousnessOften alteredNormal — infant is awake, or asleep but arousable
Eye signsMay have nystagmus or tonic deviationNormal

Demonstrate the T of STOP on the manikin, then on a volunteer's hand. Let every participant feel the difference between a tremor that stops when you hold it, and a contraction that does not. This single test prevents unnecessary phenobarbital. The SHOT Mnemonic — Rapid Etiologic Evaluation

MeansDo
SSugar & SepsisBedside glucose immediately — treat hypoglycaemia (< 2.6 mmol/L) with 10% dextrose 2–5 ml/kg IV bolus then maintenance infusion. Assume sepsis/meningitis until proved otherwise: blood culture, broad-spectrum antibiotics plus acyclovir if HSV possible.
HHypoxia & HistoryAssess for perinatal asphyxia (low Apgars, need for resuscitation). Consider HIE as the leading cause.
Quick history: maternal fever, diabetes, drug use, difficult delivery, family history of neonatal seizures.
OOsmolality & ElectrolytesCheck electrolytes, calcium, magnesium. Correct urgently. Hypocalcaemia: 10% calcium gluconate 1–2 ml/kg IV over 10 min with cardiac monitoring.
Hypomagnesaemia: 50% MgSO₄ 0.2 ml/kg IM/IV slowly.
TTrauma & Toxins / Treatable metabolicConsider intracranial haemorrhage, especially after traumatic delivery. Consider pyridoxine-dependent seizures in refractory cases — empiric trial pyridoxine 100 mg IV while monitoring EEG and respiration (risk of apnoea).

• Play each clip once without comment.
  • Each participant writes: SEIZURE or MIMIC — and which letter of STOP decided it.
  • Then reveal, and discuss only the disagreements.
Case Study: Neonatal Convulsions
A premature newborn weighing 1.5 kg begins to exhibit clinical convulsions in the NICU.

• Vitals & access: the infant has secure IV access and is currently stable on respiratory support.
  • Stat labs: a point-of-care test reveals an ionized calcium level of 0.7 mmol/L. Blood glucose and magnesium are normal.
Facilitator Q&A Guide
Task 1: Immediate intervention (0–15 minutes)
Question: According to Step 1 of the immediate intervention protocol, what is your first action based on the lab results?
Answer: You must correct the reversible cause first. The infant has hypocalcaemia (ionized Ca < 0.8 mmol/L). Action: treat immediately with 10% calcium gluconate IV.
Calculation: 1 ml/kg × 1.5 kg = 1.5 ml IV over 10 minutes, under cardiac monitoring. Avoid extravasation — tissue necrosis risk.

sections.title: Neonatal Seizures: Task 2: First-line antiseizure medication

read.text: Task 2: First-line antiseizure medication
Question: The seizures continue despite correction of the calcium level. What is the first-line antiseizure medication, and what is the exact loading dose for this 1.5 kg infant?
Answer: The first-line medication is phenobarbital. The loading dose is 20 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes.
Calculation: 1.5 kg × 20 mg/kg = 30 mg IV.
Follow-up question: What side effects must you monitor for during this infusion?
Answer: Monitor closely for respiratory depression and hypotension.
Task 3: Phase 2 escalation (15–60 minutes)
Question: It has been 20 minutes since the phenobarbital loading dose was completed, but the infant is still seizing. What is your next immediate step?
Answer: Administer an additional dose of phenobarbital: 10 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes.
Calculation: 1.5 kg × 10 mg/kg = 15 mg IV.
Task 4: Further escalation (if seizures persist)
Question: The infant has now received a total of 40 mg/kg of phenobarbital in the first 24 hours (the maximum loading dose), but seizures persist. What are your pharmacological options now?
Answer: Choose one of: Option A Levetiracetam · Option B Fosphenytoin/phenytoin · Option C Midazolam infusion · Option D Lidocaine infusion.

FACILITATOR HINT notice that this baby got calcium before phenobarbital. Ask the group why. Guide toward: a seizure with a correctable cause does not need a drug that stops breathing. Fix the cause and the seizure may simply stop.

sections.title: Neonatal Seizures: Case 2 — The Baby Who Was Never Seizing

read.text: Case 2 — The Baby Who Was Never Seizing
A 2-day-old term baby, 3 kg, is referred for “fits”. The midwife describes shaking of both arms.
On your examination the baby is awake, looking at you, and the arms are trembling rapidly.
When you gently hold the wrist, the trembling stops. Blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L. Temperature 36.9°C.
Ask the group:

• Apply STOP out loud. What do you find?
  • Does this baby get phenobarbital?
  • What would you tell the referring midwife?
Facilitator Answer Key
This is jitteriness, not a seizure. S — provoked by handling. T — stops with gentle restraint. O — fast, tremor-like, generalized; eyes normal. P — the baby is awake and alert.
No phenobarbital. It would sedate a well baby and risk apnoea for nothing.
But still: check the glucose (done — normal), check the calcium, and ask about maternal drug use. Jitteriness is not always innocent — it just is not a seizure. Thank the midwife for referring.
She was right to be worried; the answer is teaching, not blame.
Teaching point: the commonest error in this session is not missing a seizure. It is treating a tremor. Both errors are dangerous — STOP protects you from the second one.

read.label: Learners' course · Module 1, Referring a newborn

read.text: Learning objectives

• 1. Identify type of transfer and babies who need referral.
  • 2. Prepare and organize referral.
  • 3. Provide counseling and family support.
  • 4. Provide pre-referral stabilization and enroute care.
  • 5. Documentation and handover.

Facilitator Script — Opening "unplanned or non-organized newborn transfer from the labour room or delivery facility to the NICU may increase mortality and morbidity, leading to worse outcomes. A simple, timely, efficient approach without any panic is required".

“An unstable baby who is moved will deteriorate on the way and may arrive in a moribund state — which defeats the whole purpose of the referral. The ambulance is not the treatment. What you do in the 30 minutes before the ambulance leaves is the treatment. Watch me do it, step by step.”
Discussion what challenges facing neonatal transport

Ask the group to mention challenges of neonatal transport, ensure they cover the following which of these they face: Write the group’s answers on the flip chart. Keep them visible — you will come back to them in the drill.

• Facilities are scarce and not easily available.
  • Families have poor resources.
  • Organized transport services are not available — at times the baby may have to be transported on foot or by cart.
  • No health provider is available to accompany the baby.
  • Facilities are not fully geared up to receive sick neonates.
  • Communication systems are non-existent or inefficient.
Demonstration of transferee process

Facilitator: set up the manikin, transport incubator, oxygen cylinder, bag and mask, and monitoring equipment before the session. Run the demonstration in real time with a co-facilitator playing the team member. Participants observe first, then each group runs the sequence themselves.
"A baby needs to move. Watch what we do — and in what order. The order is not a suggestion. A baby who leaves before Step 3 is complete arrives worse than he left."
Demonstrate each step, narrating as you go. Pause at Steps 3, 4 and 7 for the group to practise the specific skills below.
Step 1 — Assess The attending health worker or midwife carefully assesses the baby to determine:

• Vital signs
  • Severity of distress
  • Degree of maturity
  • Presence of congenital anomalies or other complications
“Make sure there is a genuine indication for referral. Do not move a baby because you are anxious. Move a baby because the care they need is not here.” Step 2 — Decide

• The reason or indication for admission.
  • The level of care needed — intensive care, HDU or SCBU.
  • The type of respiratory support needed — nasal cannula, HHFNC, CPAP or ventilator.

Whenever possible, the transport team communicates and discusses their assessment and decision with the SCBU/NICU medical staff before moving. Step 3 — Stabilize (STABLE): Maintain Warmth, A, B, C It is of utmost importance that a neonate is stabilized before the transport is begun. Say this sentence out loud to the class.

LetterAssessAct
TemperatureBy touch or thermometerNormalize BEFORE leaving. Warmer, KMC, plastic or polyethylene bag, cover, hat. Increase incubator temperature.
AirwayNeck position, secretions in mouth/nose, chest movementsCorrect position with a shoulder roll. Suction.
Stabilize the ET tube if intubated.
BreathingBreathing effort, respiratory distressTactile stimulation. Bag and mask with oxygen.
Oxygen supplementation as needed.
CirculationPulse volume, capillary refill timeIf CRT > 3 sec and/or poor peripheral pulses with normal temperature: normal saline or Ringer lactate 10 ml/kg over 20–30 min. Reassess for further boluses. May need emergency vascular access.
FluidsCan the baby feed?If sick and unable to feed: maintenance fluid based on birth weight and day of life, plus any abnormal losses.
MedicationsNeed for antibiotics, anticonvulsants, vitamin KGive before departure if indicated.
FeedingSuck, cup, gavageIf the baby can be fed, feed enterally — breast, cup, or NG tube.
Also: place a nasogastric tube for a distended abdomen. Continue all necessary support during transport. Step 4 — Check Equipment Transport equipment must be checked by assigned staff before moving:

• Oxygen source (cylinder or concentrator)
  • CPAP
  • T-piece
  • PPV bag
  • Transport ventilator
  • Transport incubator
  • Monitors
  • Infection control equipment

Whenever a high-risk delivery is anticipated and transfer is expected, all equipment should be checked early and the transport incubator prewarmed. The team leader must confirm that the equipment check was done and assure readiness before moving. Equipment failure during transport may lead to deterioration and loss of valuable time.

Oxygen — Do the Calculation Out Loud Portable oxygen needed = 2 × [FiO₂ flow (L/min) × expected journey time (minutes)]. A full transfer cylinder contains 250 L. “The baby needs 2 litres a minute. The journey is 45 minutes. Two times two times forty-five is 180 litres. My cylinder holds 250. I have enough — but only just. What if we are delayed at a checkpoint? Take a second cylinder.”
Step 5 — Organize the Team and Assign Duties

• Assemble a qualified and experienced team — nurses and medical staff, or a trained community midwife.
  • A team leader decides the number of staff, distributes duties between members, and supervises them.
  • A stable newborn may be transferred on a cot with a nurse.
  • A sick intubated preterm needs 2 or more medical and nursing staff.

Duties include the preparation actions (assessing and deciding — usually by the most senior or the team leader, and stabilization) and the duties during transport: maintaining the airway or head position, ventilating or bagging, monitoring, and maintaining safe transport. Step 6 — Documentation Assign one team member to document and record. This includes:

• Newborn data: GA, weight, diagnosis
  • Apgar score at 1, 5 and 10 minutes
  • Serial recording of vital signs and temperature before and after transfer
  • The equipment check
  • Parental and staff communication
  • Timing of moving to the SCNU
  • Any event during transport
Step 7 — Communication The manual lists five communication channels:

• Between the neonatal unit and the obstetric department or primary facility staff
  • With the parents
  • With the receiving team in the NICU
  • Between team members
  • With the ambulance, for outborn cases
With the parents:

• Explain the need for transfer and the reasons for it. Outline the initial plan if there is time.
  • Explain the condition and the prognosis.
  • Explain where to go and whom to contact.
  • Encourage the mother to accompany the baby.

With the receiving team: establish a clear channel, usually by phone. The GA, diagnosis, level of care and type of respiratory support needed should be relayed clearly and re-read back by the receiving team. “We are going to transfer an ex-preterm, 28 weeks, RDS, intubated by size 3 ETT with stable vitals, to level 3 NICU for ventilatory support.” Between team members: the team should work in harmony. Orders from the team leader must be clear and address a specific member by name; the member gives clear feedback. “What is the baby’s temperature now, Ms. Mona?” — “Baby’s temperature now is 36.8 degrees, Doctor.” Demonstrate this exchange with a co-facilitator. Then have the whole class practise one closed-loop call-and-response before moving on. Step 8 — Transfer

• 1. Inform the SCNU of the anticipated time of arrival.
  • 2. Use the safest available method.
  • 3. Avoid delays and interruptions.
  • 4. Keep monitoring and observing the baby during transport.
  • 5. On arrival, transfer the baby to an SCNU bed and give a detailed handover to the SCNU staff.
The aim is a transfer that is simple, comfortable, safe, stable and closely monitored. Care During Transport Explain these to the accompanying person, whoever they are:

ElementWhat to do
No noxious stimuliMinimal handling. Reduce noise, light and painful procedures en route.
EmergentStabilize and arrange for early referral — do not delay once the decision is made.
No sepsisInfection control practices during transport, with minimal handling.
Stabilize prior to transportThe whole of Step 3 above. Never leave with an unstable baby.
Maintain the warm chainKMC · properly covered in cotton or cloth · improvised containers · transport incubator.
Prevent hypoglycaemiaBreastfeed if the baby can suck. Cup-feed expressed breast milk if he can take cup feeds. For a long distance, insert a nasogastric catheter and give gavage feeding.
Maintain airway and breathingNeck in slight extension. Do NOT cover the baby's mouth and nose.
Gently wipe secretions with a cotton or cloth-covered finger. Watch the breathing — if the baby stops, stimulate the soles.
Educate the parentsTeach them the danger signs to watch for during transport.

read.text: Case study – Transport Sick and small newborn
Purpose: the purpose of a clinical drill is to help participants practise responding to clinical situations that require immediate action.
How to Run It

• Assign a team of four: team leader, nurse (airway and warmth), nurse (monitoring and documentation), and one who makes the phone calls.
  • Announce the case. The team has 10 minutes to prepare the baby and “leave”.
  • The facilitator plays the mother, the ambulance driver, and the receiving NICU on the phone.
  • The other participants observe using the Transfer Checklist.
  • Rotate roles so that every participant leads once.

FACILITATOR HINT be a difficult receiving unit at least once. Say the bed is not confirmed. Say the ambulance has no oxygen. This is what the manual means by ‘facilities are not fully geared up’ and ‘communication systems are inefficient’ — practise it here, not for the first time at 2 a.m.
Case 1 — The Preterm Needing Ventilation
A baby born at 28 weeks, 1.1 kg, in a facility with no ventilator. Grunting, chest indrawing, SpO₂ 84% on nasal cannula. Temperature 35.8°C. The nearest level 3 NICU is 45 minutes away.
Ask the team:

• Is there a genuine indication for referral? What level of care and what respiratory support?
  • What must be corrected before you leave?
  • How much oxygen do you need for the journey?
  • Who accompanies the baby?

Expected: genuine indication — ventilatory support not available here. Correct the temperature FIRST (polyethylene bag, hat, prewarmed incubator) — do not leave at 35.8°C. Secure the airway; consider elective intubation if in doubt. Check glucose. Calculate oxygen: 2 × (flow ×
• 45) . Sick preterm needs 2 or more staff. Phone the NICU with a clear read-back handover.
Document the temperature before and after.
Teaching point: the commonest killer on the road is not the disease — it is the cold. Normalize the temperature before you commence transportation.

sections.title: Neonatal referral and transport: Role Play: Communication with the Family

read.text: Role Play: Communication with the Family
Use Case 2 or Case 3 above as the scenario.
Before You Start

• Define the objective of the role play.
  • Define the setting.
  • Define the time limit.
  • Define the observers’ task.

“This scenario is taken from situations you have shared in the group discussion. It gives you the chance to practise what you might say when faced with this situation at your workplace. It’s a great way to explore what works and what doesn’t. There is no right or wrong way of approaching it — just a deepening of understanding, and the chance to practise some new ways of putting words together when dealing with parents.”
Cast

• A health service provider, a mother, and a father.
  • Be creative and add more characters if you wish — a second provider, a mother-in-law, an ambulance driver.
  • The remaining participants observe.
The Eight Counselling Points The provider should counsel the family on:

• 1. The reason for the need for transfer — non-availability of higher facilities in the SNCU.
  • 2. What is likely to happen if treatment is continued at the SNCU.
  • 3. What is likely to happen during transport.
  • 4. What means of transport are available.
  • 5. The approximate cost of transport.
  • 6. The approximate time transport will take.
  • 7. What care or treatment is likely to be given at the tertiary level.
  • 8. The likely management after going to the tertiary level.
Stress the importance of KMC during transport, and of educating the primary caregiver about the baby’s needs during the journey. Debriefing

• Appreciate the efforts of the role players first.
  • Ask the players for their own feelings and their assessment of how they approached it.
  • Then invite the observers: what was addressed well — non-verbal cues, simple language, answering the parents’ queries?
  • What could be improved, and what are the strategies for that?

Effective communication reduces parental anxiety and helps parents make informed decisions on behalf of the newborn. It maintains a healthy association between providers and parents, and prevents conflict. It should preferably be done by a senior person or a person with expertise.

read.text: Lecture (Triaging Newborn at Entry of Neonatal unit) What Triage Is? Triage is a quick assessment and sorting process used to evaluate and categorize sick newborns shortly after they arrive at the special care newborn unit. It helps prioritize care and treatment based on the severity of the condition and the resources available. Triage is about priority and speed. Triage should take less than 60 seconds. “Triage is not diagnosis. You are not asking ‘what is wrong with this baby?’ You are asking one question only: ‘can this baby wait?’ That question must be answered in less than a minute.” The Three Groups The provider carries out a brief, focused assessment and places the newborn in one of three groups:

• 1. Emergency signs (danger signs) — the newborn is critically ill and at immediate risk of death if urgent intervention is not provided.
  • 2. Priority signs — the baby needs prompt attention and should be moved ahead in the queue for timely assessment and treatment.
  • 3. Non-urgent signs — signs that do not fall under emergency or priority, and can wait for further evaluation without immediate risk.
Demonstration — What You Assess in 60 Seconds
Demonstrate on the manikin. Say each one out loud as you check it:

• Temperature
  • Respiration
  • Colour
  • Capillary refill time
  • Look for seizures and level of consciousness
The Triage Chart — Classify and Act

EMERGENCY signsPRIORITY signsNON-URGENT signs
• Hypothermia (temp < 36°C)
• Apnoea or gasping respiration
• Severe respiratory distress (rate > 70, severe retractions, grunt)
• Central cyanosis
• Shock (cold periphery, CRT > 3 sec, weak and fast pulse)
• Coma, convulsions or encephalopathy		• Cold stress (temp 36.5– 36°C)
• Respiratory distress (rate > 60, no retractions)
• Irritable / restless / jittery
• Abdominal distension
• Severe jaundice
• Severe pallor
• Bleeding from any site
• Major congenital malformations
• Weight < 1.8 kg or > 4 kg		• Transitional stools
• Posseting
• Minor birth trauma
• Superficial infections
• Minor malformations
• Jaundice
• All cases not classified as Emergency or Priority
ACT: Initiate emergency treatment. Stabilize, then admit to SCNU.ACT: Assess and act rapidly.
Admit to SCNU.		ACT: Assess fully and counsel the parents.
Treating the Emergency Signs

Make sure the baby is warm.

spells, grunting, unable to feed)
