Notice what appears at the end of every single row: make sure the baby is warm. And remember DEFG — Don't Ever Forget Glucose. Common Errors

• Delayed triage
  • Waiting for the full history
  • Sending unstable babies to waiting areas

Ask the group: has any of these happened in your unit? Do not name anyone. Write the causes on the flip chart. After Triage — Further Assessment Once emergency care has been given and the baby is stabilized, carry out a detailed assessment: a comprehensive history, and identification of at-risk neonates based on maternal characteristics.

• Maternal age: under 16 or over 40 years
  • Personal factors: poor nutritional status, smoking, drug or alcohol use, trauma
  • Maternal medical conditions: diabetes, thyroid, renal, UTI, cardiac and lung disease; hypertension, anaemia, thrombocytopenia
  • Obstetric history: bleeding in early pregnancy or third trimester; PROM, fever, TORCH infection; maternal medications, trauma
  • Past history of an infant with prematurity, jaundice, RDS, or congenital anomalies

sections.title: Triage of the Newborn at the SCNU: Triage Case Scenarios

read.text: Triage Case Scenarios
Facilitator Prompt
How to Run It

• Read each scenario aloud. Give the group 60 seconds — use a watch.
  • Each participant writes down one word only: Emergency, Priority, or Non-urgent.
  • Then ask: what is your first action? Where should this baby be managed?
  • Do not correct immediately. Let the group discuss first.
Case 1 — The Cold Baby from the Rural Health Centre

A 2-hour-old male newborn is brought to the neonatal unit by a midwife from a rural health centre. He was born at 38 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery, but the delivery room was cold and immediate drying and warming were inadequate. The baby did not cry at birth and required brief stimulation, after which he had irregular breathing.
On arrival he appears lethargic and unresponsive to handling. His skin feels cold, and there is blue discolouration of the lips and tongue.

Vital signs: HR 160 bpm, RR 77/min, SpO₂ 72%, axillary temperature 35.2°C. The extremities are cold, capillary refill time is 4 seconds, and the pulse is weak and rapid. He has apnoeic episodes with occasional gasping respirations, severe chest retractions and an audible expiratory grunt.
Facilitator Answer Key

Classification: EMERGENCY. He has almost every emergency sign at once — hypothermia below 36°C, apnoea and gasping, severe respiratory distress (rate above 70 with severe retractions and grunt), central cyanosis, and shock (cold periphery, CRT 4 seconds, weak fast pulse).
First actions: manage the airway, tactile stimulation, PPV for the gasping, give oxygen, start re-warming, insert an IV line and give 10 ml/kg normal saline over 30 minutes, check the glucose.
Stabilize, then admit to the SCNU.
Teaching point: this baby is cold because of what happened in the delivery room two hours ago.
Everything else on this list follows from that. The golden minute and the golden hour are not separate from triage — they are why this baby is in front of you.

sections.title: Triage of the Newborn at the SCNU: Case 2 — The Baby with the Omphalocele

read.text: Case 2 — The Baby with the Omphalocele

A 6-hour-old male newborn is brought to the unit after delivery at a rural health facility. He was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 20-year-old primigravida with no antenatal care. The mother reports the baby cried weakly at birth and has been “not looking well” since.
On arrival he appears small and fragile, birth weight 1.6 kg. He has a large omphalocele with bowel loops visible, covered by a thin sac.

Findings: the baby is cold and irritable. PR 120 bpm, SpO₂ 90% on room air, temperature 36.2°C, RR 68/min, no chest retractions or grunting. The abdomen is distended and the omphalocele is prominent. The skin and sclera are deeply jaundiced. There is severe pallor with pale mucous membranes and delayed capillary refill, oozing of blood from the umbilical stump, and mild bleeding from a heel-prick site.
Facilitator Answer Key

Classification: PRIORITY — and read the list carefully, because this baby collects almost every priority sign there is: cold stress (36.2°C, between 36 and 36.5), respiratory distress with rate above 60 and no retractions, irritable, abdominal distension, severe jaundice, severe pallor, bleeding from more than one site, a major congenital malformation, and weight under 1.8 kg.

But: check the capillary refill and the pulse volume carefully. ‘Delayed capillary refill’ with severe pallor and active bleeding is the edge of shock. If CRT is over 3 seconds with a weak fast pulse, this becomes an EMERGENCY.

Actions: assess and act rapidly, admit to the SCNU. Cover the omphalocele with warm sterile saline gauze and plastic wrap — do not let it dry, and remember it is a huge route of heat and fluid loss. NG tube for the distended abdomen. Vitamin K and investigate the bleeding. Check the glucose and the haemoglobin. Warm the baby.
Teaching point: a baby can be ‘priority’ on paper and slipping into ‘emergency’ while you write.
Triage is not done once. Re-triage the baby who is waiting.

sections.title: Triage of the Newborn at the SCNU: Case 3 — The One-Day-Old from the Maternity Ward

read.text: Case 3 — The One-Day-Old from the Maternity Ward
A 1-day-old newborn arrives from the maternity ward. The baby is cold, not feeding, and breathing fast.
Ask:

• Is this an emergency?
  • What action must be taken immediately?
  • Where should this baby be managed?
Facilitator Answer Key
Emergency. Immediate stabilization. SCBU / NICU admission.

Note how little information you were given — and note that you did not need any more. Cold, not feeding, breathing fast is enough to act on. Waiting for the full history is one of the three common errors.
Case 4 — The Baby Who Can Wait

A 3-day-old term baby, birth weight 3.1 kg, brought by the mother because he is “yellow”. He is feeding well and is active. Temperature 36.8°C, RR 48/min, no indrawing, no grunting. There is mild jaundice of the face and chest, and a small cephalhaematoma. The cord is clean and dry.
Facilitator Answer Key
Classification: NON-URGENT. Jaundice and minor birth trauma are both on the non-urgent list. He is feeding, warm, and not distressed.

Action: assess fully and counsel the parents. That does not mean send them away — it means take a proper history, examine the baby, measure the bilirubin according to your protocol, and teach the mother the danger signs and when to come back immediately.
Teaching point: ‘non-urgent’ does not mean ‘not important’. It means this baby does not need your hands in the next 60 seconds. It still needs your attention today.
Interactive session Admission Process — Welcoming and Preparation Goals of the Admission Process

• 1. To ensure a high standard o
  • 2. f neonatal care on admission at all levels of the SCNU.
  • 3. To minimize stress, conserving the energy and time of the staff.
  • 4. To enhance awareness and ensure readiness of the SCNU team for an organized and smooth admission process.

Why It Matters The admission process can be challenging and involves several key steps to ensure the baby's immediate stabilization and comprehensive care. These steps need to be well organized, smooth and time-effective, aiming to increase Golden Hour success rates, decrease staff stress, and ultimately improve patient outcomes. Admission of newborns, particularly sick newborns, is a crucial part of the Golden Hour of the baby's life. The clock does not stop at the door of your unit.
Demonstration and Role Play: Receiving the Newborn Baby

Once the baby has arrived at the SCNU, the next interventions have to be done SIMULTANEOUSLY — not one after the other. This is the single most important teaching point of this session. Demonstrate it with three facilitators working at the same time on one manikin.

• (a) Endorsement or Handover
  • A thorough handover from the transferring unit to the SCNU team is crucial, including details about the baby's condition, medications, and any special needs.
  • Each staff member — medical and nursing — should receive their own endorsement.
  • Maternal, antenatal and perinatal history is reviewed and documented.
  • Admission orders should be reviewed carefully by the admission team.
Use SBAR

LetterMeansExample
S — SituationWho is this baby, right now?“This is a 2-hour-old male, 38 weeks, 2.9 kg, admitted for respiratory distress and hypothermia.”
B — BackgroundHow did we get here?“Born at a rural health centre, cold delivery room, did not cry, needed stimulation.
Mother 20, primigravida, no antenatal care.”
A — AssessmentWhat did you find?“Temperature 35.2, saturation 72%, gasping, CRT 4 seconds. He is shocked and cold.”
R — RecommendationWhat do you need?“He needs PPV, warming, IV access and a fluid bolus now. I need a second nurse.”

• (b) Assessment
    • Assessment, monitoring and maintenance of stability are ongoing processes during all the steps of the golden hour of life.
    • A rapid assessment, including evaluation of vital signs (heart rate, breathing, admission temperature), a physical examination, and potentially some initial lab tests such as blood gas analysis.
    • Growth parameters are measured immediately; however, the measurement may be delayed until the baby is stable enough.
    • A checklist for endorsement and assessment helps organize the admission process and prevents confusion or missing important actions.

‘Growth parameters may be delayed until the baby is stable enough’ — say this out loud to the group. Do not undress and weigh a cold, shocked baby to fill a box on a form. Stabilize first. The scale can wait; the temperature cannot.

• (c) Maintaining Stability and Monitoring Once in the SCNU, the baby is closely monitored:
    • Vital signs, oxygen saturation, body temperature and other physiological parameters.
    • Maintenance of warmth to prevent serious hypothermia is crucial.
    • Incubator temperature (servo or manual) and humidity adjustment is very vital on admission.
    • Wrapping the baby with plastic bags may be needed, especially for extreme and VLBW infants.
    • The degree of respiratory distress and the efficacy of respiratory support should be monitored and adjusted as needed.
    • Blood glucose monitoring and judicious management of hypoglycaemia is crucial to prevent serious CNS complications of hypoglycaemia.

Writing and Reviewing Admission Orders The Rule: The most senior paediatrician or neonatologist may need to give some verbal orders during the assessment. However, the final admission orders should be written and recorded immediately after finishing the assessment. The orders should be very clear and in a systematic manner. “Verbal orders are for the first five minutes only. If it is still verbal after the assessment is finished, it is not an order — it is a rumour.” The Systematic Order Set Teach the participants to write in this exact order, every time, so that nothing is forgotten:

SystemWhat to order
Level of careDecide and state it first — intensive care, HDU or SCBU
CNSSedation, imaging
CVSMonitoring, imaging, inotropes
RespiratoryType of support and machine settings, frequency of blood gases, imaging
GITNPO vs feeding, imaging, NG tube
Renal and fluidTotal fluid intake (TFI), type of IV fluid, urine output monitoring
Infectious diseasesCultures and antibiotics

SystemWhat to order
ProceduresLines (UVC, UAC), LP, needle aspiration
MedicationsAntibiotics, others
Reviewing the Orders — The Safety Step

• The orders must be recorded and reviewed by nursing staff — at least 2 nurses.
  • Any confusion or unclear order should be clarified with the medical staff immediately.
  • All requested blood samples should be withdrawn as soon as possible.
  • IV medications are administered as soon as the IV line is ready.
  • The nursing staff prepares for all procedures and assists the medical staff during procedures such as fixation of central lines.

Two nurses reviewing is not bureaucracy. It is the last barrier between a decimal point and a dead baby. Apply patient and medication safety practices: correct patient ID, double-check doses, use of order sheets.

Exercise : Writing admission order
• Give each small group the clinical details of Case 1 or Case 2 from Session 2.
• Each group writes a full admission order set on a blank order sheet, using the nine headings
above.
• Groups then swap sheets. The receiving group plays the two reviewing nurses.
• The reviewing group must find and challenge: anything unclear, any missing system, any
dose they cannot verify.
• Debrief on what was found. The errors the group finds are the curriculum — not the errors
you predicted.
ANSWER KEY

SystemExpected order
Level of careIntensive care
CNSMonitor for encephalopathy and seizures; consider cranial imaging when stable
CVSContinuous monitoring. Normal saline 10 ml/kg over 30 min, reassess.
Consider inotropes if shock persists after boluses
RespiratoryPPV → CPAP or ventilation per response. State FiO₂ and settings. Blood gas now and in 4 hours. Chest X-ray
GITNPO. NG tube on free drainage
Renal and fluidTFI 60 ml/kg/day day 1, 10% dextrose. Monitor urine output hourly
Infectious diseasesBlood culture before antibiotics. Ampicillin + gentamicin
ProceduresUVC for access. LP deferred until stable
MedicationsVitamin K. Dextrose bolus if glucose low, then infusion
Accept any clinically sound variation — what is being assessed is whether every heading was addressed and whether the orders are unambiguous.
Goals

• 1. To understand the concept of the Golden Hour.
  • 2. To know the significance of Golden Hour interventions.
  • 3. To gain an approach that uses the best available evidence, aiming to implement safe, effective and timely interventions.
  • 4. Prevention of hypothermia.
  • 5. Support of respiration.
  • 6. Support of the cardiovascular system.
  • 7. Support of nutrition and hydration.
  • 8. Prevention of sepsis.
What the First Hour Includes

• 1. Early essential newborn care and neonatal resuscitation.
  • 2. Post-resuscitation care.
  • 3. Transportation of the sick newborn to the neonatal intensive care unit.
  • 4. Respiratory and cardiovascular support, and nutrition support.
  • 5. The initial course in the SCNU.

Look at that list again. Everything you have trained on this week is in it — the golden minute, resuscitation, compressions, intubation, vascular access, transport, triage, admission. The Golden Hour is not a new topic. It is the thread that ties the whole course together. Why It Matters Neonatal management in the first hour of life has an important effect on both the immediate and the long-term outcomes of all neonates. The studies that evaluated the concept of the golden hour in preterm neonates showed a marked reduction in:

• 1. Hypothermia
  • 2. Hypoglycaemia
  • 3. Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)
  • 4. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD)
  • 5. Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)

read.text: Learning Objectives By the end of this module, participants will be able to:

• Define prematurity and classify preterm newborns according to gestational age and birth weight.
  • Describe the basic pathophysiological concepts underlying prematurity.
  • Identify common complications of prematurity, associated risk factors, and their impact on neonatal health.
  • Apply evidence-based management protocols for prematurity and its major complications.
And for the admitted baby specifically, participants will be able to:

• Decide the appropriate place of care by birth weight.
  • Describe the care of a LBW baby and the daily monitoring required.
  • Describe Kangaroo Mother Care, and help a mother start skin-to-skin care.
  • Help a mother breastfeed a LBW baby.
  • Recognise danger signs and know when to escalate or refer.
Interactive Lecture: complication of prematurity

• Ask participants to raise their hands if they have cared for a LBW baby.
  • Ask several who raised their hands to describe the problems they have seen.
  • List these on the flip chart.
  • Explain the objectives for the session.

“Keep that list on the wall for the whole session. Every problem you have just named is in this chapter. By the end of today you will have an answer for each one — and you will notice how many of the answers are free.” Set the Scale of the Problem

• Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of death among children under 5 years of age. Three-quarters of these deaths could be prevented with current, cost-effective interventions.
  • Across countries, the rate of preterm birth ranges from 4–16% of babies.
  • Approximately 900,000 children died in 2019 of complications of preterm birth.
  • Preterm births account for approximately 70% of neonatal deaths and 36% of infant deaths, as well as 25–50% of cases of long-term neurologic impairment in children.

In low-income settings, half of the babies born at or below 32 weeks die due to a lack of feasible, cost-effective care such as warmth, breastfeeding support, and basic care for infections and breathing difficulties. In high-income countries, almost all these babies survive. Sudan: in 2023 the neonatal mortality rate was estimated at 24.8 per 1,000 live births — nearly 41,690 newborns dying annually. The stillbirth rate is estimated at 21.51 per 1,000 births, translating into 36,973 annual deaths.

FACILITATOR HINT read the sentence about low-income settings out loud, slowly, twice. Then ask: ‘warmth, breastfeeding support, basic care for infection and breathing — which of those four needs a machine?’ Let the silence sit. That is the whole argument for this training.

Definitions and Classification Preterm babies are defined as babies born alive before 37 weeks of pregnancy are completed. Low birth weight (LBW) babies are those with a birth weight less than 2.5 kg, irrespective of their period of gestation. LBW infants have a 2–3 times increased risk of mortality. Classification by Gestational Age

CategoryGestational ageNote
Extremely preterm< 28 weeksSome references classify 23–25 weeks as micro preemie (birth weight should be < 500 g)
Very preterm28 to 31 6/7 weeks
Moderate to late preterm32 to < 36 6/7 weeksThe largest group — and the one most often underestimated
Classification by Birth Weight

CategoryBirth weightAbbreviation
Low birth weight1500 – 2500 gLBW
Very low birth weight1000 – 1500 gVLBW
Extremely low birth weight500 – 1000 gELBW
Micro preemie< 500 g—
Two Clinical Types of LBW — Do Not Confuse Them

TypeMeans
Preterm / prematureBorn before 37 weeks of gestation. Small because he arrived early.
Small for gestational age (SGA) / IUGRPoor fetal growth during pregnancy. Small because he did not grow — he may be term.

A preterm SGA infant has a combination of clinical features suggestive of both prematurity and IUGR — and the risks of both. “Two babies, both 1.8 kg. One is 32 weeks and grew perfectly. The other is 39 weeks and starved in the womb. Same number on the scale — completely different babies, different problems, different risks. The scale does not tell you which one you have. The examination does.”
How to Tell Them Apart at the Cot

FeaturePretermSGA / IUGR (asymmetrical)
SkinReddened, thin, gelatinousLoose, excess skin folds on buttocks and thighs
LanugoFine hair covering the bodyUsually absent
Posture / tonePoorly flexed, floppy limbsAlert, better tone — ‘long, thin, alert’
HeadAppears large in proportion to bodyHead circumference normal, exceeds chest by > 3 cm
GenitalsImmature — small or empty scrotum; large clitoris and labia minoraAppropriate for term
Sole creasesOnly on the anterior third of the soleCreases across the whole sole
Body fat/Little fat under the skinMarasmic — poor subcutaneous fat and muscle mass
Ponderal index—< 2 in asymmetrical IUGR
Other—Meconium staining; internal organs shrunken
Ponderal Index = weight (g) / length (cm)³ × 100

EXERCISE / PRACTICE
hand out the growth chart. Give the group three babies — 34 weeks/2.4 kg, 34 weeks/1.4 kg, 40
weeks/2.2 kg. Have them plot all three and name each one: preterm AGA, preterm SGA, term
SGA. Twenty minutes, and the classification is theirs for life.
Why the Preterm Baby Is Different, The Prematurity Challenges

• Need for advanced respiratory support and care
  • Maintenance of body temperature
  • Haemodynamic stability
  • Nutrition and feeding
  • Maintenance of growth
  • Dealing with very delicate and sensitive immature organs

The Rule That Explains Everything Complications are inversely proportionate to gestational age. The smaller and younger the baby, the more, and the worse. These complications can range from devastating intracranial haemorrhage, sepsis, severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia and necrotising enterocolitis totalis, down to minor feeding-related issues. Ask the Group — Then Build the Table Together “Do not let me give you this table. Build it. Tell me: what does a 28-week baby not have that a term baby has?” Let them answer; write it on the flip chart; then show this:

Immature systemWhat is missingSo the baby gets…
LungsSurfactant; alveoliRDS → needs CPAP, sometimes surfactant
Skin & fatKeratin, subcutaneous fat, ability to shiverHypothermia, huge trans- epidermal water loss
Liver / storesGlycogen storesHypoglycaemia

Immature systemWhat is missingSo the baby gets…
Respiratory centreMature central driveApnoea of prematurity
ImmunityMaternal antibody transfer (mostly 3rd trimester), skin barrierSepsis
GutCoordinated suck-swallow- breathe; mature mucosaFeeding difficulty, NEC
Brain vesselsGerminal matrix is fragileIVH
RetinaIncomplete vascularisationROP — worsened by uncontrolled oxygen
HeartDuctus closure mechanismPDA
BloodIron stores, erythropoietin responseAnaemia of prematurity

Point at the table and say: ‘every row here is a job for you. Nothing on this list is the baby’s fault, and almost nothing on this list needs equipment you do not have.’ The Place of Care Decision “Before you treat anything, decide where this baby belongs. Getting this wrong wastes a bed, or costs a life. There is no third outcome.” Appropriate Place of Care by Birth Weight

Birth weightPlace of careWhat happens there
> 1.8 kgPostnatal ward, with the motherMonitor. Train the mother: KMC and temperature by touch; breastfeeding and milk expression; LBW feeding content and technique; recognition and reporting of danger signs; answer all her questions about LBW care.
1.5 – 1.8 kgLevel II neonatal unitCloser monitoring; likely tube or cup feeding; thermal support.
< 1.5 kgNICU — Level IIIFull intensive support.

FACILITATOR HINT notice that the > 1.8 kg baby stays with his mother, and the whole intervention is TRAINING HER. She is not a visitor to this baby’s care. She is the treatment. Ask: ‘in your unit, who teaches the mother — and when?’

sections.title: Prematurity & low birth weight complications: Prematurity Case Scenarios

read.text: Prematurity Case Scenarios
Read each case aloud. Give the group 10 minutes. Encourage discussion before correction. End each case with the key message and the referral threshold.
Case 1 — Where Does He Belong?
A baby is born at 35 weeks, birth weight 1.9 kg. He is pink, active, temperature 36.8°C, RR 48/min with no indrawing. He attaches at the breast and sucks for a few minutes, then tires.
Ask:

• Is he preterm, LBW, or both? Classify him by both systems.
  • Where should he be cared for?
  • What exactly do you do?
ANSWER KEY
Classification: moderate to late preterm (32 to < 36 6/7 weeks) AND low birth weight (1500– 2500 g). Both.
Place of care: birth weight > 1.8 kg → postnatal ward WITH the mother. He does not need a nursery bed.
What you do: monitor — and train the mother. KMC and temperature assessment by touch;
breastfeeding and milk expression; LBW feeding content and technique; recognition and reporting of danger signs. Vitamin K 1 mg IM (he is ≥ 1000 g). Delay bathing.
The catch: ‘he tires’. Watch him. If he becomes unable to feed from breast or cup, or becomes sick, he is admitted to the nursery immediately — regardless of the 1.9 kg.
KEY MESSAGE the weight decides the starting place. The baby decides whether he stays there.

sections.title: Prematurity & low birth weight complications: Case 2 — The 1.2 kg Baby at 29 Weeks

read.text: Case 2 — The 1.2 kg Baby at 29 Weeks
A baby is born at 29 weeks, 1.2 kg, in a facility with CPAP but no ventilator and no surfactant.
At 10 minutes of age he is grunting, with indrawing, RR 70, SpO₂ 86% in air. Temperature 35.6°C.
Ask:

• Classify him by gestation and by weight.
  • What is the FIRST thing to correct?
  • Does he get prophylactic surfactant? Why not?
  • Where does he belong, and what do you do about that?
ANSWER KEY
Classification: very preterm (28 to 31 6/7 weeks); very low birth weight (1000–1500 g).
First: the temperature. T comes before A in this baby. 35.6°C — polyethylene bag, hat, prewarmed incubator. Then the airway and breathing.
Respiratory: early CPAP — started here, continued during any transfer. Bubble CPAP is fine.
Target SpO₂ 85–92%: start low oxygen and titrate.
Prophylactic surfactant: NO. It is no longer indicated — it showed a trend toward increasing mortality and BPD. Early CPAP reduces the NEED for surfactant.

Place of care: < 1.5 kg → NICU Level III. This facility is not it. Stabilize — warm, CPAP, glucose, vitamin K 1 mg IM — and arrange transfer. If he ends up intubated before transfer, he should get surfactant before he travels.
Caffeine: < 30 weeks — he gets caffeine routinely.
KEY MESSAGE the answer to ‘we have no surfactant’ is not despair. It is early CPAP, which the evidence says you should be doing first anyway.

sections.title: Prematurity & low birth weight complications: Case 3 — Same Weight, Different Baby

read.text: Case 3 — Same Weight, Different Baby
Two babies arrive in your unit in the same hour. Both weigh 1.7 kg.

Baby ABaby B
Gestation32 weeks39 weeks
AppearanceRed thin skin, lanugo, floppy, head looks large, creases only on the front of the soleLong and thin, alert, loose skin folds on the buttocks, marasmic, creases across the whole sole, meconium staining
MotherTwin pregnancy, spontaneous preterm labourPre-eclampsia, no antenatal care, short stature
Head circumferenceProportionateNormal for term — exceeds chest by 4 cm
Ask:

• Name each baby.
  • Which one is at higher risk of RDS? Of hypoglycaemia? Of hypothermia?
  • Do they go to the same place?
ANSWER KEY
Baby A: preterm, appropriate for gestational age. LBW because he is early.

Baby B: term SGA with asymmetrical IUGR — long, thin, alert, marasmic, excess skin folds, ponderal index < 2, head circumference exceeding chest by more than 3 cm, meconium staining, placental insufficiency from the pre-eclampsia. LBW because he did not grow.
RDS: Baby A — immature lungs. Baby B has term lungs.
Hypoglycaemia: BOTH — but for different reasons. A has not laid down glycogen yet; B has used his up. B may be the more brittle.
Hypothermia: BOTH — A has no fat and thin skin; B has no fat either. Little surface insulation on a large surface area.
Place: both are 1.5–1.8 kg → Level II. Same place, same weight — completely different watch lists.
KEY MESSAGE never let the scale do your thinking. Two babies at 1.7 kg are not the same problem.

sections.title: Prematurity & low birth weight complications: Case 4 — Day 5, Something Has Changed

read.text: Case 4 — Day 5, Something Has Changed

A 28-week baby, now 5 days old, 1.1 kg, has been stable on CPAP in your unit. This morning the nurse reports three apnoeic episodes in the last hour, each needing stimulation. He had been having none. He is on caffeine. Temperature 36.9°C. Feeds have been going in but there were 2 ml of green aspirate this morning and the abdomen looks fuller.
Ask:

• Is this ‘just apnoea of prematurity’?
  • What is your list? What do you check?
  • What is the green aspirate telling you?
ANSWER KEY
No. He was not having apnoeas; now he is. A CHANGE in a stable preterm is never ‘just prematurity’. Apnoea of prematurity does not start on day 5 in a baby already on caffeine.
The list to exclude: sepsis, hypoxaemia, shock · IVH, seizures · PDA · anaemia · drugs · hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia · temperature · obstruction · reflux.

The green aspirate plus a fuller abdomen plus new apnoea: think NEC and think sepsis. Stop feeds, NG tube on free drainage, blood culture, antibiotics, abdominal X-ray, check glucose, check haemoglobin. Look for a PDA murmur.
The trap in this case: increasing the caffeine dose and going back to the ward round. Every group has someone who does this. Let the debrief say it, not you.
KEY MESSAGE new apnoea in a preterm is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Find out what it is a symptom OF.
Learning Objectives By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

• Define KMC as a comprehensive care package, not a single intervention.
  • State the benefits of KMC for newborns, mothers, families and the health system.
  • State where and when KMC is provided — and that weight is not a barrier.
  • Distinguish immediate, continuous and intermittent KMC.
  • Demonstrate correct skin-to-skin positioning, step by step.
  • Monitor a baby in KMC and teach a mother the danger signs.
  • Support feeding in the KMC position — breast, cup and tube.
  • Coach a mother and family, and hand over the caregiving role to them.
  • Apply the criteria for transfer, down-referral, and discharge.
Training Methods

• Facilitated group discussion and experience sharing
  • Demonstration and return demonstration
  • Skills coaching in small groups
  • Case scenarios
  • Clinical practice with real mother-baby pairs, where available
Materials Required

• Newborn manikin or doll, plus KMC ties / wraps / pouches (bring more than one design)
  • Hats and nappies
  • Chairs with armrests; two pillows; a bed if possible
  • Privacy screen
  • Feeding cups, feeding tubes, syringes
  • Thermometer and baby weighing scale
  • Growth chart, monitoring chart, discharge documents, immunization card
  • Flip chart and markers
  • KMC video, if available (load it offline beforehand)
Interactive session: KMC

What KMC Is, and What It Is Not Open With a Question “What is Kangaroo Mother Care?” Let them answer. Write every answer on the flip chart. Do not correct anything yet. Most groups will say ‘skin-to-skin’ and stop there. That is exactly the gap this session closes. The Definition — Present It as Written Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is: care of preterm and low-birth-weight newborns in prolonged (as close as possible to 24 hours a day, with a minimum of eight hours a day) skin-to-skin contact initiated as soon as possible after birth, with exclusive breast milk feeding. An additional feature where KMC is initiated in health facilities is timely discharge from the neonatal intensive or special care unit to a lower level of care within the facility or at home, with continued skin-to-skin contact and close monitoring. Now go back to the flip chart and ask them to find, in their own answers, the four things the definition contains:

• 1. Prolonged skin-to-skin contact — as close to 24 hours as possible, minimum 8.
  • 2. Initiated as soon as possible after birth.
  • 3. Exclusive breast milk feeding.
  • 4. Timely discharge to a lower level of care, with continued skin-to-skin and close monitoring.
The Sentence to Underline

KMC is a comprehensive care package that includes the mother-baby pair and their family, supported by healthcare workers, aimed at minimizing separation between mother and baby during hospitalization. It is NOT merely an intervention — it is a fundamental standard of care for all preterm and LBW newborns.

“Read that last part again. Not ‘a good idea if we have time’. Not ‘a nice thing for the mother’. A fundamental standard of care. That means a preterm baby who did not receive KMC today received substandard care today — the same way a baby who did not receive his antibiotics did.”

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: The Key Points — Teach These as the Spine of the Whole Session

read.text: The Key Points — Teach These as the Spine of the Whole Session

• KMC is a comprehensive care package that minimizes separation between mother and baby, involving prolonged skin-to-skin contact and exclusive breast milk feeding.
  • KMC should be initiated as soon as possible after birth for all preterm and low-birth-weight newborns, regardless of weight or gestational age.
  • The goal is continuous KMC (as close to 24 hours as possible, minimum 8 hours daily) with zero mother-baby separation.
  • KMC provides immediate and long-term benefits for newborns, mothers, families and the health system — including improved survival, neurodevelopment, breastfeeding outcomes, and reduced hospital stay.
  • KMC is safe for both stable and unstable babies, can be practised everywhere (labour room, NICU, postnatal ward, and home), and requires no additional staff.
  • Transfer of babies should ideally occur in the skin-to-skin position, and discharge criteria focus on feeding competence and maternal readiness rather than weight alone.
  • KMC is equally important for late preterm infants (34–36+6 weeks), who are often cared for in postnatal wards and may not receive adequate skin-to-skin support.

That last point deserves a full minute. Ask: ‘who in this room has a 35-week baby on the postnatal ward right now?’ Then ask: ‘is that baby in skin-to-skin?’ The late preterm is the baby everyone forgets, because he looks fine. Benefits: Building the Case Do Not Give Them the List

• Ask participants if they are aware of the benefits of KMC.
  • List their responses on the flip chart.
  • Complete their list only afterwards.
“You will name the baby benefits easily. Now name one benefit for the mother. Now name one for the health system. Now name one for you personally, as a nurse on this ward.”
Key Evidence Highlights

• Immediate KMC significantly reduces neonatal mortality, particularly within the first 72 hours of life.
  • KMC reduces the incidence of severe infections, including sepsis and necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC).
  • KMC improves thermoregulation, reduces hypoglycaemia, and stabilizes vital signs.
  • Long-term benefits include improved neurodevelopmental outcomes, academic performance, and reduced behavioural disorders.
  • Mothers practising KMC experience less anxiety, reduced postpartum depression, and improved breastfeeding success.
The Full Benefits Table

CategoryBenefits
Immediate benefits for newborns• Better chance of survival
• Better immunity
• Decreased incidence of severe infections or sepsis (including NEC)
• More stable vital signs, from improved overall physiological regulation
• Improved thermoregulation (less hypothermia)
• Fewer episodes of hypoglycaemia
• Earlier initiation of breastfeeding, better feeding, longer exclusive breastfeeding
• Better growth and weight gain
• Decreased length of hospital stay
• Protection from pain and decreased pain with procedures
• Less crying and decreased stress (lower cortisol levels)
• Improved somatosensory system maturation (better sleep cycles)
• Optimal developmentally supportive care (neuroprotective)
Longer-term benefits for newborns• Better long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes — improved brain development and function (intelligence, attention, memory, coordination)
• Improved academic performance

CategoryBenefits
• Reduced school absenteeism, hyperactivity, aggressiveness and externalization disorders
• Likely to be more protective and nurturing as parents
• Likely to receive higher hourly wages
Benefits for mothers• Facilitates respectful maternity and newborn care, with the mother gaining greater confidence and competence as primary caregiver
• More sensitivity to the infant's signals and early social behaviour
• Promotes mother-newborn bonding and attachment
• Decreased maternal anxiety and postpartum depression
• Improved lactation: better breastmilk supply and longer breastfeeding duration
Benefits for parents and the family• Promotes meaningful participation of parents and family members as part of quality care
• Enhanced mental health and well-being, less anxiety in parents and family — increased confidence as caregivers
• Increased bonding and attachment of fathers and other family members with their newborn
• Cost savings: fewer readmissions, because of better health outcomes
Health system workforce and facilities• Enhanced job satisfaction and empowerment of the health workforce — improved staff morale
• Reduced health-care expenditure (less equipment, shorter stays, fewer readmissions)
• Promotes sustainable development

FACILITATOR HINT point at ‘likely to receive higher hourly wages’ and let the room laugh. Then say: that is a real finding, from real follow-up studies, of babies who were held. What you do at 3 a.m. on this ward is still being measured thirty years from now.
Where and When to Provide KMC

PlaceWhat happens there
Labour roomInitiate immediately after birth
Postnatal wardContinue KMC as the standard of care
Newborn care unit and NICUMothers should have a bed at the baby's bedside, to enable continuous KMC
HomeAfter discharge, KMC continues until at least 40 weeks corrected gestational age, or until the baby reaches 2.5–3 kg

No additional staff is required to implement KMC. The mother or caregiver provides the care, with support from healthcare workers. In humanitarian and conflict settings, KMC is particularly valuable: it requires no sophisticated equipment, can be practised in temporary shelters, and empowers families to provide life-saving care even when health facilities are disrupted.

FACILITATOR HINT that paragraph is written for Sudan. Read it out loud, then ask the group where they have worked in the last two years, and what they had. Let them talk. KMC is the one intervention on this whole course that a displaced mother in a tent can still receive.
The Barriers Conversation — Do Not Skip It
“Name the challenges to carrying out KMC in your facility. Not in theory — in your ward, this month.”
Write every barrier on the flip chart. Then work through them as a group. The commonest are:

Barrier they will nameWhat the protocol answers
“We have no staff”No additional staff is required. The mother is the caregiver.
“We have no KMC ward”KMC is practised everywhere — labour room, postnatal ward, NICU, home.
“The baby is too small”Weight is not a barrier to initiation.
“The baby is unstable”KMC is safe for unstable babies. The OMWaNA trial tested exactly this.
“The mother is on another ward”Mothers should have a bed at the baby's bedside. Zero separation is the goal.
“We are too busy”KMC reduces length of stay, readmissions, and expenditure. It makes you less busy.
“Cultural resistance”A real barrier — brainstorm this one properly. Fathers and family members can also provide KMC.

Keep this flip chart. It goes to the unit manager at the end of the course. When — As Soon As Possible After Birth KMC should be initiated as soon as possible after birth for ALL preterm or LBW newborns. Weight is NOT a barrier to initiation. KMC is recommended for 8–24 hours per day — as many hours as possible.
Immediate KMC Place the baby skin-to-skin immediately after birth, unless:

• The baby is haemodynamically unstable or unable to breathe.
  • The mother is critically ill, and no substitute caregiver is available.
Then:

• Attempt direct feeding at the breast within the first hour.
  • If unsuccessful, provide colostrum within the first hour of birth.
  • Delay weighing and measuring the newborn for 60–90 minutes after birth, to allow uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact.

Stop on that last one. Ask: ‘in your labour room, how many minutes after birth is the baby weighed?’ The answer is usually ‘immediately’. Ask why. There is no clinical reason. The scale can wait 90 minutes; the first skin-to-skin hour cannot be repeated. Continuous KMC

• Continuation of immediate KMC — for BOTH stable and unstable babies.
  • Provide skin-to-skin care for at least 18 hours per day, with ZERO separation between mother and baby.
  • For stable babies ≥ 32 weeks, continue KMC in a step-down low-care ward where mother and baby room together with the baby in the KMC position.
  • The baby should be on enteral and oral feeds — direct breastfeeding with supplementary expressed breast milk via cup and/or gastric tube.
Intermittent KMC

• Practise intermittent KMC when immediate continuous KMC is not possible in the NICU or newborn care unit.
  • The mother or other caregiver should provide skin-to-skin sessions of at least 60–70 minutes or longer, as many times as possible each day.
  • Sessions should coincide with feeding times, with the baby in the skin-to-skin position when receiving gastric tube feeding.

FACILITATOR HINT intermittent KMC is the fallback, not the plan. If your unit does 60 minutes twice a day and calls it KMC, you are doing the fallback. Name that honestly — then ask what would have to change to reach 18 hours.
The Three Types — Summary

TypeHow muchWhen you use it
ImmediateFrom birth, uninterruptedAlways — unless the baby cannot breathe / is haemodynamically unstable, or the mother is critically ill with no substitute
Continuous≥ 18 hours/day, zero separationThe goal. Stable AND unstable babies
Intermittent≥ 60–70 min per session, as many as possibleOnly when continuous is not possible. Coincide with feeds
Equipment and Supplies Use available, affordable equipment and supplies to help mothers stay more comfortable during KMC.

ItemRecommendation
BedsA comfortable bed for each mother if continuous KMC space is available. An adjustable bed is not necessary; two pillows allow a semi-recumbent position.
ChairsComfortable chairs with armrests facilitate good posture during breastfeeding. A chair next to the mother's bed is desirable. Chairs should have wipeable fabric for infection control.
PrivacyFoldable mobile medical privacy screens with solid or washable surfaces are practical. Traditional curtains may have infection prevention challenges.
Feeding suppliesFeeding tubes, syringes, feeding cups.
Monitoring equipmentThermometer, baby weighing scales.

ItemRecommendation
Resuscitation equipmentBasic resuscitation equipment, oxygen where possible.
MedicationsDrugs for preventing and treating frequent problems of preterm newborns may be added according to local protocols.

Walk the group around your own unit with this list in hand. Ten minutes. Tick what you have. The point is not to shame the unit — it is to notice that the entire list costs less than one incubator, and that two pillows and a chair with armrests are on it.

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Demonstration: Practice KMC: Positioning

read.text: Demonstration: Practice KMC: Positioning
Demonstrate First — Slowly, Naming Every Step

StepAction
1Place the baby in the fetal position (flexed arms and hips with slight hip abduction) on the mother's or caregiver's bare chest, in an upright position.
Baby should only wear a hat and a nappy.
3Turn the baby's head to one side in a 'sniffing' position, to keep the airway open.
4Secure the baby to the mother's or caregiver's chest with a cloth or wrap.
5The baby's head (at ear level) should be secured to prevent hyperextension or flexion of the neck, and avoid obstructive apnoea.
6The baby's stomach (diaphragm) must be able to move freely, to enable unrestricted breathing.
7Baby and parent may be covered with a shirt or blanket.
8The parent may lie down if the baby is firmly secured.
The Two Steps That Kill — Emphasize Them Hard

Step 5: the head at EAR LEVEL, secured, neither hyperextended nor flexed. A flexed neck in a preterm baby is obstructive apnoea. Step 6: the diaphragm must move FREELY. A wrap tied over the abdomen is a baby who cannot breathe. “Everything else on this list is comfort. These two are the airway. If you remember nothing else from today: ear level, and let the belly move.”
Show the Different Wraps

• Demonstrate putting the baby in the KMC position and making use of a pouch, tari, mbeleko, or whatever wrap is used locally.
  • Discuss the different ways you can tie a baby in the skin-to-skin position.
  • Emphasise the importance of continuous skin-to-skin KMC.
Bring at least two different wrap designs. Ask the group what mothers actually use at home in their area — and practise with that.
Return Demonstration

• Divide participants into groups of 4–5. One facilitator monitors each group.
  • Each participant must perform the full sequence on the manikin, or with a real mother-baby pair where available.
  • Each participant repeats until they perform it correctly.
  • If a participant cannot get it, have them watch another participant do it — this usually shows them what they are doing wrong.
  • Coach those having difficulty. Ask those who did well to take over the facilitator's role.
Where you have willing mothers on the ward: let participants practise assisting real mothers to put babies in the skin-to-skin position. Start with mothers who are already doing intermittent KMC.

Feeding and Growth during KMC

The Feeding Order — Every Session, Every Time Always start a feeding session by feeding DIRECTLY AT THE BREAST, then cup feeding, then tube feeding — with the baby in the skin-to-skin position. “Breast, then cup, then tube. In that order, every session. Not ‘he has a tube so we use the tube.’ The tube is what finishes the feed — not what starts it. Every session begins at the breast, even if he only manages a few sucks. That is how he learns.” Feeding and Growth

ActionDetails
Feeding instructionsAlways start a feeding session by feeding directly at the breast, then cup feeding, then tube feeding (with baby in skin-to-skin position)
Feeding frequency3-hourly feeds × 8 feeds in 24 hours
Supplementary feedingProvide expressed breast milk via cup and/or tube
Weight monitoringMonitor daily and plot on the growth chart
Weight loss > 10%Baby must receive supplementary expressed breast milk via cup and/or tube
Supplementary volumeCalculate 40–100% of a single feed volume, depending on the baby's ability to suckle and gestational age
Transition from tube to cupSlowly decrease tube milk volume and increase cup volume until the baby can finish the full volume via cup. Only then remove the tube
Cup Feeding Technique — Demonstrate It

• The baby is in an upright or semi-upright position.
  • The cup is held to the baby's lower lip.
  • The baby LAPS the milk with the tongue.

Do NOT pour milk into the baby's mouth. Every participant cup-feeds the manikin before leaving this session. Watch for the pour — it is the commonest error, it looks efficient, and it aspirates babies. Make them hold the cup at the lip and wait.

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Transfer in the Skin-to-Skin Position

read.text: Transfer in the Skin-to-Skin Position
Transfer to a higher level of care in the skin-to-skin position whenever possible:

• From labour ward to newborn care unit or NICU.
  • From NICU or newborn care unit to a lower level of care (intra-hospital or inter-hospital).
  • A baby born at home should be transferred in the skin-to-skin position to a health facility.

Link this back to the transport session: the manual says the transport incubator must be prewarmed and the baby must not leave cold. The mother IS a prewarmed transport incubator, and she never runs out of battery. Intra-Hospital Transfer

• Baby is secured in the skin-to-skin position; the mother may walk or be transferred in a wheelchair, or another caregiver may carry the baby skin-to-skin.
  • Mother and baby are accompanied by a healthcare worker.
  • A summary of the mother's and baby's health history should be available.
Inter-Hospital Transfer

• Baby is transferred secured skin-to-skin to the mother or other caregiver, in an ambulance or an ordinary motor vehicle.
  • A healthcare worker accompanies the mother and baby.
  • A summary of the mother's and baby's health history and follow-up arrangements should be available.
Criteria for Down-Referral Transfer

DestinationCriteria
Rural, locality, or secondary general hospital with KMC- trained staffGestational age ≥ 32 weeks · baby on enteral (gastric tube) AND oral feeds (breast and cup) · mother healthy and skilled in feeding
Primary Health Care (PHC) unit with KMC-trained staffGestational age ≥ 35 weeks · baby on oral feeds (breast and cup) · mother healthy and skilled in feeding

Notice that both rows require KMC-trained staff at the destination, and both require a mother who is skilled in feeding. You are not transferring a baby — you are transferring a mother-baby pair, to somewhere that knows what to do with them.

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Discharge Criteria from KMC ward

read.text: Discharge Criteria from KMC ward
Babies who have been receiving CONTINUOUS KMC can be discharged if these criteria are met:

CategoryCriteria
All small babiesAble to breastfeed directly AND finish all expressed breast milk given by cup. Normal vital signs and no danger signs. Note: almost all small newborns need supplementary cup feeds until weight reaches 3 kg.
Babies ≤ 1.8 kgRegained birthweight or reached 1.8 kg · > 34 weeks gestational age · consistent weight gain for ≥ 3 days (average 20 g/day) · off gastric tube and doing well on cup feeds.
Babies > 1.8 kgLate preterm (34 to < 37 weeks) must be observed for ≥ 72 hours to establish feeding and KMC skills · weight loss < 10% of birthweight (if > 10%, introduce cup feeding and keep until weight loss < 10% or birthweight regained).
MotherPractises KMC consistently · has good breast milk supply · skilled in direct breast- and cup-feeding · handles baby safely · recognizes stress signs · knows how to calm the baby · comfortable as primary caregiver · educated on danger signs and CPR.

Notice: there is a whole row for the MOTHER. She is a discharge criterion. A baby whose mother cannot cup-feed is not ready for discharge, whatever his weight is doing. The discharge criteria must be confirmed by the attending doctors. Nurses may assess readiness and schedule follow-up visits. Follow-Up Schedule 1 week · 2 weeks · 1 month · then monthly — until the baby reaches 3 kg or 40 weeks corrected gestational age, or earlier if any concerns arise.
Arrangements Before Discharge

• If the mother is very young or inexperienced, identify a supporting family member.
  • Baby should be immunized, with an immunization document and a date for the next immunization.
  • Follow-up visits should be arranged and communicated effectively.
The mother should receive the following IN WRITING:

• 5. Prescription for multivitamins and iron supplementation for the baby.
  • 6. Discharge date and weight, on the discharge documents or immunization card.
  • 7. Feeding instructions for home.
  • 8. Date and place of the first follow-up visit.

‘In writing’ is not a formality. She has just spent weeks being told things by tired people in a noisy ward. Discuss the discharge plan with her and the family BEFORE the day of discharge — including the expectation that the baby will usually be cared for in the KMC position at home until at least 40 weeks gestational age or 2.5–3 kg, or according to the baby's needs and cues.
Case Scenarios : KMC
Read each case aloud. Give 8 minutes. Encourage discussion before correction. End each case with the key message.

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Case 1 — “He Is Too Small For That”

read.text: Case 1 — “He Is Too Small For That”
A baby is born at 30 weeks, 1.1 kg. He is breathing with grunting, on CPAP, and has an IV line.
At 40 minutes of age the mother asks whether she can hold him. The doctor says: “not yet — he is only 1.1 kg and he is not stable. Maybe in a week, when he is bigger.”
Ask:

• Is the doctor right? Quote the protocol.
  • What are the ONLY two reasons to delay skin-to-skin at birth?
  • What has this baby lost in the last 40 minutes?
ANSWER KEY

The doctor is wrong on both counts. Weight is NOT a barrier to initiation. KMC is safe for both stable and unstable babies. ‘When he is bigger’ is exactly backwards — the smallest, sickest babies gain the most.

The only two exceptions: the baby is haemodynamically unstable or unable to breathe; or the mother is critically ill and no substitute caregiver is available. He is breathing, on CPAP, with a line. He does not meet either exception.
What he has lost: immediate KMC significantly reduces mortality, particularly within the first 72 hours. He is in the window right now, and he is spending it alone.
What should happen: skin-to-skin now, with the CPAP and the line arranged without tangles.
Attempt the breast; if not, colostrum within the first hour.
KEY MESSAGE ‘too small’ and ‘too sick’ are the two commonest reasons given for withholding KMC — and they are the two strongest reasons for providing it.

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Case 2 — The 35-Week Baby Nobody Is Watching

read.text: Case 2 — The 35-Week Baby Nobody Is Watching
A baby is born at 35 weeks, 2.3 kg. He is on the postnatal ward with his mother. He looks well.
He is dressed in clothes and lying in a cot beside her bed. He has fed twice in 12 hours and the nurse notes he is “sleepy”. His temperature is 36.3°C.
Ask:

• Does this baby qualify for KMC?
  • Why is nobody doing it?
  • What are the two problems already visible?
ANSWER KEY

Yes. He is late preterm (34–36+6 weeks). The protocol says explicitly: KMC is equally important for late preterm infants, who are often cared for in postnatal wards and may not receive adequate skin-to-skin support. He is the textbook case.
Why nobody is doing it: because he looks fine. He is 2.3 kg, he is pink, he is on the postnatal ward. He does not look like a KMC baby — which is precisely the problem the protocol is warning about.

The two problems already visible: (1) temperature 36.3°C — below 36.5, that is a danger sign the mother should have been taught to report. (2) ‘Sleepy’ and fed twice in 12 hours — poor feeding is a danger sign, and he needs 8 feeds in 24 hours, 3-hourly.

What should happen: undress him to hat and nappy, skin-to-skin with his mother now. Start the feeding sequence — breast, then cup. Teach her the four checks and the danger signs. Recheck the temperature.
KEY MESSAGE the late preterm on the postnatal ward is the baby this protocol was written for. He does not look sick until he is.

sections.title: Kangaroo Mother Care: Case 3 — The Wrap Is Wrong

read.text: Case 3 — The Wrap Is Wrong

You walk into the KMC room. A mother is sitting with her 1.5 kg baby skin-to-skin. She has tied the wrap firmly and neatly — it is snug across the baby's back and abdomen. The baby's chin is resting down on his own chest. He is quiet. She is proud of how well she has secured him and says he has not moved in an hour.
Ask:

• What do you see?
  • Which two positioning steps have been broken?
  • What do you say to her?
ANSWER KEY
Two errors, both dangerous: (1) The chin is down on the chest — the neck is FLEXED. Step 5:

the head must be secured at ear level, preventing hyperextension or flexion, to avoid obstructive apnoea. (2) The wrap is snug across the abdomen — Step 6: the diaphragm must be able to move freely to enable unrestricted breathing.
‘He has not moved in an hour’ is not reassurance. In this position, it is the finding.

What you say: not ‘you did it wrong’. She has done something hard and she has done most of it well. Reposition WITH her — head to the side in the sniffing position, ear level, loosen over the belly, watch the abdomen move together. Then have her show you. Praise the securing; fix the airway.
The trap in this case: a participant who says ‘tell her to redo it’ and walks on. Coaching is done with your hands next to hers, not from the doorway.
KEY MESSAGE a neat wrap and a safe wrap are not the same thing. Ear level, and let the belly move.
Case 4 — The Alarm at 2 a.m.

A mother in the KMC step-down ward wakes at 2 a.m. Her 1.6 kg baby, 34 weeks, feels limp and she thinks he stopped breathing for a few seconds. She has been taught the danger signs. She is frightened.
Ask:

• What should she do — exactly?
  • Which danger signs are present?
  • What is the one thing she should NOT do?
ANSWER KEY
Danger signs present: apnoea (any episode requiring stimulation, or > 20 seconds) and lethargy/floppiness (baby feels limp). Two of the six.
What she does: call immediately for medical assistance WHILE KEEPING THE BABY IN THE SKIN-TO-SKIN POSITION.
What she must NOT do: take him off her chest and carry him to find a nurse. That makes him colder and less stable. The position stays unless he needs emergency resuscitation.

And note: she has been coached in CPR for apnoea or sudden collapse. That is in the skill coaching row. If he needs stimulation, she can give it in the first seconds — which is where the seconds matter.
Then the team: this is new apnoea in a preterm — it is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Exclude sepsis, hypoglycaemia, temperature, anaemia, IVH, PDA.
KEY MESSAGE teaching the mother the danger signs is not a formality on a discharge form. She is the monitor for 18 hours a day. Teach her properly and she will find things before your machine does.
Case 5 — Ready to Go?

A 1.9 kg baby, born at 34 weeks, now 10 days old. He has regained his birthweight and gained 20 g/day for the last 4 days. He is off the gastric tube and finishing his cup feeds. Vital signs normal, no danger signs. He breastfeeds for a while then tires, and finishes by cup.
His mother is 17 years old. She practises KMC when reminded. She can breastfeed but has not cup-fed him herself — the nurses do it. She has not been taught CPR. Her own mother lives three hours away.
Ask:

• Does the BABY meet the discharge criteria?
  • Does the PAIR meet the discharge criteria?
  • What must happen before he goes?
ANSWER KEY

The baby: yes. ≤ 1.8 kg row — regained birthweight, > 34 weeks, consistent weight gain ≥ 3 days averaging 20 g/day, off the gastric tube and doing well on cup feeds. Able to breastfeed directly and finish expressed milk by cup. Normal vitals, no danger signs. He is ready.

The pair: NO. Read the mother row. She must practise KMC CONSISTENTLY — she does it when reminded. She must be skilled in direct breast- AND cup-feeding — she has never cup-fed him. She must be educated on danger signs and CPR — she has not been. She is not a discharge criterion that has been met.

What must happen: she cup-feeds him herself, repeatedly, until she is skilled. She is taught the danger signs and CPR. She is taught the four checks. And — because she is very young — identify a supporting family member. Her mother is three hours away; who else?

Before he goes she gets, in writing: the multivitamin and iron prescription, the discharge date and weight on the documents or immunization card, the feeding instructions for home, and the date and place of the first follow-up visit. He is immunized with a document and a next date.
Follow-up at 1 week, 2 weeks, 1 month, then monthly to 3 kg or 40 weeks corrected.

The trap: every group discharges this baby. He looks perfect on the weight chart. Discharging him is discharging a 17-year-old who has never fed her own baby, three hours from her mother, into a home where he must stay in KMC until 2.5–3 kg.
KEY MESSAGE discharge criteria focus on feeding competence and maternal readiness — NOT on weight alone.
Read the mother's row before you sign.
Learning Objectives Knowledge

• State when to start enteral feeds and what trophic feeding is for
  • State the advancement rates by birth weight
  • State when to fortify, when to stop, and what to do when no fortifier exists
  • State the vitamin, iron and mineral supplementation schedule
  • Recognise the signs of feeding intolerance and grade the response
Skills

• Give a gravity bolus feed correctly — never by plunger
  • Assess gastrointestinal and oral feeding readiness
  • Measure and interpret abdominal girth
  • Calculate a daily feed volume and an iron dose
Attitudes

• Treat the mother's milk supply as a clinical priority from hour one
  • Stop an oral feed when the baby says stop
  • Advance feeds by protocol, not by mood or by shift
Materials

• Manikin or doll · OG and NG tubes in preterm sizes · 60 mL syringes WITH removable plungers · milk substitute (water)
  • Tape measure for abdominal girth · weighing scale · Fenton growth charts · feeding charts
  • Human milk fortifier sachet (or photo) · ferrous sulphate and ferrous gluconate bottles (labelled, demonstration)
  • Breast pump or hand-expression teaching aid · milk storage containers and labels · refrigerator thermometer
  • Calculators · the colour-graded intolerance table printed A3 · copies of all four checklists
Interactive session: Nutrition Is Treatment

Facilitator Script “We give antibiotics on time because we know what happens if we do not. We give surfactant on time for the same reason. But feeds get postponed — he is too small, he is on CPAP, we will start tomorrow. Read the first line of this section: failure to meet the growth needs of a preterm baby causes IRREVERSIBLE deficits. Not delayed. Irreversible.”
Open With a Question
• “In your unit, what usually delays the first feed of a preterm baby — honestly?”

Write every answer on the flip chart. The commonest are: he is on CPAP; he is too small; no one has expressed yet; the doctor has not written it. Keep the list — you will answer each one during the session. The Goal To achieve postnatal growth approximately that of a normal foetus of the same postmenstrual age. Failure to do this results in IRREVERSIBLE DEFICITS and LONG-TERM SEQUELAE. Supporting the Mother — The First Feeding Intervention

• Provide special breastfeeding support to mothers who have delivered a preterm newborn.
  • Breast milk production relies on SUPPLY AND DEMAND. If the baby cannot feed directly, frequent expression and complete emptying of the breasts are essential.
  • Practice skin-to-skin position and kangaroo care.
  • Provide early lactation counselling and maternal nutritional support.

“The milk supply is established in the first days, or it is not established at all. A mother whose baby went to the nursery and who was not helped to express by hour six will struggle for weeks. Expressing support is not comfort care — it is the manufacture of the medicine.” Ask: ‘who in your unit teaches a mother to express, and when?’ If the answer is ‘the nurses, when they have time’, that is a system finding. Put it on the barriers list. Starting and Advancing Feeds

Facilitator Script “Two numbers to hold: within 24 hours, and no later than day 4. Trophic feeds start within the first 24 hours in a stable baby. Progression starts no later than day 4. If your unit routinely misses those two, the rest of this session is academic.”
Trophic Feeding — Gut Medicine, Not Food

What it isSmall volumes of enteral milk (10–24 mL/kg/day) to promote development of the immature GI tract
What it is NOTIt is NOT considered to contribute to nutrition
When to startWithin the FIRST 24 HOURS of life in clinically stable infants
ReviewEvaluate feeding tolerance DAILY
When to progressNo later than the FOURTH DAY of life, unless clinical reasons prevent it

“It is not food and it is not meant to be. Its job is to keep the gut alive — the villi, the motility, the hormones — while the TPN does the feeding. That is why the volume looks uselessly small. It is not nutrition; it is exercise for the bowel.” Advancement Rates

Birth weightStartIncrease by

≥ 1 kg30 mL/kg/day30 mL/kg/day
What to Feed

Facilitator Script “Mother's milk first, always. But mature breast milk alone does not contain enough protein, calcium or phosphorus to grow a 1200-gram baby at the rate the womb would have grown him.
That is not a criticism of breast milk — it is a statement about how extraordinary the third trimester is.”

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Human Milk — Why It Is First

read.text: Human Milk — Why It Is First

• Reduces rates of life-threatening conditions (NEC, sepsis)
  • Shortens hospital stay
  • Improves long-term neurodevelopmental outcome
  • Colostrum has a positive effect on immune function of preterm infants Pumped breast milk should be REFRIGERATED rather than FROZEN — it retains more anti-infective properties.

StorageUse within
Room temperature4 hours
Refrigerated5–7 days
Frozen3–4 months

Cross-reference Patient Safety (Section 9): feeding a mother's expressed breast milk to the WRONG newborn is one of the named misidentification errors. Every container is labelled with the baby's identity and the time of expression — and checked against the baby, not the cot. Substitutes Special preterm formulas (22, 24, 26, 30 kcal/oz) may be used. Diluted milk, dextrose, and oral rehydration solutions are NOT recommended. Fortification

QuestionAnswer
WhyMature breast milk lacks sufficient protein, calcium and phosphorus for a < 1500 g baby to grow at intrauterine rates
WhoVery preterm and VLBW infants fed on human milk
START whenTolerating at least 120 mL/kg/day
STOP whenAt least 2 kg, or established at breastfeeding and growing well
LongerMay continue in nutritionally compromised infants
When There Is No Fortifier — The Sudan Reality

• Fortify expressed breast milk using newborn standard formula or premature formula.
  • If nothing is available: increase expressed breast milk volume to 200 mL/kg/day in 8 feeds, UNDER CLOSE MEDICAL SUPERVISION, to avoid fluid overload.
  • Even 220 mL/kg/day may be considered IF PDA, congenital cardiac conditions and chronic lung disease are EXCLUDED.

Before you write 200–220 mL/kg/day, actively exclude PDA, congenital cardiac disease and chronic lung disease — and WRITE THE EXCLUSION IN THE NOTES. In those three conditions, high volumes cause decompensation.
Supplements Vitamin and iron supplementation starts AS SOON AS THE BABY IS ON FULL ENTERAL OR ORAL FEEDS, and continues until 6 to 12 months of age.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Prescribing Drill

read.text: Prescribing Drill
Each participant writes the day-by-day plan. Compare in pairs before revealing.

BabyDay 1Day 2–3Day 4 onward
0.9 kg, 27 wk, stableTrophic 10–24 mL/kg/day within 24 hContinue trophic; review tolerance dailyStart nutritional feeds 15– 20 mL/kg/day, increase 15–20/day
1.3 kg, 30 wk, stableTrophic within 24 hReview dailyNutritional feeds 30 mL/kg/day, increase 30/day
1.8 kg, 33 wk, stableTrophic within 24 h; may progress soonerAdvance30 mL/kg/day increments

Return to the flip chart from Session 1. ‘He is on CPAP’ — does CPAP contraindicate feeding? No: it changes the TUBE (orogastric, not nasogastric). ‘He is too small’ — the 0.9 kg baby still starts within 24 hours. Answer each barrier with the protocol
How to Feed: The Gravity Bolus

Facilitator Script “This is the most important twenty minutes of the session and it is about a piece of plastic. The plunger. If you push a feed into a preterm baby you can put milk in his lungs. Gravity is not the slow option — it is the only option.”
The Four Rules

• 1. Enteral feeds are given by gastric tube to deliver expressed breast milk to the stomach.
  • 2. OROGASTRIC tubes are preferred in preterms with respiratory complications or on nasal CPAP — nasogastric tubes interfere with ease of breathing.
  • 3. All preterm babies should receive enteral feeds UPRIGHT IN THE KMC (SKIN-TO-SKIN) POSITION, to improve absorption.
  • 4. INTERMITTENT BOLUS feeds are preferred to continuous feeds.

Why bolus is preferred: more physiological — mimics normal feeding, promotes natural cycles of gut hormone release (gastrin, insulin) and normal digestion; allows smaller stomach volumes at any time, reducing reflux and associated apnoea or desaturation. Continuous feeding may be acceptable in certain circumstances. The Gravity Rule The milk MUST RUN IN BY GRAVITY. Speed it up or slow it down by RAISING OR LOWERING THE SYRINGE. IT IS DANGEROUS TO PUSH THE MILK USING THE PLUNGER — pushing may lead to respiratory aspiration and severe complications. “The plunger comes out and stays out. The barrel is a funnel. Your hand controls the height, and the height controls the speed. If your thumb is on a plunger, stop — you are doing a different procedure.”
Demonstration — Step by Step

• Wash hands. Confirm the baby's identity with two identifiers (cross-reference Patient Safety).
  • Check the milk: correct baby, correctly labelled, within storage time, at the right temperature.
  • Position the baby UPRIGHT in the KMC position on the mother's chest where possible.
  • Confirm the tube position by your unit's method before every feed.
  • REMOVE THE PLUNGER from the syringe. Attach the barrel to the tube.
  • Pour the measured milk into the barrel.
  • Hold the syringe so the milk runs in by GRAVITY. Raise to speed up, lower to slow down.
  • Watch the BABY, not the syringe — colour, breathing, tone, comfort.
  • If the baby shows stress, LOWER the syringe or pause. Do not push.
  • Allow the feed to finish. Flush as per unit protocol.
  • Keep the baby upright afterwards.
  • Document volume, time, tolerance and any observations.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Common Errors at This Station

read.text: Common Errors at This Station

• The plunger stays in ‘just to get it started’ — that is the error, and it always starts that way.
  • Holding the syringe too high — the feed runs in fast, the baby regurgitates.
  • Watching the syringe instead of the baby.
  • Baby lying flat rather than upright in KMC position.
  • NG tube in a baby on CPAP.
  • Not confirming which baby the milk belongs to.
Interactive session: Readiness of feeding
Facilitator Script “Two different readinesses, often confused. Gut readiness asks: can I put milk in the stomach?
Mouth readiness asks: can he take it himself? A baby can be ready for gavage on day one and not ready for the breast for six weeks. Do not test the second when you mean the first.”
Gastrointestinal Readiness

READYNOT READY
SOFT, non-tender, non-distended abdomen — the key indicator of GI tolerance and readinessRIGID or DISTENDED abdomen with PROFUSE VOMITING — signals intolerance or obstruction
The Practice Change — Routine Gastric Residuals Routine checks of gastric residuals OFTEN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD in premature babies.

• Disrupts acid production — drawing out stomach contents stops natural hydrochloric acid creation.
  • Increases infection risk — without strong acid, dangerous bacteria grow and multiply.
  • Harms milk digestion — low acid deactivates pepsin, the enzyme that breaks down milk proteins.
  • Causes feeding problems — inactive enzymes plus bacterial overgrowth lead to worse intolerance.

ONLY check GRV if there are CLEAR SIGNS of gastrointestinal pathology. Do NOT stop feeding because of a GRV alone unless the baby ALSO shows bile-stained vomit, severe distension, bloody stools, or systemic instability.

FACILITATOR HINT this reverses what many participants were taught, and it differs from the Level II manual which describes routine pre-feed checks. Name that openly. Then ask: does your feeding chart have a pre-printed ‘aspirate’ column? If so, the chart is teaching the old practice every shift, and the chart needs changing.

“The finding drives the test, not the timetable. You check residuals when the baby is telling you something is wrong — not because it is four o'clock.” Oral Feeding Readiness — The Three Domains A baby must be able to MANAGE THEIR OWN SALIVA before oral feeding can be considered.

DomainSigns
Behavioural (alertness)Quiet alertness — awake, eyes open, engaged, not fussy · increased activity of arms, legs, face · rooting · mouth movements: lip smacking, opening and closing, tongue out
Motor and sucklingHand-to-mouth movements · gently flexed normal resting tone — not limp, not rigid · STRONG non-nutritive suckle on a gloved finger
Physiological stabilityStable breathing, usually 40–60/min, no increased effort or nasal flaring · stable heart rate, no bradycardia, no desaturation
Feeding cues may be REDUCED OR ABSENT in sick or very preterm newborns. Their absence is not proof of unreadiness — it means look harder at the other two domains.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: The Suck–Swallow–Breathe Pattern

read.text: The Suck–Swallow–Breathe Pattern

Even with cues present, the baby is only ready if the body can coordinate SSB. Observe DURING active feeding. If a baby struggles to coordinate SSB, they are at risk of CHOKING or ASPIRATING milk into the airways.

CategoryIncoordination signs during or after feeds
Stress cuesForehead furrowing, splayed fingers, watery eyes, turning away
Work of breathingFlaring nostrils, rapid breathing, chest retractions during breaks
Clinical distressCoughing, gagging, wheezing during the feed
FatigueFalling asleep very quickly, or taking over 30 minutes for a minimal amount of milk
STOP Signs — Not Ready

If the baby shows stress signals during a feeding attempt, STOP THE ORAL FEED ENTIRELY. Colour changes — pale, bluish, greyish. Respiratory distress — gulping, coughing, choking, apnoea. Agitation and fatigue — excessively floppy, immediate sleep, panicked strained fussing. “Stopping a feed is not a failure. Pushing on through those signs is how a baby aspirates. The baby is allowed to say no, and your job is to hear it the first time.” Observation Practice

• Where you have consenting mothers on the ward: observe a real feed together, and have each participant call out the domain signs as they see them.
  • Where you do not: use the manikin and have one facilitator role-play the stress cues while participants name them and decide to stop.
Interactive session: Feeding Intolerance and Monitoring Growth

Facilitator Script “Every preterm baby will have a difficult feeding day. The skill is not avoiding intolerance — it is grading it. Most of what frightens us needs the feed reduced. A small amount of it needs everything stopped and an X-ray. Knowing which is which is this session.”
The Signs

SignWhat counts as significant
VomitingSmall volume of altered milk is usually benign. Significant, frequent, BILE- or BLOOD-stained must be assessed. Continued BILE-STAINED vomiting may mean BOWEL OBSTRUCTION OR ILEUS
Abdominal distensionSignificant if MORE THAN 2 cm compared with the previous measurement, or with bilious residual or abdominal wall erythema.
Mild fullness < 2 cm after bolus feeds or on CPAP is not uncommon
Gastric residuals> 30% (50%) of the previous feed · blood or bile stained · with systemic manifestations
Bloody stoolsAlways significant
SystemicThermal instability · apnoea · bradycardia · lethargy

‘More than 2 cm compared with the PREVIOUS measurement’ requires that a previous measurement exists. MEASURE the girth — same point, same time in the feed cycle, every shift. An estimated abdomen is not a measurement. Demonstrate girth measurement on the manikin: mark the point, measure at the same phase of the feed cycle, record it. Then have two participants measure the same manikin and compare — if they differ by more than a few millimetres, discuss why technique matters.
Grading the Response — The Traffic Light

ResidualAbdomen / colourAction
LOWNo bile, no blood, benign examCONTINUE feeding · monitor and follow up
MODERATE 30–50%No bile, no blood, benign examREDUCE feed volume · monitor and follow up
LARGE > 50%No bile, no blood, benign examSTOP 2–4 feeds · assess clinically, investigate if indicated · monitor
BILE or BLOOD stainedAnySTOP FEEDS · assess clinically · septic workup, labs, abdominal X-ray · gastric tube for FREE DRAINAGE · consider IV fluids and antibiotics · consider TPN · follow up

“Notice that only the bottom row stops everything. The other three adjust. A unit that stops feeds every time there is a residual starves babies; a unit that never stops misses NEC. The grading is the skill.” Monitoring Growth

MeasurementStandard
Weight frequencyDAILY if critical · at least 3×/week if stable
Initial weight lossLimit to ≤ 10%
Daily gainPRETERM 15–20 g/day · TERM 25–30 g/day, once stable and on full feeds
Regain birthweightPRETERM 10–16 days · TERM 7–13 days

MeasurementStandard
PlottingFenton preterm growth charts
