Biochemistry — The Four Tests That Change Management

TestThresholdAction
Blood glucoseKeep 2.6–7.0 mmol/LTest every 1–3 hours during feeding adjustments
Serum urea< 1.8 mmol/L = too little proteinIncrease milk volume or fortify feeds
Bicarbonate< 18 mmol/L = acidoticConsider oral sodium bicarbonate 8.5%, 0.5– 1 mL per feed × 8/24 h until acidosis improves
Serum phosphateScreen at 3–4 weeks or before discharge.
Normal > 1.9; treat if < 1.8 mmol/L		Oral phosphate — fleet enema fluid is sterile and given orally, 0.2 mL with each feed × 8 = 1.6 mL/day for 7–10 days. Recheck after 5–7 days

Too much phosphate, or too high a dose, causes HYPOCALCAEMIA WITH TETANY. Give it divided with feeds — never as a single large volume, which also causes vomiting. Ask: who screens phosphate at 3–4 weeks in your unit? Metabolic bone disease of prematurity is invisible until the baby fractures. This one blood test, at one point in time, is the whole screening programme.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Case 1 — The Feed That Was Never Started

read.text: Case 1 — The Feed That Was Never Started

A 1.1 kg baby, 29 weeks, now 4 days old. He is stable on CPAP. He has had IV fluids only since birth. The notes say each day: “Nil by mouth — on CPAP.” His mother has not been shown how to express and says her breasts are now soft and comfortable.
Ask:

• What has gone wrong, and on which day?
  • Does CPAP prevent feeding?
  • What has happened to the milk supply, and what do you do about it?
ANSWER KEY

What went wrong: trophic feeding should have started within the FIRST 24 HOURS in a stable baby, and progression no later than DAY 4. He has had neither. Four days of gut rest in a 29- weeker is four days of villous atrophy and lost time.

CPAP does not prevent feeding. It changes the TUBE — orogastric is preferred in preterms on nasal CPAP, because nasogastric tubes interfere with ease of breathing. ‘Nil by mouth — on CPAP’ is not a clinical decision, it is a habit.

The milk supply: ‘soft and comfortable’ on day 4 means the supply is failing. Breast milk production relies on supply and demand; without frequent expression and complete emptying, it stops. This is urgent — start intensive expression support today, every 2–3 hours including overnight, with skin-to-skin.
What you do now: start trophic feeds via OG tube today; begin expression support immediately;
put him in KMC; document a daily feeding plan so it cannot drift again.
The trap: groups focus on the baby and miss the mother. The milk supply is the harder problem and the one with the shorter window.
KEY MESSAGE ‘Nil by mouth’ written four days running is not a plan. Every day without a feeding decision is a decision.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Case 2 — The Feed That Was Pushed

read.text: Case 2 — The Feed That Was Pushed

A nurse is feeding a 1.4 kg baby by OG tube. The ward is busy. She attaches the syringe with the plunger in, pushes the 18 mL feed in over about 30 seconds, and moves on. Ten minutes later the baby is found desaturated with milk at the mouth.
Ask:

• What happened?
  • What are the immediate actions?
  • What do you say to the nurse — and what do you say to the unit?
ANSWER KEY

What happened: the feed was PUSHED. The manual is explicit — it is dangerous to push milk using the plunger; it may lead to respiratory aspiration and severe complications. A rapid bolus into a small stomach caused reflux and probable aspiration.
Immediate actions: position, suction the mouth, assess airway and breathing, oxygen and support as needed, call for help. Stop feeds and assess. Consider chest X-ray. Watch for aspiration pneumonia.

To the nurse: not blame — the manual says this happens under time pressure. Show her the technique WITH the plunger out, hands together, and let her do it. She is more likely to change with a demonstration than a reprimand.

To the unit: this is a system finding, not an individual one (cross-reference Patient Safety, Swiss-cheese model). Why was the ward so busy? Are the syringes the right type? Is the gravity rule in the written feeding policy? Is it taught at orientation?
The single most preventable feeding injury in any newborn unit. It takes 30 seconds to cause and it is entirely avoided by removing a piece of plastic.
KEY MESSAGE gravity, not pressure. The plunger stays out.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Case 3 — The Residual

read.text: Case 3 — The Residual

A 1.2 kg baby, day 9, on 100 mL/kg/day by OG tube and tolerating well. At the 6 a.m. feed the nurse aspirates routinely and finds 4 mL of milky residual from a 15 mL feed. The abdomen is soft, the baby is pink, active and afebrile. She withholds the feed and documents “feed intolerance”.
Ask:

• Was the aspiration indicated?
  • Is 4 mL from a 15 mL feed significant?
  • Was withholding correct?
ANSWER KEY
The aspiration was NOT indicated. Routine gastric residual checks do more harm than good — they disrupt acid production, increase infection risk, deactivate pepsin, and worsen intolerance.
Check GRV ONLY if there are clear signs of GI pathology. This baby had none.
The volume: 4 mL of 15 mL is about 27% — below the 30% threshold, not bile or blood stained, with a benign abdominal exam. By the grading table this is LOW: continue feeding, monitor and follow up.

Withholding was WRONG on both counts: the test should not have been done, and the result did not meet the threshold for action. Do not stop feeding a baby because of a GRV unless the baby also shows clear signs of illness — bile-stained vomit, severe distension, bloody stools, or systemic instability.
The system question: why did she aspirate? Almost certainly because the feeding chart has an ‘aspirate’ column. The chart is teaching the old practice every shift. Change the chart.
Every group will debate the 4 mL. The more important answer is that the number should never have been generated. The finding drives the test, not the timetable.
KEY MESSAGE a missed feed is a real harm. Do not create a reason to miss one.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Case 4 — No Fortifier

read.text: Case 4 — No Fortifier

A 1.3 kg baby, 31 weeks, day 14, on full expressed breast milk at 150 mL/kg/day and tolerating well. Weight gain is 8 g/day. Serum urea is 1.4 mmol/L. The unit has no commercial human milk fortifier and none is expected.
Ask:

• What is the urea telling you?
  • Is his weight gain adequate?
  • What are your options, in order?
ANSWER KEY
The urea: 1.4 mmol/L is below 1.8 — which indicates TOO LITTLE PROTEIN in the diet. The action stated in the manual is to consider increasing milk volume or fortifying feeds.
Weight gain: 8 g/day is below the preterm target of 15–20 g/day. The biochemistry and the growth chart agree — he is underfed.

Options in order: (1) fortify EBM using newborn standard formula or premature formula; (2) if nothing is available, increase EBM volume to 200 mL/kg/day divided into 8 feeds, under close medical supervision to avoid fluid overload; (3) 220 mL/kg/day may be considered ONLY IF PDA, congenital cardiac conditions and chronic lung disease are excluded.

Before increasing volume: examine for a murmur and signs of PDA, review the respiratory history for chronic lung disease, and document the exclusion. And note the ceiling — do not exceed 200 mL/kg/day without senior specialist consultation.
KEY MESSAGE no fortifier is not no options. But the volume route has an explicit safety gate, and that gate is three diagnoses you must actively exclude and write down.

sections.title: Feeding the Preterm Newborn: Case 5 — The Baby Who Said No

read.text: Case 5 — The Baby Who Said No

A 1.9 kg baby, 34 weeks, has been on tube feeds and is now being offered the breast. He roots and latches. After two minutes he goes quiet, then pale; his nostrils flare and he coughs. The mother is anxious and asks whether she should keep trying — “he was doing so well.”
Ask:

• What are you seeing?
  • Do you continue?
  • What do you say to the mother?
ANSWER KEY

What you are seeing: suck–swallow–breathe incoordination with STOP signs — colour change (pale), increased work of breathing (nasal flaring), and clinical distress (coughing). He rooted and latched, which are readiness CUES, but cues alone are not enough; the physiological stability is what failed.
Do you continue? NO. If the baby shows stress signals during an attempt, STOP THE ORAL FEED ATTEMPT ENTIRELY. Continuing risks choking and aspiration.

What you say to the mother: not ‘he failed’. He showed you exactly what he could manage today and told you when to stop — which is a good sign, not a bad one. Complete this feed by tube in the KMC position, keep offering non-nutritive suckling at the emptied breast, and try again at the next feed. Reassure her the supply is protected by continuing to express.
The trap: ‘he was doing so well’ is the sentence that makes people push on. Rooting and latching are the easy part; the coordination is what matures last.
KEY MESSAGE stopping is not failure. The baby is allowed to say no, and hearing it the first time is the skill.

  • Blank bilirubin plotting sheets · calculators · pens
  • Phototherapy unit · eye covers · nappies · manikin or doll · thermometer

Interactive session: Neonatal Jundice
Ask participant to open Chrtbooklet

Facilitator Script “Sixty to eighty per cent of term babies go yellow. Almost all of them are fine. Your job in this session is not to learn to spot jaundice — you can all do that. It is to learn to spot the ONE baby in that yellow crowd who is on his way to permanent brain damage, and to spot him today rather than tomorrow.”

sections.title: Neonatal Jaundice: overview: Open With Questions

read.text: Open With Questions

• “How many jaundiced babies did you see last month? How many did you treat?”
  • “How did you decide which ones to treat?”
  • “Has anyone here seen a baby with kernicterus?”
Let the last question sit. In most Sudanese units at least one person has. That memory is the reason for this session, and it is worth naming before any teaching starts.
Teach the Physiology — Briefly
Three factors, all normal, all newborn:

• 1. Higher red blood cell mass with a shorter lifespan
  • 2. Immature hepatic conjugation (UDP-glucuronyl transferase)
  • 3. Enhanced enterohepatic circulation “Every newborn is built to go a bit yellow. More red cells, dying faster, hitting a liver that has never worked before. That is why 60–80% of them do it — it is not a disease, it is a design.”
The Central Distinction

PHYSIOLOGICALPATHOLOGICAL
OnsetAFTER 24 hoursWITHIN 24 hours
PeakDay 3–5Rises rapidly
ResolutionBy 1–2 weeksLasts > 2 weeks
LevelModestExcessively high
What you doMonitorInvestigate and treat

THE 24-HOUR RULE. Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is NEVER physiological. Not sometimes. Never. Any baby yellow on day one is a baby being investigated — that is the single highest-yield sentence in this whole session. The Red Flags Write these on the flip chart. Then close the manual and ask the room to give them back to you.

• 1. Onset < 24 hours
  • 2. Bilirubin rises > 5 mg/dL (85 µmol/L) per day
  • 3. TSB > 17 mg/dL (290 µmol/L) in a term infant, OR > 15 mg/dL (255 µmol/L) in the first 48 hours
  • 4. Jaundice lasting > 2 weeks (unconjugated) or > 3 weeks (conjugated)
  • 5. Conjugated bilirubin > 20% of total

Run this as an oral drill in a circle, the way the ToT module describes: ask one participant, they answer quickly, move to the next. Not a test — practice for speed and confidence. Five flags, twenty participants, four times round. Why It Matters — Say It Plainly Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes BILIRUBIN ENCEPHALOPATHY or KERNICTERUS — preventable, potentially devastating, permanent. “Preventable is the important word in that sentence. Not treatable — preventable. Which means every case of kernicterus that walks out of a hospital is something a system failed to do, not something a disease did.” The Risk Factor Drill Give the list. Then give the babies, and ask which risk factors apply.

Risk factors — primary level screening
Preterm (< 37 weeks)Bruising or cephalohaematoma
Low birth weight (< 2500 g)Poor feeding / dehydration
Sibling with neonatal jaundiceG6PD deficiency
ABO / Rh incompatibility
Demonstration Nomograms: Plotting and Deciding

Facilitator Script “A bilirubin number on its own means nothing. Fifteen at six hours old is an emergency. Fifteen at five days old in a term baby may be nothing at all. The number only becomes information when you plot it against the age in HOURS. This session is about that one habit.”

sections.title: Neonatal Jaundice: overview: Before Anything — The Unit Trap

read.text: Before Anything — The Unit Trap
Some chart use µmol/L. 1 mg/dL = 17.1 µmol/L. A TSB of 17 mg/dL is 290 µmol/L. If you plot ‘17’ on a µmol/L chart, you will read it as safe when the baby needs urgent treatment.

• Ask every participant: what unit does YOUR laboratory report in? Have them say it out loud.
  • Have them write the conversion at the top of their plotting sheet before they plot anything.
This is the highest-consequence, lowest-difficulty error in the entire session. Do not move on until every person in the room has stated their own lab's unit.
The Two Charts

ChartTells you
A. Phototherapy thresholdWhen to START phototherapy — by gestational age, age in hours, and TSB
B. Exchange transfusionWhen urgent exchange is required. Immediate treatment if
thresholdrising > 8.5 µmol/L/hr (> 0.5 mg/dL/hr) or approaching/exceeding the threshold
Practical Case: Neonatal Jaundice
Every participant plots all four, on paper, individually. Then compare in pairs before the facilitator gives the answers.
Case 1 — Baby 1
Term, 38 weeks, 40 hours old. TSB 240 µmol/L. No risk factors.

Answer: Plot 240 µmol/L at 40 hours on the phototherapy threshold chart for ≥ 38 weeks with no risk factors. This sits BELOW the phototherapy line. Action: no phototherapy; repeat TSB and reassess. The teaching point — a number that sounds high is not high for this age.
Case 2 — Baby 2
Term, 38 weeks, 18 hours old. TSB 180 µmol/L.

Answer: The plot matters less than the CLOCK. This baby is jaundiced at 18 hours — under 24 hours — which is pathological by definition, whatever the chart says. Action: start phototherapy per the chart AND investigate the cause (Coombs, blood groups, FBC, retics, G6PD). Every group that only plots and does not notice the age has missed the point.
Case 3 — Baby 3 35 weeks, 30 hours old, TSB 220 µmol/L, Coombs positive, mother O negative.

Answer: 35 weeks WITH risk factors — use the lower (risk-factor) threshold line, not the term line. Coombs positive means isoimmune haemolysis. Action: start phototherapy at the lower threshold; recheck TSB in 6 hours; watch the RATE of rise; consider IVIG (500–1000 mg/kg over 2 hours) if TSB keeps rising despite phototherapy; prepare for possible exchange.
Case 4 — Baby 4
Term, 60 hours old. TSB was 280 µmol/L at 54 hours, now 340 µmol/L. Already on phototherapy.
Answer: Calculate the RATE: 60 µmol/L in 6 hours = 10 µmol/L/hr. That exceeds 8.5 µmol/L/hr (0.5 mg/dL/hr) DESPITE intensive phototherapy — an exchange transfusion indication. Action:
escalate to tertiary now; cross-match blood; do not wait for the next level to be crossed.

Baby 4 is the case that teaches the rate. Two numbers and a clock give you a slope, and the slope decides before the threshold does. Any group that reports ‘340, still under exchange threshold, continue phototherapy’ has missed the most important calculation in the session.
Demonstration: Phototherapy

Facilitator Script “Phototherapy is the most effective treatment on this course that requires no drug, no needle and no consent. It is also the one most often set up badly — baby dressed, lights too far, eyes uncovered, and a family wondering why the number is not falling.”

sections.title: Neonatal Jaundice: overview: How It Works — One Minute, No More

read.text: How It Works — One Minute, No More

Light of specific wavelengths converts bilirubin in the skin into more water-soluble forms that can be excreted without requiring hepatic conjugation. The mechanisms are photoisomerization and structural isomerization.
“It bypasses the liver. That is the whole idea — the newborn's liver is the bottleneck, and the light goes round it.”
The Five Device Types — Show Whatever You Have

TypeWhat it isWhen
ConventionalFluorescent blue/white tubes, overheadAvailable and cheap; less intense; longer exposure

TypeWhat it isWhen
IntensiveIntensiveHigh-intensity blue LED or halogen, single or multiple banksHigh-intensity blue LED or halogen, single or multiple banksPREFERRED for severe or rapidly rising TSB, or when exchange is being considered
Fibre-optic (Biliblanket)Flexible pad on the skinMild–moderate, or in COMBINATION. Allows feeding and cuddling
LEDBlue light-emitting diodesThe modern GOLD STANDARD — efficient, durable, less heat, higher irradiance
Double / tripleTwo or more sources combinedSevere hyperbilirubinaemia needing rapid reduction

Ask the room: what do you actually have in your unit? Then teach to that. If a unit has one conventional overhead and a biliblanket, the useful lesson is that using BOTH together is double phototherapy — which they may not have realised they can do. Setting Up Phototherapy

• Confirm the indication against the nomogram, and document the TSB, the age in hours, and the threshold.
  • Explain to the mother what is happening and why — including that the baby will be undressed and that she can still feed.
  • Undress the baby to a nappy only — MAXIMUM SKIN EXPOSURE is the point.
  • Apply EYE COVERS. Check they fit, are secure, and do not occlude the nostrils.
  • Position the light source at the manufacturer's specified distance (see Module 2 Section 8.6 — 45 cm).
  • Start the unit. Note the time.
  • Ensure adequate hydration and feeding — phototherapy increases insensible water loss.
  • Monitor temperature 2–4 hourly — hyperthermia AND hypothermia both occur.
  • Turn the baby regularly to expose all surfaces.
  • Remove eye covers during feeds so the parents see the baby's eyes and bonding continues.
  • Repeat TSB every 6–12 hours initially.
  • Document: device type, start time, TSB trend, temperature, fluid status.
Safety — The Complications

ComplicationPrevention / action
Increased insensible water loss → dehydrationEnsure adequate feeding; IV fluids if intake poor; monitor urine output and weight
Loose stoolsExpected; maintain hydration
Skin rashUsually benign; document
Hyperthermia or hypothermiaTemperature 2–4 hourly; adjust environment
‘Bronze baby syndrome’Rare, in CHOLESTATIC jaundice — another reason to check the conjugated fraction first
Retinal damageEYE COVERS AT ALL TIMES the lights are on

Facilitator Script “This is the procedure nobody in this room wants to do, and the one that saves the brain when everything else has failed. Most of you will do it rarely. Which is exactly why we walk through it slowly now — because the night you need it, you will not have time to read.”
The Three Indications

• TSB ≥ threshold DESPITE intensive phototherapy — thresholds vary by age in hours, gestation, and risk factors.
  • Signs of ACUTE BILIRUBIN ENCEPHALOPATHY — lethargy, hypotonia, poor feeding, high-pitched cry, opisthotonus, apnoea or seizures.
  • SEVERE HAEMOLYSIS — rapidly rising bilirubin (≥ 0.5 mg/dL/hr or ≥ 8.5 µmol/L/hr)
despite intensive phototherapy, or haemolytic disease with anaemia plus high bilirubin.
Indication 2 has no number attached. If the baby shows signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy, EXCHANGE IS URGENT REGARDLESS OF BILIRUBIN LEVEL. The baby is the test result.

“A high-pitched cry and opisthotonus in a jaundiced baby is not a sign to document and recheck in the morning. It is the brain being injured while you watch. That is a call-the-consultant-now finding.”
Preparation — Walk It

• Confirm the indication.
  • Obtain informed consent from parents.
  • Arrange cross-matched, screened, FRESH blood (< 5 days old).
  • CMV-negative, irradiated, leukocyte-depleted — usually O negative, Rh and ABO compatible with infant AND mother.
  • WARM the blood to 37 °C.
  • Calculate the exchange volume: ≈ 2 × blood volume = 160–180 mL/kg (term blood volume ≈ 80–90 mL/kg).
  • Correct hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and acidosis BEFORE starting.
Ensure aseptic technique, resuscitation equipment, and monitoring are ready.
Worked Volume Calculation — Do It Together

WeightBlood volume (80–90 mL/kg)Double volume exchangeAliquot size
1.5 kg (preterm)120–135 mL240–270 mL2–5 mL
2.5 kg200–225 mL400–450 mL5–10 mL
3.0 kg (term)240–270 mL480–540 mL5–10 mL
3.5 kg (term)280–315 mL560–630 mL5–10 mL

Have every participant calculate the 3 kg row independently before you show it. 160–180 mL/kg × 3 kg = 480–540 mL. Then ask how many aliquots of 10 mL that is (about 50) and how long at 1–2 minutes each. The arithmetic makes the 60–90 minute duration real. Route, Rate and the Procedure

ParameterSpecification
RouteUmbilical venous catheter PREFERRED; or peripheral line + arterial access
VolumeDouble volume, 160–180 mL/kg — replaces ~85% of the infant's blood
TechniquePUSH–PULL (manual syringe) or continuous (pump / automated device)
Aliquot5–10 mL term, 2–5 mL preterm — withdrawn slowly over 1–2 minutes
ReplacementEqual volume of donor blood over 1–2 minutes
Total duration60–90 minutes
The duration is bounded on BOTH sides. Too fast → haemodynamic instability. Too slow → rebound bilirubin. Not a target to beat — a window to stay inside.
During the Exchange

• Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring.
  • Frequent checks: glucose, calcium, electrolytes, haematocrit, bilirubin.
  • Observe for arrhythmias, apnoea, bradycardia, hypotension, seizures.

CALCIUM: 10% calcium gluconate 1 mL/kg SLOW IV after every ~100 mL exchanged, WITH CARDIAC MONITORING. Cross-reference the convulsions session — calcium gluconate requires a monitor there too, for the same reason.
• Provide glucose support (5–10% dextrose infusion if needed).
After the Exchange

• Flush the line with saline to clear residual donor blood.
  • Continue INTENSIVE PHOTOTHERAPY — rebound is common.
  • Monitor vital signs, urine output, acid–base, electrolytes, calcium, glucose.
  • Recheck bilirubin at 2 hours, then every 4–6 hours.
  • A second exchange may be required if bilirubin rebounds.
  • Treat the underlying cause — e.g. IVIG for isoimmune haemolysis.
  • Document: total volume, aliquot size, duration, complications, blood details (type, donor unit, expiry, irradiation).
  • Watch for late complications: NEC, sepsis, portal vein thrombosis, infection.
Complications — Name Them All

CategoryComplications
MetabolicHypocalcaemia · hypoglycaemia · acidosis · hyperkalaemia
HaematologicThrombocytopenia · coagulopathy · anaemia · polycythaemia
InfectiousSepsis (blood product related)
Catheter-relatedArrhythmias · embolism · perforation
Mortality< 1–2% in experienced centres — HIGHER in sick or preterm infants

That mortality figure is why indication matters. This procedure has a real death rate. It is done because kernicterus is worse — but it is never done casually, and never without the indication written down.

sections.title: Exchange Transfusion: Case 1 — The Day-One Baby Who Looks Well

read.text: Case 1 — The Day-One Baby Who Looks Well

A term baby, 3.2 kg, normal delivery, is noticed to be slightly yellow at 20 hours of age. He is feeding, active, afebrile. The midwife says: “He is only a bit yellow and he is feeding beautifully — all babies go yellow, we will look again tomorrow.”
Ask:

• Is the midwife right?
  • What does the timing tell you?
  • What happens next — exactly?
ANSWER KEY
The midwife is wrong. Jaundice within the first 24 hours is NEVER physiological. ‘He looks well’ is not reassurance — he looks well now, and bilirubin rises.

What happens next: measure TSB now and plot against age in hours. Investigate the cause — blood group (mother and baby), Coombs, FBC and reticulocytes, G6PD. Start phototherapy per the nomogram. Do not wait for tomorrow.
The thinking error: using the baby's appearance instead of the clock. The 24-hour rule is a rule precisely because well-looking babies with early jaundice are the ones who get missed.
KEY MESSAGE in the first 24 hours, the clock overrules the eye.
Case 2 — The Referral That Did Not Happen

A 36-week baby, 2.2 kg, born at a health centre. Day 3. Deep jaundice including the palms and soles. Feeding poorly, sleepy. The health centre has no bilirubinometer. The nearest district hospital is two hours away and the family has no transport money.
Ask:

• Which referral criteria are met?
  • What can the health centre do while arranging transfer?
  • What must be communicated to the district hospital?
ANSWER KEY
Referral criteria met — FOUR: deep jaundice especially palms and soles; poor feeding and lethargy; preterm; low birth weight. Any ONE of these was enough.
While arranging transfer: keep the baby warm; support feeding/hydration; document the age in HOURS and the time jaundice was first seen; do not delay transfer to ‘observe’.
Communicate: age in hours, when jaundice was first noticed, feeding history, risk factors (preterm, LBW), and that no TSB is available. Use SBAR (cross-reference Patient Safety).

The real issue: ‘no transport money’ is a clinical problem here, not a social one. This is the Sudan-specific delay the manual names. Ask the group how their own units solve it — and whether anyone has a written referral-support pathway.
KEY MESSAGE at primary level you cannot measure bilirubin — but you can measure the clock, the feeding and the palms. All three said refer, on day one of noticing.
Case 3 — The Rate, Not the Number

A 38-week baby on intensive phototherapy since 48 hours. At 54 hours TSB was 280 µmol/L. At 60 hours it is 340 µmol/L. The registrar says: “Still under the exchange line — keep the lights on and recheck in the morning.”
Ask:

• Calculate the rate of rise.
  • Is the registrar right?
  • What do you do now?
ANSWER KEY
The rate: 340 − 280 = 60 µmol/L over 6 hours = 10 µmol/L per hour.

The registrar is wrong. A rise of ≥ 8.5 µmol/L/hr (≥ 0.5 mg/dL/hr) DESPITE intensive phototherapy is itself an exchange transfusion indication. Ten exceeds 8.5. He does not need to cross the line — the slope has already answered.
What you do now: escalate to tertiary; cross-match fresh, irradiated, leukocyte-depleted blood;
continue intensive phototherapy meanwhile; check for haemolysis (Coombs, G6PD) and consider IVIG if isoimmune; correct glucose, calcium and acidosis in preparation.
The trap: ‘still under the line’ is the most dangerous sentence in jaundice management. The threshold is where you must act; the slope is where you should act.
KEY MESSAGE two numbers and a clock give you a slope. The slope decides before the threshold does.
Case 4 — The Baby Who Is Telling You

A 4-day-old term baby, deeply jaundiced, brought from home. He is lethargic, will not feed, has a high-pitched cry, and arches backwards when handled. The laboratory is closed and no TSB is available until morning.
Ask:

• What are you looking at?
  • Does the absence of a bilirubin level change anything?
  • What is the immediate management?
ANSWER KEY
This is ACUTE BILIRUBIN ENCEPHALOPATHY. Lethargy, poor feeding, high-pitched cry and opisthotonus are the named signs. This is bilirubin in the brain, now.

The missing TSB changes NOTHING. Exchange transfusion is urgent REGARDLESS OF BILIRUBIN LEVEL when there are signs of acute bilirubin encephalopathy. Waiting for a number until morning is waiting while the injury completes.

Immediate management: intensive phototherapy immediately, while everything else is arranged. Call the consultant. Arrange urgent cross-matched blood. Establish access (UVC preferred). Correct hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and acidosis. Prepare for exchange. Treat any underlying cause — sepsis screen, Coombs, G6PD.
Also: this baby needs long-term follow-up — hearing test and neurodevelopmental assessment — whatever happens tonight.
Every group will ask about the bilirubin level. That question is the teaching moment: the baby IS the result. Signs of encephalopathy authorise action on their own.
KEY MESSAGE when the brain is already showing you the diagnosis, the laboratory is not the decision-maker.

read.text: Facilitator Script “Eight babies in three weeks. Two died. Every one of you has lived through a run like that — and every one of you knows what happened next: nothing. Because nobody counted. Surveillance is not a form. Surveillance is the difference between eight tragedies and one outbreak you can stop.”

A surveillance system for neonatal sepsis is essential to monitor and prevent healthcare-associated infections and to ensure the health and safety of newborns. Aim: to systematically detect, report and analyze cases of neonatal sepsis in order to guide prevention, control and quality improvement interventions, and to contribute to reduction of neonatal morbidity and mortality. Scope: this system surveys sepsis (blood stream infection) among preterm and sick neonates admitted to Sudanese paediatrics and obstetrics hospitals' NICUs. It targets ALL neonates born inside or outside hospital, whatever their clinical cause of admission. It works by identifying cases clinically or by laboratory confirmation, collecting appropriate clinical samples (blood, CSF, swab). The Six Objectives — Teach in This Order

• 1. Monitor the incidence and prevalence of neonatal sepsis.
  • 2. Identify risk factors associated with neonatal sepsis.
  • 3. Detect antimicrobial sensitivity and resistance patterns.
  • 4. Evaluate the effectiveness of IPC interventions.
  • 5. Provide data for benchmarking and quality improvement in neonatal care.
  • 6. Facilitate timely response to outbreaks or clusters of neonatal infections.
FACILITATOR HINT put these six on the flip chart and leave them up ALL DAY. Every session that follows serves one of them. Blood culture technique serves objective 3. Hand hygiene serves objective 4.
Stewardship serves objective 3. At the end of the day, point back.
Why Objective 3 Is the One That Bites

“Detect antimicrobial sensitivity and resistance patterns. Which of you can tell me, right now, what your unit’s Klebsiella is sensitive to? Not what the textbook says — what YOUR unit’s isolates said last quarter. If nobody can answer, then every empirical antibiotic you start is a guess, and stewardship is impossible. Surveillance is what makes stewardship possible. That is why it comes first today.”
Role Play — The Surveillance Process
Scenario: over three weeks, eight babies in your unit were treated for sepsis and two died.
Roles:

• NICU nurse in-charge
  • Medical officer
  • Laboratory focal person
  • Infection control focal person The team demonstrates the surveillance workflow: what data are collected · how cases are detected and reported · how laboratory samples (blood, CSF, swab) contribute to confirmation · how findings guide IPC actions and quality improvement.

sections.title: Surveillance system: Facilitator Prompts — Ask These If the Team Stalls

read.text: Facilitator Prompts — Ask These If the Team Stalls

• “Who noticed it was eight and not three? How?”
  • “Were all eight cultured? If not, what are they in your data — clinical sepsis, or nothing?”
  • “What grew? Was it the SAME organism? How would you know?”
  • “Lab focal person: how long did the results take to come back, and to whom?”
  • “IPC focal person: what was your first action — and what was your first action based on?”
  • “Who outside this unit was told?”
ANSWER KEY What a Good Team Produces

ObjectiveWhat the team should have shown
1 — IncidenceThey counted. Eight cases and two deaths in three weeks is a NUMBER, and it is compared against something
2 — Risk factorsThey looked for what the eight shared — gestation, weight, lines, ventilation, day of onset, which nurse, which incubator
3 — SensitivityCultures were taken BEFORE antibiotics; isolates and sensitivities were collated, not just filed
4 — IPC effectivenessThey asked what changed before the run started, and what they will change now — and how they will know if it worked
5 — BenchmarkingData go somewhere. To the hospital, to the state, and back to the unit
6 — Outbreak responseSame organism in a cluster = outbreak until proved otherwise. Report to the hospital infection control committee to search for cases in other departments
Close the role play by linking each of the group's outputs back to a numbered objective on the flip chart. Common Errors in This Session

• The team investigates the two deaths and ignores the six survivors — the survivors are the data.
  • Nobody asks whether the eight had cultures taken before antibiotics.
  • The group blames a nurse. Errors result from multiple system failures; individual blame is insufficient — link this to the Swiss-Cheese model in Section 9.
  • They design a beautiful form nobody will fill in at 3 a.m.

Facilitator Script “Four definitions. They exist because ‘the baby looks septic’ is not data. If your unit and mine both say ‘we had eight cases’ but we mean different things, neither number means anything, and nobody can compare us, help us, or fund us.”
Suspected Sepsis
WHO defines suspected sepsis in a hospitalized infant aged 0–59 days as the presence of ONE OR MORE of the following clinical signs:

1. Not feeding well or not able to feed at all7. Fast breathing (≥ 60 breaths per minute) in infants aged 0–6 days
2. Movement only when stimulated or no movement at all8. Drowsiness or unconsciousness
3. High body temperature (≥ 38 °C)9. Grunting
4. Low body temperature (< 35.5 °C)10. Central cyanosis
5. Severe chest indrawing11. Severe jaundice
6. Convulsions12. Severe abdominal distention
ONE sign is enough. This is the lowest bar of the four definitions, and deliberately so — it is a trigger to act, not a diagnosis.
Maternal risk factors also suggest sepsis:

• PROM > 18 hours and mother not given antibiotics 4 or more hours before labour
  • Positive GBS screening
  • History of fever more than 38 degrees, or offensive vaginal discharge
Practical Case Drill — With Answer Key
Case A: A day-2 newborn who is not feeding well, RR 66/min with grunting.
Answer: SUSPECTED SEPSIS. Three criteria present — (1) not feeding well; (7) fast breathing ≥ 60/min in an infant aged 0–6 days; (9) grunting. Only one was needed.

sections.title: Case Definitions and Classification: CASE-BASED DISCUSSION

read.text: CASE-BASED DISCUSSION
Case B: A day-1 newborn with mild respiratory distress whose mother had PROM > 18 hours and did not receive antibiotics 4 or more hours before labour.

Answer: SUSPECTED SEPSIS. The maternal risk factor is explicitly listed as suggesting sepsis, and the baby has respiratory distress. Do not wait for him to look worse — that is what ‘suspected’ means.
FACILITATOR HINT after Case B, ask ‘how many of you would have started antibiotics on this baby?’ Then hold that.
You will come back to it in stewardship this afternoon. Suspected sepsis triggers investigation and treatment — it does NOT commit you to ten days.
Clinical Sepsis — No Positive Culture But Meets Criteria
All THREE must be present:

• Absence of positive microbiological blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid culture, AND
  • Treatment with FIVE or more days of intravenous antibiotics was initiated, AND
  • Patient has at least TWO of the following clinical or laboratory features of generalized infection:

CategoryFeatures
CNSConvulsion, bulging fontanel, irritability, lethargy, apathy
GITRefusal of feeding, feeding intolerance, abdominal distension or ileus
TemperatureUnexplained instability, or fever (> 38 °C), or hypothermia (< 36.5 °C)

CategoryFeatures
Heart rateUnexplained tachycardia (> 160/min) or bradycardia episodes (< 100/min)
PerfusionCapillary refill time > 3 seconds, or skin mottling
RespiratoryNew or more frequent episodes of apnoea (> 20 s)
LocalLocal infection — umbilical discharge, eye discharge
Laboratory (at least one)Platelets < 100 × 10³/µL · WBC < 4 × 10³/µL or > 20 × 10³/µL · CRP > 1 mg/dL · hyperglycaemia > 140 mg/dL or hypoglycaemia < 46 mg/dL

sections.title: Case Definitions and Classification: Group Exercise — clinical sepsis

read.text: Group Exercise — clinical sepsis
CASE-BASED DISCUSSION
Scenario: A preterm baby has no positive culture, has received IV antibiotics for 6 days, and has lethargy plus feeding intolerance. CRP is > 1 mg/dL.

Answer: YES — this meets the definition of clinical sepsis. Map it: (1) no positive culture ✓ (2) five or more days of IV antibiotics — he has had six ✓ (3) at least TWO features — he has three: CNS (lethargy), GIT (feeding intolerance), and a laboratory finding (CRP > 1 mg/dL) ✓

FACILITATOR HINT notice what criterion 2 does. ‘Five or more days of IV antibiotics’ is not a clinical feature of the baby — it is a feature of YOUR decision. A baby only becomes ‘clinical sepsis’ because somebody kept treating him. Ask the group what that means for the numbers. It means this category counts your uncertainty, not just his illness — and it is exactly the category stewardship is trying to shrink.
Laboratory Confirmed Sepsis — Recognized Pathogen
A recognized pathogen is recovered from a blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid culture. ONE culture is enough.

Gram-POSITIVE bacteriaGram-NEGATIVE bacteria
Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA)Escherichia coli — most common in early- and late- onset neonatal sepsis
Group B Streptococcus (GBS)Klebsiella pneumoniae
Streptococcus pneumoniaeEnterobacter cloacae
Enterococcus faecalis / faecium (including VRE)Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Beta-haemolytic streptococci (Groups A, C, F, G)Serratia marcescens
Listeria monocytogenes — especially in early-onset sepsisAcinetobacter baumannii
Citrobacter spp.
Proteus spp.
“One culture. One organism from that list. That is all it takes — because none of these belong in a newborn’s blood, ever. Contrast that with the next definition, and you will understand why.”
Laboratory Confirmed Sepsis — Common Commensals
If blood cultures show growth of one or multiple common commensals (e.g. coagulase-negative staphylococci), BOTH are required:

• A common commensal is recovered from TWO blood culture and/or CSF culture specimens, AND
  • Patient has at least TWO of the clinical or laboratory features of generalized infection (the same list as 10.3).
TWO cultures. Not one. A commensal in one bottle is your skin, not his blood — unless you have a second bottle and a sick baby to prove otherwise. Case Discussion — sepsis by common commensal
Case 1: One blood culture grows a common commensal. There is no second culture.

Answer: NO — criteria are NOT met. The definition requires the commensal from TWO specimens. With one bottle you cannot distinguish infection from contamination at the moment of collection. This is why blood culture technique this afternoon matters: a re-palpated site produces exactly this result, and this argument.
Case 2: Two cultures grow the commensal, and the baby has temperature instability plus apnoea.
Answer: YES — criteria are met. Two specimens ✓ and at least two clinical features — unexplained temperature instability, and new/more frequent apnoea > 20 s ✓

FACILITATOR HINT this pair is the best teaching moment in the whole section. Same organism, same lab, different answer — and the difference is entirely in how the sample was taken and whether anyone looked at the baby. Say that out loud.
The Four Definitions Side By Side

DefinitionCultureAlso needsWhat it tells you
SuspectedNot requiredONE clinical sign, or a maternal risk factorAct now
Clinical sepsisNEGATIVE≥ 5 days IV antibiotics AND ≥ 2 featuresYou treated; you never proved it
Confirmed — pathogenONE positiveNothing elseCertainty
Confirmed — commensalTWO positive≥ 2 featuresCertainty, earned the hard way

Facilitator Script “Everything you did this morning — the four definitions, the surveillance objectives, the resistance patterns — all of it rests on this one skill. A badly taken culture does not just fail this baby. It puts a false organism into your unit’s resistance data, and that wrong number will change what the next hundred babies are prescribed.”
The Technique Prepare the patient

• Verify identity.
  • Calm the neonate.
  • Position for access — peripheral or umbilical vein.
  • Clean the site with 70% alcohol — 30-SECOND SCRUB, then AIR DRY.
Confirm indication
• Suspected neonatal sepsis. No absolute contraindication; avoid sites with oedema or infection.
Prepare materials
• Sterile gloves · 70% alcohol or chlorhexidine · sterile syringes and needles (23–25G) · aerobic blood culture bottles · labels · transport bag
Collect

• Use appropriate aseptic technique and follow IPC protocols — wear gloves, and DO NOT RE-PALPATE the cleaned site.
  • Collect the sample in sterile, labelled containers.
  • BLOOD VOLUME: 1–2 mL per bottle — critical for detection.
  • CSF VOLUME: 1 mL per bottle — critical for detection.
  • If the baby is ALREADY receiving antibiotics, take the blood culture immediately BEFORE the next dose.
Label, send, record

• Label with the neonate's name, file ID, date/time, collector's name and sample type.
  • Complete the culture request form and send to the public lab using the standard transferee procedure.
Record the sample collection in the main case record registry.
The Four Errors That Destroy a Culture

ErrorWhat it does to the resultWhat it does to the unit
Re-palpating the cleaned siteContaminant — usually a commensalA false 'commensal sepsis' argument, and a baby on 10 days of antibiotics for your finger
Insufficient blood volumeFalse NEGATIVE — the organism is there, below the detection thresholdA 'culture-negative' baby who becomes 'clinical sepsis' at day 5
Incomplete labellingUnusable sample, or worse — attributed to the wrong babyCorrupted surveillance data
Delay in transportReduced yieldA false negative that looks like good news

sections.title: Blood Culture Collection Technique: Demonstration and Return Demonstration

read.text: Demonstration and Return Demonstration

• Demonstrate the full technique ONCE with narration.
  • Repeat SLOWLY, highlighting the common errors above as you deliberately nearly-make them.
  • Participants then perform return demonstration in PAIRS while facilitators observe using the checklist.

Facilitator trick: on your slow repeat, clean the site properly, then casually re-palpate it with a gloved finger while talking about something else. See who stops you. Whoever does gets to run the next station.
Role Play — Filling Forms

• Roles: nurse collecting the sample · doctor ordering · laboratory receiver.
  • Scenario: a suspected sepsis case.
  • Participants complete the blood culture request form and record the collection in the main case record registry.
The facilitator reviews for: identity accuracy · date and time · sample type · legibility — and all identifiers and timestamps complete.
“Laboratory receiver: you are allowed to reject this sample. Say why. That is your job, and doing it politely at the hatch saves a baby ten days of the wrong antibiotic.”
Other Investigation

There is NO role for CRP measurement in the golden hour. The half-life of CRP is 24 to 48 hours and it takes around 10 to 12 hours for the level to increase — making CRP in the golden hour unreliable.
Lumbar puncture for CSF culture, biochemical and microbiological analysis is usually NOT recommended as a routine investigation for early-onset sepsis screening. It should be done in:

• Neonates whose blood culture is positive
  • Infants with a strong clinical suspicion of sepsis
  • Neonates presenting with seizure activity, apnoea, or depressed sensorium

Facilitator Script “This morning you learned to find sepsis. Now the harder half: how to treat it without creating the organism that kills the next baby. Every antibiotic you start is a decision. Every antibiotic you fail to STOP is also a decision — and it is the one nobody remembers making.”
The Core Regimen and Decision Pathway

• START: Ampicillin + Gentamicin for 3 days awaiting culture results.
  • If NO GROWTH, repeat CRP/PCT: if negative and clinically stable, STOP ANTIBIOTICS.
  • Otherwise continue: ampicillin IM/IV 50 mg/kg every 12 hours in the first week of life, and every 8 hours after the first week, for a total of at least 10 days; PLUS gentamicin IM/IV 5 mg/kg once a day in the first week, and 7.5 mg/kg once a day after the first week, for a total of at least 10 days.
  • If CULTURE POSITIVE, continue as indicated for at least 10 days.
  • Alternative: third-generation cephalosporins for a total of 2–17 days — but no or trivial difference.
Step 2 is the whole of stewardship in one line. NO GROWTH + negative CRP/PCT + clinically stable = STOP. Not ‘finish the course’. Not ‘just to be safe’. STOP The Dose Table — Read It Twice

DrugFirst week of lifeAfter first weekDuration
Ampicillin50 mg/kg every 12 hours50 mg/kg every 8 hoursAt least 10 days
Gentamicin5 mg/kg once a day7.5 mg/kg once a dayAt least 10 days
FACILITATOR HINT note what changes with age. Ampicillin changes its FREQUENCY (12 → 8 hourly), same dose.
Gentamicin changes its DOSE (5 → 7.5 mg/kg), same frequency. Participants reliably get this backwards. Say it twice, and put it on the flip chart.
Other Management Points

• Fungal prophylaxis: in very preterm or VLBW infants, fluconazole prophylaxis within the golden hour — provided the incidence of fungal sepsis in the unit is significant (> 5% at baseline; European guidelines suggest 2% as the threshold).
  • Congenital infection at time of birth (viral infection like TORCH) should be treated promptly during the golden hour of life.

“Read the fluconazole line carefully. ‘Provided the incidence in the neonatal care unit is significant.’ That is a surveillance question. You cannot answer it without this morning’s session. Stewardship without surveillance is just guessing with extra steps.”
Antibiotic stewardship limits the development of antimicrobial-resistant organisms, and it can be done by improving the use of antibiotics. The components:

• Use NARROW-SPECTRUM antibiotics.
  • Have FIXED PROTOCOLS for starting AND stopping antibiotics.
  • Start antibiotics ONLY WHEN CLINICALLY INDICATED.
  • DOWNGRADE antibiotics after seeing the blood culture sensitivity pattern.
  • Consider LOCAL antibiotic resistance patterns.

There is high risk of development of antibiotic resistance with the widespread use of antibiotics — thus making careful and selective use of antibiotics to the highest-risk patients a UNIVERSAL GOAL. The Five Components, Turned Into Five Questions Put these on a card. They are the ward round.

ComponentThe question to ask at the cot
Only when indicated“Why did we START this? Is that reason still true?”
Fixed protocols for stopping“What is the STOP date? Who set it? Is it written?”
Downgrade after sensitivity“The culture is back. Have we narrowed?”
Narrow spectrum“Is this the narrowest drug that covers what we have?”
Local resistance patterns“What does OUR unit's data say about this organism?”

“Notice that four of those five questions are about STOPPING or NARROWING, and only one is about starting. That ratio is not an accident. Starting an antibiotic takes ten seconds and nobody is ever criticised for it. Stopping one takes courage, and this is the room where we practise it.” Practical Session — Dose Calculation and Double-Check

• Provide three newborn weights and two ages (within the first week, and after).
  • Participants calculate ampicillin and gentamicin dose and interval using the manual schedule.
  • Run a DOUBLE-CHECK routine: a second participant independently verifies the calculation before ‘administration’.
  • The facilitator corrects calculation AND INTERVAL errors immediately.

The commonest error is not the arithmetic — it is the interval. A participant who gives the right milligrams at the wrong frequency has made a bigger error than one who is 10% out on the dose. Score the interval. Specific Case Management

• Use one scenario for each category in the manual table.
  • Participants select the regimen DIRECTLY from the manual table without modification.
This is deliberate. The exercise is finding the right row, not inventing a regimen. Improvisation is the opposite of a fixed protocol.

FungiALARMING ORGANISMS · shift to antifungal treatment · isolate the neonate · assign one nurse and dedicate equipment · use CHLORHEXIDINE as hand rub agent

fungi ‘alarming organisms’ and changes your hand rub. That is the only place in this entire manual where the agent itself changes. Ask the group why — alcohol is unreliable against some fungal spores. If you grow a fungus, your hand rub has been failing.
Tabletop Exercise

• Give each group an isolate.
  • They choose actions and explain HOW they would implement isolation and dedicated equipment IN THEIR UNIT.

“Do not tell me what the manual says. Tell me where in YOUR unit the isolated baby goes. Which incubator. Which nurse, given tonight’s rota. Which stethoscope. If you cannot answer, you have not implemented isolation — you have written it down.”

sections.title: Antibiotic Stewardship: The Stewardship Ward Round

read.text: The Stewardship Ward Round

Run it as the last thing before the tea break, when everyone is tired — which is when real ward rounds happen. Four beds. Each group gets all four. Five minutes per bed. Every bed gets the five questions and a decision: CONTINUE · NARROW · STOP.
Bed 1
Day 4. Started on ampicillin + gentamicin day 1 for suspected sepsis (PROM > 18 hours, mother no antibiotics). Blood culture: NO GROWTH at 72 hours. CRP negative. Baby is feeding, afebrile, active.
Answer: STOP. This is step 2 of the pathway, exactly. No growth + negative CRP + clinically stable = stop antibiotics. Every group will find a reason to continue. Make them read step 2 aloud.
Bed 2
Day 6. Blood culture grew E. coli, sensitive to ampicillin AND to gentamicin AND to ceftriaxone. Currently on ceftriaxone, started by the night team ‘because he looked bad’.

Answer: NARROW. Downgrade after seeing the sensitivity pattern; use narrow-spectrum antibiotics. He goes back to ampicillin + gentamicin, and completes at least 10 days. Continuing the cephalosporin because it is working is the single commonest stewardship failure in any unit.
Bed 3
Day 8. No culture was ever taken — the bottles had run out. On ampicillin + gentamicin since day 1. Baby has had feeding intolerance and one apnoea. CRP 2 mg/dL.

Answer: This baby is now CLINICAL SEPSIS by definition (no positive culture; ≥ 5 days IV antibiotics; ≥ 2 features — GIT, apnoea, CRP). Continue to at least 10 days. But the real answer is upstream: he has no culture because the bottles ran out, which means he will be treated blind for 10 days and contribute nothing to your resistance data. THAT is the finding. Who orders the bottles?
Bed 4
Blood culture grew coagulase-negative staphylococcus — ONE bottle. Baby is well, feeding, normal temperature, normal CRP.
Answer: This does NOT meet the commensal definition — one bottle, and no clinical features.

This is a contaminant. It is a blood culture technique failure, and it is about to cost this well baby a course of vancomycin if nobody stops it. STOP. Then go and look at who took the sample and whether they re-palpated.

Bed 4 closes the loop of the entire day: bad technique (10.6) → a false result (10.5) → an unnecessary antibiotic (10.7) → resistance (10.1, objective 3). One re-palpated finger, four sessions of consequence. End the exercise there.
Multiple forms are used for documentation of neonatal sepsis, including the blood culture request form and the blood culture result form.

Facilitator Script “This is the least popular half hour of the day. It is also the half hour that turns eight sick babies into an outbreak report that gets you the bottles you ran out of in Bed 3. The form is not administration. The form is advocacy.”

Facilitator Script “Everything today has been about what happens after. This is the only session about what happens instead. And the whole of it fits in one sentence from the manual: the most important interventions are hand washing and asepsis. Not a drug. Not a machine. Your hands.”
The Core Statements

• Many interventions are done to prevent neonatal sepsis, but the MOST IMPORTANT are the standard infection control precautions — mainly hand washing and using asepsis precautions while handling the newborn.
  • The newborn should be handled with strict asepsis starting FROM THE TIME OF BIRTH. All invasive procedures — umbilical line or peripheral cannula insertion, administration of surfactant, preparation of IV fluids, TPN, and antibiotics — should be done using aseptic precautions, and a BUNDLE APPROACH should be used.
  • A clear WRITTEN POLICY for infection control should be maintained and strictly implemented during all SCNU procedures.
Do NOT wear artificial fingernails or extenders when having direct contact with patients. Natural nails should be kept SHORT — ≤ 0.5 cm long, approximately ¼ inch.

FACILITATOR HINT read the nail rule and then look at the room. Do not shame anyone. Just let it be quiet for a moment. This is the cheapest intervention in the entire manual and it is written down because it does not happen.
The Eight Interventions — Teach in This Order

• 1. Hand hygiene
  • 2. Personal protective equipment (PPE)
  • 3. Safe injections and sharps injury prevention
  • 4. Environmental cleaning
  • 5. Appropriate handling and transport of linen
  • 6. Waste management
  • 7. Decontamination and reprocessing of reusable patient care items and equipment
  • 8. Aseptic technique
Note the order. Hand hygiene is first because it is first — not alphabetically, but in importance.
Practical Session — Four Skills Stations
Four supervised stations, 4–6 participants per group, rotating. 20 minutes per station.

Station 1 — Hand Hygiene
SituationMethod and duration
Hands NOT visibly soiledAlcohol-based hand rub — 20–30 SECONDS
Hands VISIBLY soiledSoap and water — 40–60 SECONDS
Turning off the tapUse a SINGLE-USE TOWEL — never your clean hand
Fungal isolate on the unitChlorhexidine as the hand rub agent
● Time them. Every participant, with a watch. Almost nobody reaches 20 seconds unaided.
● Have them state WHEN — before touching the baby, before a procedure, after body fluid
exposure, after touching the baby, after touching the baby's surroundings.
“Twenty seconds feels like a very long time when someone is watching you do nothing else. That
feeling is why this fails on a busy ward. Learn the feeling now.”

sections.title: Prevention of Sepsis: Station 2 — PPE and Glove Use

read.text: Station 2 — PPE and Glove Use

• Correct selection based on RISK ASSESSMENT.
  • Hand hygiene BEFORE donning and AFTER doffing.
  • Correct glove-use timing.
  • Examples of UNSAFE glove use, as listed in the manual.
Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. The commonest unsafe glove use in any unit is the same pair moving from one baby to the next — which is not protection, it is transport.
Station 3 — Safe Injection and Sharps Safety

• Clean workspace preparation.
  • Sterile syringe and needle use.
  • Vial handling guidance.
  • Skin disinfection with 60–70% alcohol.
  • Sharps container use AT POINT OF CARE.
  • NO RECAPPING.
  • Discard sharps containers when THREE QUARTERS full.

Ask at this station: ‘where is the sharps container in your unit?’ If the answer is ‘by the door’ rather than ‘at the cot’, you have found a needlestick waiting to happen. Point of care means point of care.
Station 4 — Decontamination of Reusable Equipment

• Use the decontamination station and the FULL manual sequence of steps.
  • 0.1% CHLORINE working solution.
  • 20-MINUTE contact time.
Cross-reference: device-specific reprocessing (incubator, CPAP, warmer, oximeter) is scored on the disinfection checklists in the Equipment volume. This station teaches the general principle;
those checklists score the device.

Twenty minutes means twenty minutes. An item pulled out at eight minutes because the round is starting is a contaminated item with a clean reputation — which is more dangerous than a visibly dirty one.

read.text: Procedures and equipment are NOT taught as standalone sessions. Every procedure and every device is taught inside the clinical session that gives the reason for using it. This document tells you where each one lives.
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of this neonatal procedures module, participants should be able to:

• Demonstrate correct preparation and aseptic technique for neonatal procedures.
  • Perform selected neonatal procedures safely and competently according to standard protocols.
  • Apply appropriate pain prevention and comfort measures before, during, and after procedures.
  • Identify indications, contraindications, and potential complications of common neonatal procedures.
  • Document procedures accurately, including consent, technique, and monitoring.
ROLE OF THE FACILITATOR Facilitators play a central role in ensuring safe learning and patient protection during procedural training. Prior to each session, facilitators should:

• Review all procedural steps and equipment requirements.
  • Identify appropriate neonates or simulation alternatives.
  • Coordinate with neonatal unit staff to ensure clinical safety.
  • Ensure informed consent is obtained from caregivers where applicable.
  • Supervise all procedures closely, intervening immediately if patient safety is compromised.
Facilitators must emphasize patient-centered care, adherence to infection prevention standards, and reflective learning throughout all procedural demonstrations and practice sessions
GENERAL PRINCIPLES FOR NEONATAL PROCEDURES
Procedure Documentation Facilitators must reinforce that every procedure performed on a neonate must be documented clearly, including:

• Date and time of procedure
  • Indication and diagnosis
  • Consent process and caregiver discussion
  • Procedure performed and technique used
  • Complications (if any)
  • Post-procedure monitoring and plan
Refusal of procedures and associated counseling must also be documented comprehensively
Infection Prevention and Safety All procedures must follow universal precautions:

• Strict hand hygiene
  • Use of sterile or high-level disinfected equipment
  • Maintenance of a clean and organized procedural field
  • Appropriate disposal of sharps and contaminated materials
These principles are reinforced during clinical practice sessions within the neonatal unit
Pain Prevention and Comfort Measures Facilitators should ensure that participants consistently apply pain-prevention strategies, including: Environmental and Behavioral Measures

• Swaddling during procedures
  • Non-nutritive sucking
  • Minimizing noise and light
  • Skin-to-skin contact (Kangaroo Mother Care) following procedures
Physiological Measures

• Oral glucose/sucrose administration according to gestational age
  • Gentle tactile stimulation as competitive sensory input

read.text: TEACHING APPROACH AND SESSION STRUCTURE
Each neonatal procedure session should follow a standardized structure:

• 1. Brief theoretical overview (indications, risks, anatomy)
  • 2. Facilitator demonstration using manikin
  • 3. Supervised participant practice
  • 4. Group reflection and feedback
  • 5. Safety check and documentation review
Scoring

ScoreMeans

1Attempted but incomplete · minor errors not immediately endangering the baby · needed verbal prompting · correct but poorly sequenced

• Score ONLY what is directly observed. Do not infer from seniority or confidence.
  • Verbal explanation does not substitute for correct performance unless the row says so.
  • One checklist = one observed procedure. If interrupted for patient safety, score completed steps and document why.

Facilitator Script “Remember this morning’s baby — heart rate still under 60 after 60 seconds of good compressions. You said adrenaline. Now I am asking you: through what? This is the session that answers that question.”
Competency

• Emergency vascular access indications
  • Catheter length calculation methods
  • Safe insertion technique
  • Confirmation of catheter position

Indications

• Emergency situation when urgent IV access is required
  • To administer adrenaline during resuscitation
  • Bolus of fluid for volume expansion
  • To correct severe hypoglycaemia
  • Single and double volume exchange transfusion
  • Measurement of central venous pressure
  • TPN, or dextrose concentration above 12.5%
  • Vasopressors / inotropes
Contraindications
• Omphalitis · omphalocele · peritonitis · necrotising enterocolitis
Depth — The Number That Changes By Context

ContextInsert to
Emergency resuscitation2 to 4 cm (less in preterm) — until free flow of blood. STOP there

Confirmed positionJust above the dome of the right diaphragm, T9–T10
“In resuscitation you are not placing a long line. You are opening a road for the adrenaline. Two to four centimetres, free blood, stop. Every extra centimetre you push is liver.”
Demonstration UVC

• 1. Arrange equipment; follow aseptic technique of infection prevention. Prepare the solution to be infused.
  • 2. Restrain the baby on a padded crucifix splint, under a radiant warmer with good light.
  • 3. Cap and mask. Wash hands, sterile gown and sterile gloves.
  • 4. Prepare the umbilicus in a spiral motion inward to outward: spirit → povidone iodine → spirit, a different swab each time. Allow to dry.
  • 5. Change to a second pair of sterile gloves. Drape with a sterile cloth.
  • 6. Fill the catheter with normal saline via an attached syringe — no air.
  • 7. Tie sterile umbilical tape around the base of the cord, tight enough to prevent bleeding.
  • 8. Cut the stump horizontally with a sterile blade, 1.5–2 cm from the skin.
  • 9. Hold the stump with toothed forceps and identify the vein: two thick-walled arteries; ONE thin-walled vein with a wider opening, sitting towards the baby's head.
  • 10. Remove any clot and debris from the vein.
  • 11. Insert the saline-filled catheter gently, aiming towards the baby's head and to the baby's RIGHT (towards the right shoulder). Do not force.
  • 12. Apply gentle suction periodically as you advance. Once blood flows back freely — STOP. Do not advance further.
  • 13. If resistance is met, especially in the first 2–3 cm: do NOT continue. Remove and try again. Do not infuse into the liver.
  • 14. Tie the cord tie or suture around the stump to hold the catheter and prevent bleeding around it or from an artery.
  • 15. Remove the syringe, connect the infusion set — no air bubbles.
  • 16. Secure with suture material or adhesive tape.
  • 17. Confirm the tip by X-ray or ultrasound — T9–T10. If in the hepatic or portal vein, remove and retry.
  • 18. The catheter may be pulled back but NEVER advanced once the sterile field is broken.
  • 19. Inspect hourly. Redness or swelling around the umbilicus → stop the infusion, remove the catheter, establish peripheral IV, treat the umbilical infection.
Common Errors

• Choosing an artery — thick-walled, two of them, constricted lumen.
  • Forcing through resistance in the first 2–3 cm.
  • Advancing after blood return — ‘just a bit more to be safe’ — straight into the liver.
  • Advancing a catheter after the field is broken.
  • Skipping the second glove change.

Whatever position you choose, the tip must NEVER sit between T10 and L2. That is where the coeliac, superior mesenteric and renal arteries come off. A catheter parked there is a gut or a kidney.
Demonstration — What Differs From the UVC

• 1. Preparation, asepsis, draping, cord tie and stump cut: IDENTICAL to the UVC. Do not re-teach — say ‘everything up to here is what you just did’.
  • 2. Identify the two arteries — thick-walled, small lumen, usually towards the feet.
  • 3. Dilate the arterial lumen gently with fine forceps. Wait. The artery is in spasm; it will open.
  • 4. Insert the saline-filled catheter aiming CAUDALLY — towards the feet.
  • 5. Advance with gentle steady pressure. Resistance at 1–2 cm (abdominal wall) and again at 5– 6 cm (bladder level) is normal — steady gentle pressure, never force.
  • 6. Blood return confirms intraluminal placement.
  • 7. Advance to the pre-calculated length for the chosen position.
  • 8. Secure. Confirm by X-ray — and read the tip against the vertebrae, not the ruler.
  • 9. Then, every hour: look at the legs, the feet and the buttocks.
Complications to Name Out Loud

• Vasospasm — white or blue leg, foot or buttock. The commonest, and the earliest warning.
  • Thrombosis and embolism.
  • Ischaemia of the gut (NEC), kidney, or limb.
  • Haemorrhage — a disconnected arterial line exsanguinates a newborn in minutes.
  • Infection. Hypertension. False tract.

If a leg blanches or goes blue after a UAC: that is the catheter, until proved otherwise. Warm the OPPOSITE leg reflexly. If it does not resolve quickly — remove the line. A line is replaceable; a foot is not. Common Errors

• Forcing at the two normal resistance points instead of waiting with steady pressure.
  • Aiming cephalad, like the vein.
  • Not dilating the lumen and declaring the artery ‘impossible’.
  • Leaving the tip at T10–L2.
  • Not looking at the legs afterwards — the whole complication set is visible on the skin.

Facilitator Script “Your 1.1 kg baby is on day 3. He needs TPN for two weeks. Every peripheral line lasts a day and a half and costs him a cannulation. This is how you stop hurting him — once, properly, and then leave him alone.”
Competency (from the guide)

• Indications for prolonged intravenous therapy
  • Site selection and measurement techniques
  • Aseptic insertion and securing of lines
  • Prevention of malposition and infection
Indications

• Prolonged IV therapy — more than 5–7 days
  • Total parenteral nutrition
  • Dextrose concentration above 12.5%
  • Vasopressors / inotropes
  • Drugs that are irritant or vesicant
  • The VLBW baby who will exhaust peripheral access
Site Selection and Measurement

SiteMeasure from insertion point to
Basilic (preferred)Right axilla, then to the sternal notch — tip in the SVC
CephalicAs above — but note the sharp angle at the shoulder
Long saphenousGroin, then to the xiphisternum — tip in the IVC above the diaphragm
Scalp veinsOnly if others fail
The tip must NOT sit inside the heart. A tip in the right atrium causes tamponade and arrhythmia. Central means the SVC or IVC outside the cardiac silhouette — not ‘as deep as it will go’.
Demonstration — The Steps

• 1. Select the vein. Measure the distance BEFORE opening the set — measure twice.
  • 2. Full aseptic precautions: cap, mask, sterile gown, sterile gloves, large sterile drape. This is a central line, not a cannula.
  • 3. Prepare the skin: spirit → dry → iodine → dry → spirit.
  • 4. Achieve venous access with the introducer.
  • 5. Advance the catheter SLOWLY with non-toothed forceps, a few millimetres at a time.
  • 6. If it stops: do not force. Reposition the limb — abduct or adduct the arm, turn the head towards the insertion side to close off the jugular. Then try again.
  • 7. Advance to the measured length. Not further.
  • 8. Aspirate for blood return; flush gently.
  • 9. Secure the line and apply a sterile transparent dressing so the site stays visible.
  • 10. Request imaging confirmation with contrast if needed. Read the tip position before you use the line.
  • 11. Then: never use it before the X-ray is seen; inspect the site every shift; minimise access.
Common Errors

• Measuring after opening the set — or once.
  • Treating it like a cannula: gloves only, no drape, no gown.
  • Forcing when it stops, instead of repositioning the limb or head.
  • Using the line before seeing the film.
  • Leaving the tip in the heart.
Opening the line repeatedly for sampling — every entry is a sepsis risk.

Facilitator Script “Capillary refill five seconds. Heart rate 180. Two nurses have tried four times and there is no vein. Six minutes have gone. What do you do? — You stop trying for a vein. The bone is a vein that cannot collapse.”
The chicken thigh is not a joke prop. It has cortex, it has marrow, and it gives the exact ‘give’ the participant must learn to feel. Let everyone feel the pop before they ever meet a shocked baby.
Competency

• Indications and contraindications
  • Correct site of insertion
  • Skin preparation
  • Stepwise insertion technique
  • Monitoring and complication recognition
Indications and Contraindications

IndicatedContraindicated
Emergency — IV access failed or will take too longFracture in that bone
Shock, cardiac arrest, severe dehydrationPrevious IO attempt in the SAME bone — use the other leg
Any resuscitation drug, fluid or blood can go IOInfection or burn over the site
Osteogenesis imperfecta
The Site

• Proximal tibia: 1–2 cm BELOW and 1 cm MEDIAL to the tibial tuberosity, on the flat antero-medial surface.
  • Aim away from the joint — direct the needle slightly caudally, at 90° or angled away from the growth plate.
Aim AWAY from the growth plate. A needle through the physis is a leg that grows short.
Demonstration — Intraosseous (IO) Access

• 1. Identify the landmark. Say it out loud: below and medial to the tuberosity.
  • 2. Clean the skin — aseptic technique.
  • 3. Insert with a firm rotating motion, perpendicular or angled slightly away from the joint.
  • 4. Feel for the sudden loss of resistance — the pop. Stop advancing immediately.
  • 5. The needle should STAND FIRMLY WITHOUT SUPPORT. That is your first confirmation.
  • 6. Remove the stylet. Attempt to aspirate marrow — note that it is NOT necessary to aspirate marrow to confirm placement.
  • 7. Slowly inject 3 ml of IV fluid to check placement.
  • 8. LOOK for swelling — at the front of the leg, and in the calf muscle at the back. Swelling = extravasation. Remove the needle and try the OTHER leg.
  • 9. If infusion is difficult but there is NO swelling: the needle may have entered the posterior cortex. Withdraw about 0.5 cm and cautiously inject again.
  • 10. If no problems: secure the needle. Attach standard IV tubing.
  • 11. Increased pressure — pressure bag or push — may be needed. There is a high risk of obstruction if continuous high-pressure fluids are not flushed through.
  • 12. Marrow can be sent for glucose, chemistry, blood type and crossmatch, haemoglobin, blood gas and culture.
Remove the IO needle as soon as alternative IV access is available, and WITHIN EIGHT HOURS if possible. Common Errors

• Pushing past the pop — straight through the far cortex.
  • Aiming at the joint.
  • Re-attempting in the same bone after a failure — the fluid leaks out of the first hole.
  • Not looking at the calf. The swelling is behind the leg where nobody looks.
  • Waiting for marrow aspirate to ‘confirm’ — it is not necessary and it wastes seconds.
Leaving it in beyond 8 hours.

Facilitator Script “A ventilated 28-weeker. Sudden desaturation, bradycardia, the chest is not moving on one side.
You do not have time for an X-ray. This is the one procedure on this course where waiting for a film is the wrong answer.”
Recognise It First — The Procedure Is the Easy Part

• Sudden deterioration in a ventilated or CPAP baby
  • Desaturation and bradycardia
  • Reduced or absent air entry on one side
  • Asymmetrical chest movement
  • Displaced apex beat
  • Transillumination positive — useful in the dark, in a small baby
Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis. In an unstable baby, do not wait for the X-ray. The X-ray comes after the needle. The Landmark — and the Rule That Prevents Bleeding

• 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line — or 4th–5th space, mid-axillary line.
  • Insert over the SUPERIOR margin of the rib below.
Over the TOP of the lower rib. The neurovascular bundle runs under the rib above. Go under the rib and you hit the artery, the vein and the nerve.
Demonstration — Needle Thoractomy

• 1. Recognise it clinically. Say the findings out loud as you go.
  • 2. Position: supine, affected side up slightly if using the axillary approach.
  • 3. Aseptic skin preparation — fast, but done.
  • 4. Attach a 23–25G butterfly or cannula to a three-way tap and syringe BEFORE you puncture.
  • 5. Insert perpendicular, over the superior margin of the rib below.
  • 6. Advance while aspirating. Air rushes back — that is your confirmation.
  • 7. Aspirate until resistance. Do not over-evacuate.
  • 8. Withdraw the needle if using a butterfly; leave the cannula if you are bridging to a drain.
  • 9. Reassess: air entry, saturation, heart rate, chest movement. It should be immediate.
  • 10. Plan the chest tube. A needle is a bridge, not a treatment.
  • 11. Then get the X-ray.
Common Errors

• Waiting for the film in an unstable baby.
  • Going under the rib — into the bundle.
  • Puncturing before the three-way tap and syringe are attached.
  • Over-evacuating.
Treating the needle as definitive and not planning the drain

Facilitator Script “The needle bought you ten minutes. It is now minute nine. The needle is not a treatment — it is a bridge, and this is the other side of it.”
Competency

• Recognize indication of chest tube
  • Select correct tube size
  • Identify correct site for insertion
  • Insert tube at correct depth
  • Stepwise insertion technique
  • Connect drain correctly
  • Monitoring and complication recognition
Size and Site

WeightTube size
< 1000 g8 Fr
1000–2000 g8–10 Fr
> 2000 g10–12 Fr

• Site: 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line — in the ‘safe triangle’.
  • Air rises: direct the tube anteriorly and towards the apex.
  • Fluid falls: direct it posteriorly and basally.

Stay ANTERIOR to the mid-axillary line and stay AWAY from the nipple. The internal mammary vessels run just lateral to the sternum; the long thoracic nerve runs posteriorly. In a preterm the whole chest is the width of your palm.
Demonstration — chest tube insertion

• 1. Confirm the indication and select the tube size for the weight.
  • 2. Position: supine, arm abducted above the head, affected side up 30–45°.
  • 3. Full aseptic technique — cap, mask, gown, gloves, sterile drape.
  • 4. Local anaesthetic and analgesia. This baby feels this. Module (2) 7.1 applies here.
  • 5. Small skin incision, one space BELOW the target space.
  • 6. BLUNT dissection with mosquito forceps, over the superior margin of the rib below, until you feel the pleura give.
  • 7. Insert the tube WITHOUT the trocar, guided by the forceps. Direct it anteriorly for air.
  • 8. Advance to the pre-measured depth — all side holes inside the chest, and no further.
  • 9. Look for misting in the tube and bubbling in the drain.
  • 10. Connect to an underwater seal or a one-way valve drainage bag.
  • 11. Secure the tube with a suture and dressing. Do not kink it.
  • 12. Confirm the position with X-ray.
  • 13. Monitor: bubbling, swinging, output, and the baby.
Chest drains are NEVER clamped — including for transport. Use a one-way valve drainage bag rather than an underwater bottle if the baby is moving. Common Errors

• Using the trocar. It goes through the lung.
  • Sharp dissection instead of blunt.
  • Going under the rib.
  • Advancing too far — the tube ends up in the mediastinum or across the midline.
  • Not advancing far enough — a side hole outside the chest gives a surgical emphysema and no drainage.
  • Clamping for transport.
Forgetting the analgesia because the baby is sick.

Facilitator Script “Remember the golden hour rule: LP is not routine for early-onset sepsis screening. You do it when the blood culture is positive, when clinical suspicion is strong, or when the baby presents with seizures, apnoea or depressed sensorium. Not because the form has a box.”
Competency

• Recognize indication of LP
  • Position baby correctly
  • Identify correct site for insertion
  • Insert needle correctly
  • Stepwise insertion technique
  • Monitoring and complication recognition
Indications and Contraindications

Do it whenDo NOT do it when
Blood culture is positiveThe baby is haemodynamically unstable — stabilise first
Strong clinical suspicion of meningitisSigns of raised intracranial pressure
Seizures, apnoea or depressed sensoriumSevere respiratory compromise — the position will apnoea him
Bleeding diathesis / thrombocytopenia
Local skin infection over the site
It is not routine for early-onset sepsis screening. And an unstable baby does not get an LP — the antibiotics do not wait for the CSF. Position — This Is Where the Procedure Succeeds or Fails

• Lateral decubitus, or sitting.
  • Flex the hips and knees. Flex the spine.
  • Do NOT flex the neck. It obstructs the airway and does not open the interspaces.
  • The assistant holds the baby, watches the airway, and watches the monitor — not the needle.

The assistant is a clinical role, not a pair of hands. Neck flexion and over-flexion cause apnoea and desaturation during LP. Whoever holds the baby has one job: the airway. “Ninety per cent of failed taps are failed positions. If the back is not perpendicular to the bed and the spine is not flexed, do not put the needle in — fix the position first. You cannot rescue a bad position with a good needle.” The Landmark

• L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace — on the line joining the top of the iliac crests.
  • The neonatal cord ends lower than in an adult. Going higher risks the cord.
Demonstration — Lumber Puncture

• 1. Confirm the indication and exclude the contraindications out loud.
  • 2. Assign the assistant and brief them: airway and monitor.
  • 3. Position: lateral decubitus, hips and knees flexed, spine flexed, NECK NEUTRAL.
  • 4. Identify the interspace on the intercristal line.
  • 5. Sterile technique: gloves, drape, skin prep spirit → dry → iodine → dry → spirit.
  • 6. Analgesia — topical or local. Module (2) 7.1.
  • 7. Insert the needle in the midline, angled slightly towards the umbilicus, bevel up.
  • 8. Advance slowly. Remove the stylet frequently to check for CSF — the ‘give’ is often not felt in a newborn.
  • 9. Collect CSF into the tubes: cell count, protein/glucose, culture, and glucose to be paired with a blood glucose.
  • 10. Replace the stylet before withdrawing.
  • 11. Apply pressure and a dressing.
  • 12. Reassess the baby — saturation, heart rate, breathing.
Common Errors

• Flexing the neck — the commonest cause of desaturation on the table.
  • Starting with a bad position and hoping.
  • Not removing the stylet often enough — you have been in the CSF and gone straight through.
  • Going too high.
  • Doing it in an unstable baby.
Nobody watching the monitor.

Facilitator Script “Your admission orders say ‘monitor urine output hourly’. Good. Now tell me how. Urine output above 1.5 ml/kg/hour is one of your best signs that the shock is resolving — but only if you can actually measure it.”
Competency (from the guide)

• Recognize indication of urinary bladder catheter
  • Select correct catheter size
  • Insert catheter correctly
  • Stepwise insertion technique
  • Monitoring and complication recognition
Indications and Contraindications

IndicatedContraindicated
Accurate hourly urine output in the sick or shocked babySuspected urethral trauma
Urinary retentionBlood at the meatus
Sterile urine sample when suprapubic aspiration is not possibleKnown urethral anomaly — hypospadias, posterior urethral valves

Never force a catheter in a boy with hypospadias or blood at the meatus. A false passage in a neonatal urethra is a lifelong stricture.

WeightCatheter
