Demonstration — urinary bladder catheterization

• 1. Confirm the indication. Exclude the contraindications out loud.
  • 2. Position supine; frog-leg for girls.
  • 3. Sterile gloves. Clean the meatus outward in circles — different swab each time.
  • 4. Lubricate the catheter.
  • 5. Boys: hold the penis perpendicular, apply gentle traction to straighten the urethra. Advance gently. Slight resistance at the external sphincter is normal — pause, steady pressure, do not force.
  • 6. Girls: separate the labia, identify the meatus ABOVE the vaginal opening. If you enter the vagina, leave that catheter in place as a marker and use a fresh one for the urethra.
  • 7. Advance until urine flows, then 1–2 cm more — for a Foley, only inflate the balloon once urine is flowing.
  • 8. Never inflate a balloon against resistance.
  • 9. Secure the catheter to the thigh without tension. Keep the bag below bladder level.
  • 10. Monitor: output, blood, and signs of infection. Remove as soon as it is not needed.
Common Errors

• Forcing at the sphincter.
  • Inflating the balloon before urine flows — in the urethra.
  • In girls, entering the vagina and not noticing.
  • Leaving it in ‘because it is there’ — every day is a CAUTI risk.
Bag above the bladder.

Facilitator Script “This is the gold standard for a clean urine sample in a newborn — no urethra, no skin flora, no argument about contamination. It looks alarming. It is safer than the catheter.”
Competency

• Recognize indication of urinary bladder aspiration
  • Identify correct site of insertion
  • Insert needle correctly
  • Stepwise insertion technique
  • Monitoring and complication recognition
Indications and Contraindications

IndicatedContraindicated
Sterile urine sample for culture — the gold standardBladder empty — wait, or use ultrasound
Suspected UTI or sepsis workupBleeding diathesis / thrombocytopenia
Catheterisation failed or contraindicatedAbdominal distension, organomegaly, or bowel loops over the bladder
Local skin infection · known genitourinary anomaly · recent abdominal surgery

Timing is the whole procedure. At least one hour since the last void. If you have ultrasound, look first — an empty bladder is a dry tap and a needle in the bowel for nothing. If the baby voids while you are prepping, catch it and abandon.
The Site

• Midline, 1–2 cm ABOVE the symphysis pubis.
  • Needle perpendicular to the skin, or angled 10–20° towards the head.
  • Depth is shallow — the neonatal bladder is an abdominal organ, not a pelvic one.
Midline. Perpendicular. Shallow. Going lateral risks the iliac vessels; going deep risks the bowel.

sections.title: Suprapubic Bladder Aspiration: Demonstration — suprapubic aspiration

read.text: Demonstration — suprapubic aspiration

• 1. Confirm the indication; exclude contraindications; confirm at least an hour since the last void.
  • 2. An assistant holds the legs in the frog position and occludes the urethra gently — boys: hold the penis; girls: gentle pressure at the meatus.
  • 3. Sterile gloves. Prepare the skin: spirit → dry → iodine → dry → spirit.
  • 4. Analgesia — sucrose, non-nutritive sucking, or local. Module (2) 7.1.
  • 5. Identify the midline, 1–2 cm above the symphysis.
  • 6. Insert a 22–24G needle perpendicular, or angled slightly cephalad, WHILE ASPIRATING.
  • 7. Advance only 2–3 cm. Urine appears. Stop.
  • 8. Aspirate the sample slowly.
  • 9. Withdraw in one movement. Apply pressure and a dressing.
  • 10. Reassess. Look at the next nappy for blood — transient microscopic haematuria is common and self-limiting.
  • 11. If the tap is dry: do NOT redirect the needle inside the abdomen. Withdraw completely, wait 30–60 minutes, and try once more.
Common Errors

• Going too deep — through the bladder and into the bowel.
  • Going off the midline.
  • Not aspirating on the way in, so you pass through the bladder without knowing.
  • Fanning the needle around inside to ‘find’ the bladder.
  • Doing it on an empty bladder because nobody asked when he last voided.
Skipping analgesia because ‘it is quick’.

• Radiant Warmer

  • Pulse Oximeter
Facilitator Preparation

• Review SOPs and disinfection standards
  • Ensure equipment is functional, clean, and complete
  • Coordinate with neonatal unit staff
  • Prepare competency checklists and scoring sheets
  • Identify appropriate babies or simulation scenarios
Standard Demonstration Framework

• Indication for use
  • Equipment and baby preparation
  • Operation and correct settings
  • Monitoring and documentation
  • Safety considerations
  • Cleaning, disinfection, and storage
Taught in: Admission — preparation before receiving the baby

Facilitator Script “The phone has just rung. A 34-weeker is coming from theatre, ten minutes. What is the first thing you touch? — Not the trolley. This. Because it takes twenty minutes to prewarm and you have ten. Which means the honest answer is: you should have turned it on when the labour ward first called.”
Indications

• 1. Newborn resuscitation
  • 2. Short-term procedures
  • 3. Severe hypothermia requiring rapid warming

Infants with suspected perinatal asphyxia should NOT be placed under a radiant warmer or in an incubator — it puts them at risk of hyperthermia. Ask the group why that matters. The answer is the cooling protocol. Parts — Name Them on the Machine, Not on a Slide

• Bed / bassinet · overhead unit (radiant heat source) · skin probe · air probe
  • Control panel: mode selector · heater output control · heater output display · temperature selection · temperature display · alarm display
  • Storage tray · X-ray tray
Preparation — Two Lists, Both Checked

Machine preparationBaby preparation
Direct power sourceAlcohol-based hand rub
Temperature sensor (probe)Medical adhesive tape
Clean mattressA thermometer
Linen to cover the mattressPlastic wrap (if below 32 weeks GA)
Cotton swabs with 70% alcoholItems for the specific procedure
• Room temperature must be ≥ 22°C for the warmer to function optimally.
Standard Operating procedure for Warmer

• 1. Turn the warmer on 20 minutes BEFORE the baby, to prewarm the linen and mattress.
  • 2. Ensure the mattress and linen are clean.
  • 3. Select the mode.
  • 4. Set the target temperature to 36.5–37.0°C.
  • 5. Apply the probe over the RIGHT HYPOCHONDRIUM in supine position, or the FLANK in prone position.
  • 6. Connect the skin probe to the abdomen with sticking tape. Cover with a reflective pad if available.
  • 7. Check the probe is in place every 2–3 hours.
  • 8. Check and record the temperature every 2–3 hours.
  • 9. Change the probe site every 24 hours.
The Two Modes — Teach the Difference or the Rest Is Meaningless

MANUALSERVO
Heater outputYou increase or decrease itAutomatic, based on skin temperature
Used forInitial preparation of the bed; rapid warming of a severely hypothermic babyOnce the baby is 36.5–37.5°C — switch to servo
MonitoringAxillary temperature at 30 minutes, then 2-hourlyAlarm activates at 0.5°C above set temperature
The dangerThe baby cooks if you walk awayProbe displacement — or a febrile baby, where servo turns the heater OFF and you miss it
RuleNEVER leave a baby unattended in manual modeProbe must be well secured
ONE radiant warmer, ONE baby. Two babies under one heater means the heater is centred on neither of them.
Common Errors

• Turning it on when the baby arrives — twenty minutes too late.
  • Leaving a baby unattended in manual mode.
  • Probe on bruised skin, or removed with a fingernail.
  • Probe taped to the mattress, not the baby — the heater runs forever.
  • Never switching from manual to servo once the baby is warm.
  • Forgetting the extra fluid a warmer costs.
  • Using spirit or an organic solvent to clean it.

• External surfaces: cleaned DAILY with light detergent or soap, then chlorine solution or glutaraldehyde.
  • Reusable probe: isopropyl alcohol swab.
  • After use: clean, disinfect, and cover with a linen cover to store properly.
  • Self-maintenance: inspect the heating element weekly. Calibrate control and power units every 4–6 months. Thorough servicing annually.
NO SPIRIT. NO ORGANIC SOLVENT on the external surfaces. It degrades the housing. The alcohol swab is for the probe only.
Taught in: Transport — methods of transport

Facilitator Script “Your baby is 35.8°C. The referral hospital is 45 minutes away. You have no transport incubator, and the ambulance has no power. Everything you learned about the radiant warmer is now useless — it needs a wall socket and it is bolted to that room. This device needs neither.”
This is the one device on this list built for exactly the constraints Module (1) names: no organised transport, no power, families with no resources. Teach it that way.
How It Works — Explain the Wax, or Nobody Trusts It

PartWhat it does
WarmPakContains a wax that MELTS at 37°C and releases heat as it SOLIDIFIES — maintaining the baby's temperature for 4–6 hours
AccuTemp HeaterA small electric heater to prepare the WarmPak
BabyWrapThe sleeping-bag-like garment that holds the WarmPak and the baby

“The wax cannot go above 37 degrees — that is the physics, not a setting. It cannot burn him. That is why this device is safe in a vehicle where nobody is watching a dial.” Standard operating procedure portable warmer

• 1. Wash hands. Ensure the BabyWrap is clean and disinfected.
  • 2. Plug the AccuTemp Heater into the power source and put the WarmPak inside the heater for 30 MINUTES.
  • 3. Once warm, place the warmed WarmPak inside the pouch in the BabyWrap.
  • 4. Place the infant in the BabyWrap.
  • 5. Use the RAINBOW SIGN to monitor the target temperature.
  • 6. After use, clean the BabyWrap and the AccuTemp Heater.
Thirty minutes to charge, 4–6 hours of warmth. Ask the group: when do you start heating the WarmPak? Same answer as the radiant warmer — when the phone rings, not when the baby is at the door.
The Rainbow Indicator

• It is the only monitor this device has. Teach the participant to read it and to say out loud what it means.
  • It does not replace a thermometer. Check the baby's axillary temperature as well — the rainbow tells you about the pak, the thermometer tells you about the baby.
Common Errors

• Not allowing the full 30 minutes — a half-charged pak does not last the journey.
  • Using a BabyWrap that was not cleaned between babies.
  • Reading the rainbow and never touching the baby.
  • Assuming it replaces skin-to-skin. For a stable baby, the mother is still better.

• AccuTemp Heater: disinfect with an appropriate solution (spirit or chlorine-based) BEFORE EACH USE, by wiping the device surface.
  • WarmPak: has no direct contact with the neonate. Clean whenever needed — wipe with a towel immersed in soap and water, then wipe with an appropriate disinfectant.
  • BabyWrap: clean with soap and water BETWEEN PATIENTS.
  • Blood exposure: chlorine-based solution 0.05% for 20 minutes only, then wash thoroughly in distilled water and dry.
Taught in: Golden Hour — prevention of hypothermia; revisited in Prematurity — thermal protection

Facilitator Script “This machine is the difference between a 900-gram baby surviving the week and not. And the commonest way it fails is not a fault — it is two people opening both sides at once to change a nappy.”
Who Goes In One

• ALL preterm infants ≤ 30 weeks gestation and/or ≤ 1000 g should be nursed in incubators.
  • Incubators are the admission bed of choice for all babies born < 33 weeks or ≤ 1800 g.
  • Some babies ≥ 33 weeks may need one if hypothermic on admission.
  • Term and near-term infants may be swaddled and nursed in a cot if stable.
  • For those requiring respiratory care, an open care system should be used.
Infants with suspected perinatal asphyxia should NOT be placed in an incubator — it puts them at risk of hyperthermia. Why the Double Wall, and Why One Side at a Time

• Incubators are fully enclosed cots that add heated air and humidity while reducing stimuli including light and sound.
  • They are DOUBLE WALLED to reduce radiant and conductive heat loss.
  • They are efficient when ONE side is opened for cares or procedures — but NOT when both sides are opened together, which causes high convective and evaporative heat loss.

Demonstrate this. Open one side, then open both. Ask the group what just happened to the air inside. This single habit costs nothing and is one of the five interventions the manual lists as proven to reduce hypothermia in very preterm infants. Standard Operating Procedure — Infant Incubator

• 1. Ensure the incubator is clean and disinfected before use.
  • 2. Connect to a reliable power source; ensure the power cable is intact.
  • 3. Switch on using the main power button.
  • 4. Select the mode — servo or manual.
  • 5. Attach the skin temperature probe to the abdomen or back. Change the probe site every 8–12 hours.
  • 6. Ensure the water reservoir is filled with STERILE or DISTILLED water.
  • 7. Adjust the humidity.
  • 8. Then: minimise the time doors on OPPOSITE sides are open during procedures and cares.
The Settings — The Numbers Your Checklist Assumes

ModeSetting
SERVO (skin control)Set the temperature to 36.5–37°C. The manual's Golden Hour section specifies servo targeting an abdominal skin temperature of 36.5°C
MANUAL (air mode) — extremely preterm < 28 wks34–36°C
MANUAL — very preterm 28–32 wks33–34°C
MANUAL — near- term / term32–33°C

Servo and manual are set differently and this confuses everyone. In SERVO you set the temperature you want the BABY to be (36.5–37°C) and the incubator works out its own. In MANUAL you set the temperature you want the AIR to be (32–36°C by gestation). Setting a servo incubator to 34°C, or a manual one to 36.5°C, are both dangerous errors.
Humidity

BabyHumidity
Usual start40–70%, depending on weight and condition
ELBW / VLBW (< 1500 g), first week70–90%
After 1 weekGradually reduce to 40–50%

• Water reservoir: sterile or distilled water only, changed DAILY.
  • Any baby requiring humidity should NOT be dressed or covered by fabrics.
“Humidity is not comfort. In a 900-gram baby the skin is not a barrier — water pours out of it. Ninety per cent humidity in week one is a fluid prescription.”
Common Errors

• Both doors open at once.
  • Confusing servo and manual set-points.
  • Tap water in the reservoir.
  • Reservoir water not changed daily — it becomes a bacterial nebuliser.
  • Probe loose or detached in servo mode.
  • Dressing a baby who is in humidity.
  • An asphyxiated baby in an incubator.
The Schedule

PartFrequency
Frequent touch points — door handles and latches3 times per day
Water reservoir for humidification (always sterile water)Change the water daily
IV pole · hood external surfaceDaily
Mattress sheets and incubator coverDaily, or if stained with blood
Inner double wallWeekly
Water reservoir, heater impeller cover, duct cover assemblyWeekly
Gasket, grommets, hand ports, access panel, locking button, sensor module openingWeekly
Mattress, trays, cover, scale, T bars, temperature probesWeekly
Incubator trolley and shell — heater well, controller, shell, trolleyWeekly (proper disassembly first)
Heater radiator and fan impellerWeekly — DO NOT immerse the heater assembly in liquid
Air inlet filter chamber and coverEvery 3 months, or after use on an infected baby — do NOT attempt to clean the filter itself
• Incubators should be COVERED after cleaning and when not in use. Store in a dedicated place, away from contamination sources such as splashes from sinks.
Taught in: Prematurity — RDS session
Facilitator Script “Twenty-nine weeks, 1.2 kg, grunting, saturation 86. You have no ventilator and no surfactant.
Yesterday you would have called that hopeless. The evidence says early CPAP reduces death, reduces BPD, reduces intubation — and reduces the NEED for the surfactant you do not have.
This machine is not second best. It is first line.”
The Prerequisite — Say It Before Anything Else

The most important prerequisite for starting CPAP is the PRESENCE OF GOOD RESPIRATORY EFFORT. CPAP splints an airway; it does not breathe for a baby. A baby with poor respiratory effort needs PPV, not CPAP.
Indications and Contraindications

IndicatedContraindicated
Spontaneously breathing preterm with respiratory distressPoor respiratory effort
Recurrent apnoea not responding to medical measuresTracheo-oesophageal fistula
Post-extubation from mechanical ventilationChoanal atresia
Term babies with respiratory distress or low lung volumeCleft palate
Very preterm (< 32 weeks) immediately after birth, with or without distressSevere cardiovascular instability
pH < 7.25 and PaCO₂ > 60 mmHg — progressive respiratory failure

sections.title: Bubble CPAP: Standard Operating Procedure — Portable CPAP

read.text: Standard Operating Procedure — Portable CPAP

• 1. Ensure all components are clean and disinfected.
  • 2. Assemble the system according to manufacturer guidance; ensure correct connections.
  • 3. Fit the cap — covering up to the ears, ears lying FLAT under it. A cap that is too small causes oedema and discomfort.
  • 4. Select the prong size by birth weight (table below). Moisten the prongs with saline before insertion.
  • 5. Secure the prongs. The bridge of the prongs must NOT abut the columella and must NOT blanch the skin.
  • 6. Connect the prongs to the circuit. Stabilise the head so the prongs do not dislodge.
  • 7. INSERT AN OROGASTRIC TUBE. CPAP inflates the stomach.
  • 8. Set the pressure, FiO₂ and flow.
  • 9. Ensure CONTINUOUS BUBBLING at all times.
  • 10. Monitor the devices and the patient.
  • 11. Confirm the oxygen cylinder pressure regularly.
Prong Size by Birth Weight

SizeBirth weightSizeBirth weight
0< 700 g32000–3000 g
1700–1000 g43000–4000 g
1000–2000 g5> 4000 g

The best-fitting prong is the BIGGEST that comfortably fits the nostril without distending it. Too tight causes pressure necrosis; too loose causes a large air leak and no CPAP. Periodically check the nasal mucosa for hyperaemia and the columella for blanching. Device Monitoring — The Housekeeping That Keeps It Working

• Refill the humidifier BEFORE water drops below the ‘REFILL’ line.
  • Refill the pressure generator when water drops below the ‘fill mark’.
  • Replace water in jars every 24 hours.
  • Replace the filter disk every 24 hours — earlier if discoloured, or after each patient.
No bubbling = no CPAP. If the bubbling stops, the baby is receiving nothing but expensive humidified air, and the only sign is on the machine, not on the baby — until he tires. Common Errors

• Starting CPAP on a baby with poor respiratory effort.
  • Prongs too small — a leak, and no pressure.
  • Prongs too big — pressure necrosis of the columella.
  • No orogastric tube — the abdomen distends and splints the diaphragm.
  • Not noticing the bubbling has stopped.
  • Waiting for an X-ray before increasing the pressure on a grunting baby.
  • Water jars and filter not changed at 24 hours.

• Empty the jars, remove any gross soiling, then FULLY disassemble the device.
  • Soak in clean water until ready to reprocess.
  • Clean with enzymatic detergent or dish soap, using a soft-bristled brush or sponge.
  • Brush lumens AND flush lumens THREE TIMES.
  • Rinse all components.
  • High-level disinfection — flushing each lumen with disinfectant at least THREE TIMES.
  • Air dry completely before storage.
Do NOT autoclave or boil components.
Taught in: Golden Hour — respiration

Facilitator Script “This is the smallest device on the list and the only one that tells you the dose of a drug. Oxygen is a drug. It is the drug that causes ROP. This machine is how you prescribe it — and ‘100% because he looks blue’ is not a prescription.”
Indications

• All sick newborns — oxygen saturation as the FIFTH vital parameter
  • Assessment of response to resuscitation
  • Titration of oxygen therapy in newborns
  • Apnoea monitor
  • Valuable during transport of the newborn
The Targets — The Numbers Your Checklist Assumes

BabyTarget SpO₂
Usually85–95%
Preterm89–95%
< 29 weeks85–92%
Module (1) ruleGive oxygen below SaO₂ 85%; gradually withdraw above 92%
NeverPersistent value > 95%

Avoid persistent values above 95%. In the preterm baby, a saturation of 99% is not a good result — it is a retina being damaged, and it is your fault, not the disease's. “Every ROP risk factor in the manual is something you control on this ward: hypoxia, hypothermia, hypotension, sepsis, poor weight gain. This machine is the one that controls the first one — in both directions.”
Standard Operating Procedure — Pulse Oximeter

• 1. Clean the probe with spirit / alcohol and let it dry.
  • 2. Switch on the pulse oximeter.
  • 3. Apply the probe to a site that is WARM and WELL PERFUSED.
  • 4. Ensure both sides of the probe are DIRECTLY OPPOSITE each other.
  • 5. Secure the probe in place.
  • 6. Set high and low alarm limits for saturation and heart rate — 2% above and below the desired limit.
  • 7. Observe and CHANGE THE SITE every 6–8 hours if applied continuously.
  • 8. Record the reading every 2 hours.
  • 9. After use, switch it off, clean the probe with spirit, and keep it covered.

Pre-ductal means the RIGHT hand. Teach this alongside the Golden Hour targeted saturation table — a post-ductal reading in the first minutes of life is a different number and a different decision. When It Does Not Work — The Row Your Checklist Calls ‘Identifies Limitations’

• 10. Hypovolaemic states or low perfusion states.
  • 11. Dyshaemoglobinaemias — carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin.
  • 12. Optical interference from external light sources — phototherapy unit, fluorescent light, sunlight.

Read that first one again. The shocked baby is exactly the baby whose oximeter lies to you — and exactly the baby you most want to believe it. In shock, trust the capillary refill and the pulses, not the number. Complications
• Pressure necrosis on prolonged contact — which is what the 6–8 hourly site change prevents.
Common Errors

• Probe on a cold, poorly perfused foot, then treating the low number as real.
  • Emitter and detector not directly opposite — a plausible but wrong number.
  • Probe under a phototherapy light with no cover.
  • Alarms not set, or set so wide they never sound.
  • Site not changed — pressure necrosis.
  • Accepting 99% in a preterm baby as good news.
  • Believing it in a shocked baby.
Pulse Oximeter — Disinfection

• Clean with a spirit swab and let it dry BEFORE and AFTER any use.
  • Clean the probe with a spirit swab and let it dry before using on another baby.
  • After use: switch it off, clean the probe, keep it covered if not required for any baby.

read.text: Facilitator approach:

• Use interactive questioning before reading goals.
  • Ask: “What types of preventable harm have you seen in newborn units?” “What makes newborns especially vulnerable?”

Allow 5–10 minutes discussion before formally reviewing the stated goals. Emphasize throughout that patient safety in neonatal care is proactive, systematic, and team-based. Definition, Importance, Objectives

Facilitator Script “Every other session on this course is about a sick baby. This one is about the system around the baby — the labels, the checks, the handovers. It is the least dramatic session on the course and it prevents some of the worst harm, because the harm here is harm WE cause, on top of the illness.”
Goals

Open with the two questions from your draft before reading anything: ‘what preventable harm have you seen in newborn units?’ and ‘what makes newborns especially vulnerable?’ Allow 5–10 minutes. THEN read the goals, unchanged:

• 1. Improve the accuracy of patient identification.
  • 2. Improve the effectiveness of communication among caregivers.
  • 3. Improve the safety of using medication.

Definition Patient safety is defined as freedom from accidental injury. Ensuring patient safety involves the establishment of operational systems and processes that minimise the likelihood of errors and maximise the likelihood of intercepting them when they occur. Then explain WHY neonatal care carries higher risk — the three reasons from your draft:

• Weight-based dosing — every dose is a fresh calculation that changes as the baby grows
  • Rapid deterioration — small errors become life-threatening quickly
  • Invasive procedures

“Read the definition again — it has two halves. Minimise the likelihood of errors, AND maximise the likelihood of INTERCEPTING them. That second half is the whole session. We will never stop all errors. We can build a unit that catches them before they reach the baby.” Importance According to the WHO, medical errors affect 1 IN 10 PATIENTS globally, with consequences including death, lasting or temporary harm, financial setbacks, and psychosocial distress for the patient and sometimes the caregiver.
• The distinctive, complicated SCNU environment plus the heightened vulnerability of newborns amplifies the likelihood of error.

Landmarks: the IOM report of 1999; the IOM 2001 report — care should be effective, evidence-based, patient-centred, timely, efficient and equitable, and patients should not be harmed by the care they receive.
Case Scenario
A 1.5 kg preterm baby received 10 TIMES the intended antibiotic dose, due to a decimal error.
Ask: where did the system fail? What could have prevented it?
ANSWER KEY

Answer key — the layers that should have caught it: the prescriber's calculation (three-quarters of neonatal medication errors occur at the PRESCRIBING stage); the pre-administration routine; the independent double-check by a second person; a unit formulary or emergency dose sheet listing the correct dose by weight; adequate lighting and freedom from interruption at the point of preparation. A tenfold decimal error passes only when ALL of these are missing or skipped at once.

This scenario is the Swiss-cheese model in miniature, and it returns at Topic 10. Plant it here; harvest it there. Do not let the group settle on ‘the nurse was careless’ — the manual is explicit that individual blame is insufficient.

Facilitator Script “Newborns are the easiest patients in the hospital to mix up. Same birth date, similar file numbers, identical surnames, no way to tell you their name, and often a twin in the next cot.
Everything that lets an adult confirm their own identity is missing. That is why this is Goal number one.”
Why Newborns Are High-Risk

• Born with similar birth dates and similar medical record numbers
  • Multiples with identical surnames, hospitalised at the same time
  • Unable to talk to confirm identity
  • Lack the distinguishing physical characteristics adults have
Real errors that have resulted from misidentification:

• Two vaccines given to the same infant
  • The wrong infant circumcised
  • A mother's expressed breast milk fed to the wrong newborn
  • A breastfed infant given formula, or a mother breastfeeding the wrong infant
Misidentification causes 11–25% of reported adverse events involving medication in the SCNU. This is not a rare, theoretical risk — it is up to a quarter of the serious medication events. The Rules

• 1. Use at LEAST TWO patient identifiers when providing any care, treatment or service.
  • 2. Distinct naming systems — mother's first and last name plus the newborn's gender: ‘Smith, Judy Girl’; for multiples ‘Smith, Judy Girl A’ and ‘Smith, Judy Girl B’.
  • 3. Standardized banding — two body-site identification, barcoding, and the medical record number on BOTH bands.
  • 4. Communication tools — signage alerting staff to newborns with similar names.

Use a wrist or foot band ONLY if it is attached to the patient. DO NOT use the bed number, or a band attached to the bed or cot. If a parent is present, ask them for the child's first and last name. Match name, date of birth, and file number on the lab form to the patient before taking blood.
Skill Station
CASE-BASED DISCUSSION
Scenario: twins in SCBU — Baby A 2.3 kg, Baby B 1.9 kg. The participant must confirm identity using two identifiers, check the medication chart, and administer to the correct baby.
The facilitator watches for exactly this:

The participant shouldFail the station if they
Verify the name on the bandIdentify the baby by which cot they are in
Check the hospital / file number — a SECOND identifierUse only one identifier
Confirm the number matches the chart AND the bandRead the chart but never check the band
Confirm the dose is for THIS baby's weightAssume A and B are interchangeable

The single error to catch, from your draft: assuming identity based on INCUBATOR LOCATION. Babies get moved. The band moves with the baby; the cot does not. Anyone who reaches for the baby without reading the band has failed — whatever else they do correctly.

Facilitator Script “Communication failures are one of the leading causes of accidental patient harm. Not knowledge failures — communication failures. The doctor knew, the nurse knew, but the message between them dropped a word, or was never read back. Getting everyone on the same page has been shown to reduce adverse events.”

• The plan of care must be actively WRITTEN.
  • Care providers must READ BACK verbal medical orders for verification — closed-loop.
  • All written orders must use standard acronyms and abbreviations agreed across the organisation.

Verbal and telephone orders must be read back to the person who gave them. ‘Closed-loop’ means the order is not complete until the giver has heard it repeated and confirmed it. An order that is not read back is an error waiting for a witness.
Huddles and Handovers

• Huddles enhance communication and safety — they plan and coordinate anticipated deliveries, discharges, transfers, surgeries, and diagnostic testing.
  • A main morning meeting before rounds (nurse manager, charge nurses, discharge coordinator, nurse practitioners, attending neonatologists, fellow, transport team, lead respiratory therapist, social worker), and an evening meeting for overnight issues.
  • Communication with parents; incident reporting.
  • A rounding script for nurses — an outline for patient presentations and a shift-to-shift bedside handoff tool.
SBAR — Teach It, Then Drill It

LetterContent
S — SituationWho you are, which baby, and the problem in one sentence
B — BackgroundThe relevant history — gestation, day of life, diagnosis, current support
A — AssessmentWhat you think is going on, and how sick the baby is right now
R —What you want to happen, and how soon
Recommendation
Role Play: Handle handover
Scenario: a night nurse calls the doctor about a baby with RR 80/min, grunting, SpO₂ 86% on room air.
Model SBAR — What Good Sounds Like

S: ‘This is [name], the nurse in SCBU. I'm calling about Baby Fatima A — she has sudden respiratory distress and I need you to come.’ B: ‘She's a 34-week baby, day 1, was stable on room air until 20 minutes ago.’ A: ‘Now her respiratory rate is 80, she's grunting, and her saturation is 86% in room air. I think she's in respiratory distress and needs support now.’ R: ‘I've started oxygen and put her on the monitor. I need you to come and assess for CPAP within the next few minutes — can you come now?’
Debrief against four questions:

• Was the situation clearly stated?
  • Was background included?
  • Was the assessment clear?
  • Was a recommendation made — with a timeframe?

The commonest failure: the nurse lists numbers but never says what they WANT. ‘Her sats are 86’ is a fact; ‘I need you here in five minutes to assess for CPAP’ is a recommendation. Drill the R — it is the letter people drop under stress.

Facilitator Script “Medication is where this unit most often hurts a baby by accident. The dose changes every time the baby gains weight, the margin for error is tiny, and the contents of a needle hub alone can overdose a premature baby. This is the highest-yield twenty minutes of the whole safety session.”.
Why Medication Is the Sharp End

• Errors occur MOSTLY in premature infants under 1500 g — they need the most pharmacological support.
  • Enteral nutrition and medication errors account for 13.3% of potentially harmful SCNU errors.
  • Three-quarters of neonatal medication errors occur at the PRESCRIBING stage.
  • The contents of the DEAD SPACE in a needle hub and syringe may be enough to overdose a premature neonate.
  • The three environmental factors: under-illumination of the preparation area, distractions, and interruptions while handling medications.
Every prescription needs a specific calculation, and it must CHANGE as the newborn gains weight. Yesterday's correct dose is today's error. Re-calculate against today's weight, every time
The Preadministration Process

• 1. A routine preadministration process before giving ANY medication.
  • 2. Double-check — right PATIENT, right DRUG, right DOSE, right TIME, right ROUTE — before administration.
  • 3. Replace concentrated stock with a single-dose system.
  • 4. Increase the number of personnel who must check for accuracy.
  • 5. Clinical pharmacists monitoring orders; a SCNU-specific formulary; emergency dose sheets listing calculated doses by weight.

The manual's paradox, worth teaching out loud: increasing the number of checkers helps — UNLESS each assumes someone else has already checked. A double-check where the second person rubber-stamps the first is not a double-check. It must be INDEPENDENT.
Practical — Calculation and the Independent Double-Check
Worked example (from your draft): Baby weight 1.8 kg, antibiotic 50 mg/kg.
The facilitator watches, per your draft, for:

• Decimal placement — 50 × 1.8 = 90 mg, not 900 mg and not 9 mg
  • Unit conversion — mg vs mL after dilution
  • Dilution calculation — the concentration in the syringe, and the volume to draw How to Run the Double-Check
  • 1. Participant 1 calculates the dose and prepares it — working alone.
  • 2. Participant 2 calculates INDEPENDENTLY, without seeing the first answer, then compares.
  • 3. They reconcile any difference before ‘administration’ — and the discrepancy, if any, is the teaching moment.
  • 4. Document after administration — not before.

Make participant 2 turn away and calculate from the order and the weight, THEN compare. If they just glance at participant 1's number and nod, stop the exercise and explain why that nod is exactly the failure the manual warns about.

Facilitator Script “Alarms exist to save babies, and they harm them in two opposite ways. Set wrong, they miss the sick baby. Set to shriek at everything, they train you to ignore them — and one day the alarm you silence is real. Alarm fatigue is a patient safety problem, not a nuisance problem.”
The Two Rules

• 1. Alarm settings must be APPROPRIATE — set to the individual baby, not left on a default.
  • 2. NEVER silence an alarm without ASSESSING the baby first.

Silencing before assessing is the cardinal alarm error. The alarm is a question about the baby — ‘is he alright?’ — and the only valid way to answer it is to look at the baby, not to press the button.
Bedside Simulation (from your draft) — With Answer Key
Scenario: the monitor alarms HR 85/min in a TERM baby.
The participant must:

• 3. ASSESS the baby — colour, tone, breathing, activity — first.
  • 4. Check the leads and the probe — is this real, or a signal artefact?
  • 5. Interpret clinically.
ANSWER KEY

The reasoning: HR 85 in a TERM baby is below the usual range — but a well, pink, active term baby with a good trace may simply have a low resting or sleeping heart rate, OR this may be a genuine bradycardia. You cannot tell from the number. Assess the baby AND confirm the signal is real (lead contact, probe position) BEFORE acting. The wrong answer is to silence it; the other wrong answer is to treat a number without looking at the baby.

Discuss alarm fatigue explicitly: on a busy unit where every alarm is a false alarm, staff learn not to respond — and that learned deafness is what kills the baby whose alarm was real. Appropriate limits per baby are how you keep alarms meaningful.

This topic is taught in FULL in the Neonatal Sepsis — Surveillance, Prevention and Stewardship session (Module 2, Section 10). Do not duplicate it here. Here it is framed as a patient-safety goal; there it is practised as skill stations.
The Patient-Safety Framing

• Ask (from your draft): where are infection risks highest in your unit? Which procedures carry the highest risk?
  • In small groups, walk through: hand hygiene demonstration; equipment handling; invasive line insertion preparation.

“Every healthcare-associated infection is, by definition, harm we caused. That is why it sits inside patient safety and not only inside sepsis. The hand you do not wash is a patient-safety failure before it is ever a microbiology result.” For the full technique, scored checklists (hand hygiene, blood culture, stewardship) and the four skill stations, use the Section 10 guide.

sections.title: Medical Errors and the Swiss-Cheese Model

read.text: Facilitator Script “The most important idea in this whole session is this: serious harm is almost never one person's mistake. It is several small holes, in several defences, lining up on the same day. Which means the fix is never just ‘be more careful.’ The fix is building more layers, so the holes stop lining up.”
The Model

• Errors result from MULTIPLE system failures, not a single act.
  • Individual blame is insufficient — and it is actively harmful, because it stops you finding the other holes.
  • Each defence is a slice of cheese with holes; harm occurs only when the holes in every slice line up and a hazard passes straight through.

Draw it: several slices, each with holes in different places. Most days, a hole in one slice is blocked by the solid part of the next. Harm happens on the rare day the holes align. Every check in this session — two identifiers, read-back, the independent double-check — is one more slice.
Group Exercise
Case: a preterm infant received the wrong IV fluid concentration.
Participants identify the holes. Your draft names four — here is what each looks like and which slice it belongs to:

The holeThe defence that failed
Communication breakdownThe plan of care was not clearly written or read back — the order itself was ambiguous (Topic 6)
Labelling issueThe fluid bag or syringe was not labelled clearly, or looked like another — no barrier to picking the wrong one (Topics 5 & 7)

The holeThe defence that failed
Lack of double-checkNo independent second person verified the concentration before it ran (Topic 7)
Staffing issueToo few staff, or too rushed — the interruptions and distractions the manual names as error factors (Topic 7)

The conclusion to reach: no single one of these caused the harm. Any ONE slice, intact, would have stopped it — a clear label, or a real double-check, or a written order, or a less rushed nurse. The harm required ALL of them to fail together. So the improvement plan has four items, not one, and none of them is ‘the nurse should be more careful.’ Link this back to the tenfold-dose scenario from Topic 3 — same structure, different holes. When the group sees that both cases are the same shape, the model has landed.
Critical Incident Analysis

• When an event happens, conduct a thorough examination based on DATA and FACT, not assumption.
  • Disseminate the lessons — an incident analysed and not shared has no preventive value.
“The purpose of looking at an error is never to find who to blame. It is to find which slice to thicken, so the next baby is caught by a layer that was missing this time.”

read.text: This chapter builds on the CPAP equipment SOP (taught in the Prematurity — RDS session and detailed in the Equipment volume). Here the device becomes a decision: who needs NIV, which mode, what settings, how to read the response, and when it has failed. Learning Objectives

• 1. Identify respiratory disorders requiring non-invasive ventilation (NIV).
  • 2. Explore non-invasive ventilation options and consider the pros and cons.
  • 3. Explore monitoring and assessment strategies for neonates on NIV.
And, added for competence:

• 4. Initiate CPAP safely at the correct starting settings.
  • 5. Adjust CPAP and FiO₂ using the traffic-light protocol.
  • 6. Recognise NIV failure early and escalate.
  • 7. Prevent and stage nasal injury.
  • 8. Wean and remove CPAP by protocol.
Materials

• CPAP machine (bubble / Vayu) and HFNC circuit · manikin or doll · caps/bonnets in several sizes
  • Nasal prongs in all sizes · transparent measuring tape · granuflex / barrier dressing · saline
  • Pulse oximeter · blender · humidifier · orogastric tubes · blood-gas access if available
  • Monitoring charts · the traffic-light protocol poster · nasal-injury staging photos · copies of all checklists

sections.title: Recognising the Baby Who Needs NIV

read.text: Why NIV, and Why It Replaced the Ventilator Over the past few decades, invasive mechanical ventilation has been replaced by NIV, because invasive ventilation is associated with major morbidities: bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), pulmonary hypertension, increased susceptibility to respiratory infection, neurodevelopmental impairment, and cerebral palsy. Definition: NIV refers to any method of providing respiratory support where an endotracheal tube is NOT used. “Every day a baby spends on a ventilator is a day their lungs are being injured to keep them alive. NIV is how we support breathing without paying that price. The whole of this chapter is about staying on the near side of the tube.”
Scenario 1 — The Baby Who Is Tiring
A preterm baby with respiratory distress. Increasing oxygen has been tried. The baby is now working hard to breathe.
Facilitator questions:

• What signs suggest respiratory FAILURE, not just distress?
  • Is oxygen alone sufficient?
  • What is the next appropriate intervention?
Expected Participant Reasoning

• Persistent hypoxia despite oxygen
  • High respiratory rate with severe work of breathing
  • Prematurity + RDS risk
  • Baby tiring → impending failure
Correct Action — Facilitator Emphasises Start CPAP IMMEDIATELY. Do NOT wait for further deterioration. Do NOT increase oxygen blindly.
Key Teaching Points

• RR > 70 + retractions + poor response to oxygen = NIV indicated.
  • Early CPAP prevents intubation.
  • Delayed action worsens outcomes.
Common Errors to Correct

• Increasing oxygen flow repeatedly
  • Waiting for consultant review
  • No baseline documentation before NIV

FACILITATOR HINT the trap in this scenario is that raising the oxygen LOOKS like doing something. Saturation may even nudge up for a while. Meanwhile the work of breathing is unchanged and the baby is tiring toward apnoea. Oxygen treats the number; CPAP treats the breathing. Say that out loud.
Indications for NIV

1. Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)6. Apnoea of prematurity — CPAP is the standard
2. Transient Tachypnoea of Newborn (TTN)7. Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH)
3. Meconium Aspiration Syndrome (MAS)8. Post-operative support
4. Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension (PPHN)9. Neuromuscular disorders affecting respiratory muscles
5. Bronchiolitis (often RSV)10. Tailor the choice of method and settings to the clinical need

sections.title: Recognising the Baby Who Needs NIV: Contraindications — When NIV Is the Wrong Answer

read.text: Contraindications — When NIV Is the Wrong Answer

• 1. Severe respiratory distress, especially with cardiovascular instability — invasive ventilation may be required.
  • 2. Haemodynamic instability — positive pressure can affect cardiac function.
  • 3. Severe air leak syndrome — pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum; NIV could worsen it.
  • 4. Facial abnormalities preventing a proper seal or interface placement.
  • 5. Unstable neurological status — may not tolerate treatment.
  • 6. Upper airway obstruction.
  • 7. Gastrointestinal conditions — abdominal wall anomalies or massive distension.
  • 8. Inability to protect the airway.
  • 9. Uncooperative neonate — extreme agitation or non-compliance.

The manual's rule: always consult the neonatal specialist / senior, and consider the individual patient's clinical status — contraindications can vary. NIV is not for the baby who is already too sick for it.

FACILITATOR HINT hold contraindication 3 up next to Scenario 4 (later today). A tension pneumothorax is BOTH a reason NIV can fail AND a reason it should never have been pushed harder. The same finding appears in both places — that is not a coincidence, it is the lesson.

Facilitator Script “There are six names on this list and they frighten people. But they are only three ideas: flow with no reliable pressure (HFNC), one pressure (CPAP), and two pressures (everything else).
Learn the three ideas and the six names sort themselves out.”
The Modalities — One Table

ModePressure levelsWhat it is
HFNCVariable, unreliableHeated humidified high flow, 2–8 L/min via loose nasal prongs. Washes out dead space, reduces work of breathing. Pressure NOT reliably measurable
CPAPONE (PEEP)Constant distending pressure throughout inspiration and expiration. The workhorse of neonatal NIV
NIPPVTWO (PIP + PEEP)CPAP with superimposed inflations to a set PIP, via a ventilator. May be synchronized. Used when CPAP is failing
BiPAPTWO (lower)High and low pressures differing by no more than 3–4 cmH₂O; longer Ti (0.5–1 s); rates 10–30/min. Often considered the same as NIPPV
nHFOVOscillatorySmall tidal volumes at supraphysiological rates for better CO₂ elimination. Infrequently used; needs further evaluation
The Evidence — What to Teach, and What Not to Overstate

ComparisonWhat the evidence says (as written in the manual)
Early CPAP vs mechanical ventilationProphylactic or very early CPAP reduced BPD, the combined outcome of death or BPD, and mechanical ventilation
NIPPV vs CPAPEarly NIPPV reduced respiratory failure, the need for intubation, treatment failure and mechanical ventilation — without increasing complications (Cochrane)
HFNC as PRIMARY supportNo significant difference vs CPAP in most outcomes EXCEPT a HIGHER treatment failure rate. Decreased nasal injury. No robust evidence in extreme low gestational age
HFNC post- extubationNo significant difference vs CPAP in extubation failure. Decreased nasal injury

The one line to make participants remember: HFNC is gentler on the nose but fails more often as PRIMARY support, and the pressure it delivers is UNKNOWN. It is a comfort trade-off, not a free upgrade. Advantages of NIV — Ask Before You Tell

• Preserves airway integrity; avoids invasive ventilation and its complications
  • Reduces ventilator-associated pneumonia and lung injury
  • Enhances parental involvement — the baby stays accessible for kangaroo care
  • Improves respiratory muscle function by minimising work of breathing
  • Enhances gas exchange — CPAP creates and maintains PEEP, recruits alveoli
  • Decreases risk of chronic lung disease; better tolerated in preterms
  • Decreases need for intubation; flexible; allows earlier weaning
Disadvantages — The Reasons This Chapter Has Six More Sessions

• Interface challenges — leak or skin breakdown
  • Gastric distension → regurgitation and aspiration (why an OG tube is mandatory)
  • Nasal injury — trauma, irritation, septal necrosis, especially with prolonged use
  • Discomfort and agitation
  • Difficulty with synchrony — no flow sensor as in invasive ventilation
  • Limited ventilatory support — NIV failure can occur
  • Risk of air leak — the pressure reaching the lungs cannot be measured; auto-PEEP
  • Needs SKILLED monitoring — bedside nurses must be trained in NIV care

FACILITATOR HINT point at the last disadvantage. ‘Needs skilled monitoring.’ That is you. That is the entire reason this is a full-day session and not a device demonstration. The machine is easy. The watching is the skill.

Facilitator Script “The prerequisite for CPAP is good respiratory effort. CPAP splints an airway open — it does not breathe for the baby. A baby with poor respiratory effort does not need CPAP; they need PPV. Get that one thing wrong and everything after it is dangerous.”
PREREQUISITE: the most important prerequisite for starting CPAP is the presence of GOOD RESPIRATORY EFFORT.
Demonstration — CPAP Step by Step

• 1. Confirm the indication.
  • 2. Explain the procedure to the mother.
  • 3. Check the equipment — assemble, connect air and oxygen, humidifier with distilled water, ensure the heating wire is in the inspiratory limb.
  • 4. Choose the correct nasal interface — the biggest prong that fits the nostril without distending it (size table below).
  • 5. Fit the cap covering up to the ears, ears lying FLAT under it. A cap too small causes oedema.
  • 6. Apply granuflex / barrier dressing under the nose and over the bridge to prevent necrosis.
Moisten the prongs with saline before insertion.

• 7. Secure the interface — the bridge of the prongs must NOT abut the columella and must NOT blanch the skin.
  • 8. INSERT AN OROGASTRIC TUBE — CPAP inflates the stomach.
  • 9. Start CPAP at the correct settings (below).
  • 10. Ensure continuous bubbling in both phases of respiration.
  • 11. Document the time and the settings.
Nasal Prong Size by Birth Weight

SizeBirth weightSizeBirth weight
0< 700 g32000–3000 g
1700–1000 g43000–4000 g
1000–2000 g5> 4000 g
Too TIGHT causes pressure necrosis. Too LOOSE causes a large air leak and no CPAP. Periodically check the nasal mucosa for hyperaemia and the columella for blanching.
Starting Settings — By Indication (Module 3 initiation protocol)

Preterm with RDRecurrent apnoeaPost-extubation
CPAP5 cmH₂O4–5 cmH₂O5 cmH₂O
FiO₂30%< 25% (room air if SpO₂ target met)As on the ventilator (titrate to target SpO₂)
Flow6–8 L/min6–8 L/min6–8 L/min

nasal CPAP is usually started at 5 cmH₂O, flow 5 L/min, FiO₂ 30%; then titrated — pressure to reduce work of breathing, flow to obtain adequate continuous bubbling, and FiO₂ to the saturation target (90–95% for preterm neonates).

FACILITATOR HINT there is a documented discrepancy across the manuals on the SpO₂ target — 89–92% (Level II), 90–94% (MSSN practical), 90–95% (Module 3). Do not paper over it. Tell participants to state and follow THEIR unit's written protocol, and to write which one on the chart.
Skills Station Tasks (CPAP assembling)

• Assemble CPAP and do the wall connections.
  • Apply the interface correctly.
  • State the initial settings.
  • Identify the danger signs after initiation.
  • Safety emphasis: a poorly fitted CPAP causes nasal injury, air leaks, and treatment failure.
The fit IS the therapy.

Facilitator Script “Never judge NIV by oxygen alone — look at the baby. Write that on the board and leave it there. A saturation of 92 tells you almost nothing on its own. The work of breathing tells you everything.”
Scenario 3 — Response to CPAP 30 minutes after CPAP initiation: RR 62/min · HR 148/min · SpO₂ 92% on FiO₂ 0.30 · chest indrawing mild · baby more active.
Facilitator questions:

• Is this improvement or failure?
  • What parameters tell you the baby is responding?
  • What should be documented now?
  • What is the plan for the next 2 hours?
ANSWER KEY

IMPROVEMENT. Compare to a distressed baby: the rate has settled, the indrawing is now only mild, the baby is more active, and the saturation is on target at a LOW FiO₂ of 0.30. Every trend is the right way.
The parameters that prove it: reduced work of breathing (mild indrawing), a settling respiratory rate, improved activity — not the saturation alone.
Document: the settings, the full set of vitals, the work of breathing, and the time.
Plan: continue CPAP, maintain monitoring, avoid unnecessary changes.

Teaching point: this is the GREEN column of the traffic light. The instinct of an anxious team is to keep adjusting a baby who is getting better. Do not. ‘Avoid unnecessary changes’ is an active decision, not passivity.
The CPAP Adjustment Traffic Light (Module 3)

The golden rule of adjustment: FiO₂ and pressure go hand in hand. If there is a mismatch, something is wrong. Bring down the FiO₂ FIRST, then the pressure.
Monitoring — What You Check, and How Often

FrequencyCheck
EVERY HOUR (visual)The nose is not squashed or pushed upwards · the eyes are clearly visible · tapes not too tight, no indentation, pitting or ocular oedema
At least 4-HOURLY (physical)Hat fit — not too tight/loose, not rubbing · remove prongs/mask to rest the nose from pressure · inspect the nose for redness, breakdown, bruising, indentation, altered shape, bleeding · prongs clean and patent before replacing · ears not creased or folded

Remember (manual): remove prongs/mask by LOOSENING the tapes, not by pulling them off the face. Perform regular mouth care. Suctioning should NOT be routine — only as the baby dictates. Document whenever the nose is checked.
• Also monitor: capillary refill, blood pressure, urine output; tone, activity and response; a respiratory distress score (e.g. Downe's); chest X-ray at start and if deterioration occurs.
Feeding on NIV

• Babies are initially kept nil per mouth until stabilised.
  • Thereafter, commence feeds by orogastric tube.
The NCPAP System — Four Things Right, Every Round

• Tubes in the nose
  • Nasal airway clear
  • Mouth closed
  • Neck slightly extended
Ward Round (your draft) — Run It Live

• Conduct a ward round of 3–4 patients on NCPAP (or simulated stations).
  • For each baby, demonstrate: pressure · FiO₂ and oxygen saturation · clinical signs · any complications · whether adjustments are needed.
  • Each pair of participants answers for each patient, then places the baby in a traffic-light column and justifies it.

Facilitator Script “Nasal injury is the price of CPAP, and it is almost entirely preventable. A baby who survives RDS and goes home with a hole in the septum was failed — not by the disease, but by the watching. This is the session that prevents it.”
Why It Happens

• Nasal prongs cause trauma, irritation or septal necrosis, particularly with PROLONGED use.
  • The commonest mechanism is a prong bridge pressing on the columella — the strip of skin between the nostrils — which blanches, then breaks down.
Prevention — Built Into Every Step Already

• 1. Correct prong size — biggest that fits without distending.
  • 2. Barrier dressing (granuflex) under the nose and over the bridge.
  • 3. The prong bridge must NOT abut the columella; must not blanch.
  • 4. Remove prongs/mask 4-hourly to rest the nose — more often if the baby's condition dictates.
  • 5. Loosen tapes to remove; never pull off the face.
  • 6. Inspect and DOCUMENT at every check.
Inspect — What You Are Looking For

SiteSigns of injury
Columella / septumRedness, blanching, indentation, altered shape, breakdown, bleeding
NaresRedness, skin breakdown, bruising
Around the eyesOcular oedema, pitting, indentation from tapes
EarsCreasing, folding, redness, bruising, swelling, discharge, bleeding
Stage It — A Simple Working Scale

StageAppearanceAction
IPersistent redness / hyperaemia, blanching that recoversReassess fit NOW; barrier dressing;
increase rest periods; document
IISuperficial skin breakdown, bruising, altered shapeChange interface type (alternate prongs/mask); dressing; senior review;
document with time
IIINecrosis — septal erosion, deep breakdown, bleedingStop that interface; escalate to senior immediately; consider alternative NIV mode; wound care; incident report

Blanching is stage I and it is your window. Once the columella is white under the prong bridge, injury has started — act on the blanch, not on the ulcer. By the time it is stage III you are managing a complication that should never have happened.

FACILITATOR HINT rotate the interface. If your unit has both prongs and a nasal mask, alternating them gives each pressure point a rest — the same logic as turning a bed-bound patient. Show the group how to swap without losing the pressure.
Scenario 4 — Sudden Deterioration, With Answer Key
Baby on CPAP for 6 hours: RR 84/min · HR 182/min · SpO₂ 85% despite FiO₂ 0.60 · asymmetric chest movement · reduced breath sounds on the right · baby pale and lethargic.
Facilitator prompts:

• Is this CPAP failure or a complication?
  • What is your FIRST concern?
  • What immediate actions are required?
ANSWER KEY

This is a COMPLICATION, not simple failure. Asymmetric chest movement + reduced breath sounds on one side + sudden deterioration = PNEUMOTHORAX until proved otherwise — a known complication of CPAP (auto-PEEP, air leak).
First concern: tension pneumothorax. Do not reach for the FiO₂ dial.

Immediate actions: call for help · assess for tension · transilluminate · if unstable, needle decompression BEFORE the X-ray (cross-reference: needle thoracotomy, taught in Prematurity — RDS) · prepare for chest drain · escalate to the paediatrician · this baby may now need intubation.

The trap: this baby's saturation is 85% on 60% oxygen, so the reflex is to turn the oxygen to 100% and increase the pressure. In a tension pneumothorax, increasing the pressure makes it WORSE. Recognise the asymmetry first. Every group has someone who reaches for the dial — let the debrief teach it.
When Has NCPAP Failed? (Module 3 / MSSN)
Any ONE of these is CPAP failure — all require immediate consultation with a paediatrician for further management and retrieval if possible:

• 1. FiO₂ rising to above 0.6
  • 2. Respiratory acidosis — pH < 7.28 with rising PaCO₂ > 60 mmHg
  • 3. Development of recurrent apnoea requiring stimulation
  • 4. Worsening indrawing / grunting / tachypnoea
  • 5. Agitation not relieved by simple measures

FACILITATOR HINT note that four of these five are about the BABY, and only one is a number on the blender. A baby who needs more and more oxygen, or who keeps having apnoeas, has failed CPAP even if a single gas looks acceptable. Failure is a trajectory, not a threshold.
Complications to Look Out For

• Pneumothorax · pulmonary interstitial emphysema — from excessive pressure and over-distension
  • Decreased venous return, increased pulmonary vascular resistance, reduced cardiac output
  • Nasal trauma / septal necrosis
  • Gastric distension → regurgitation and aspiration
  • Agitation · continued deterioration
Criteria for Weaning

• Absence of significant episodes of apnoea
  • Minimal work of breathing
  • Decreasing oxygen requirements to less than 30%
The Four Steps

StepPhaseAction
1Initial FiO₂ reductionWhen SpO₂ > 95%: reduce FiO₂ by 5% steps. Continue until ready for CPAP reduction
CPAP reduction phaseWhen FiO₂ reduced to ~50% AND retractions mild or absent: reduce CPAP by 1 cmH₂O steps. Goal: CPAP to 5 cm, FiO₂ to 50%
3Further FiO₂ reductionAt CPAP 5 cm, FiO₂ 50%: reduce FiO₂ by 5% steps. Goal: FiO₂ < 30%
4Final weaning & removalCPAP 5 → 4 cm when FiO₂ < 30%.
REMOVE when FiO₂ < 25% AND CPAP at 4 cm
The rule underneath all four steps: decrease FiO₂ BEFORE decreasing pressure. Wean the oxygen down first; the pressure is what is holding the lung open, so it comes off last.

• Trial off NCPAP once the baby is stable for 6–12 hours on CPAP 5 cmH₂O, FiO₂ < 0.3, RR < 70.
  • Reduce CPAP by 1 cmH₂O every 6 hours until at 5 cmH₂O once RR < 70, FiO₂ < 0.3, and less effort.
  • If CPAP was given for apnoea, it can be removed within 24–48 hours of an apnoea-free period.

FACILITATOR HINT warn the group — it is not uncommon to see a mild rise in respiratory rate and inspired oxygen in the FIRST HOUR after coming off CPAP. That is expected, not failure. Do not put a baby straight back on CPAP for a wobble at 20 minutes; give the hour.

read.text: Learning Objectives

• 1. Know the basic physiology of respiration.
  • 2. Be familiar with common ventilation terminology.
  • 3. Understand the concept and common principles of mechanical ventilation.
  • 4. Be aware of common types and modes of mechanical ventilation.
  • 5. Know the common indications of mechanical ventilation.
  • 6. Develop the skills to use the ventilator safely from initiation to weaning and extubation.
  • 7. Know how to improve the care of ventilated babies and to monitor them.
  • 8. Be familiar with common complications and how to prevent them.

“The responsibility of the intensivist is to optimise ventilation and prevent the harmful effects of OVER- or UNDER-ventilation. Read that twice. The ventilator is the only treatment on this course that harms in both directions — too much and too little are both injuries.” Materials

• Neonatal ventilator(s) · test lung · manikin · ventilator circuits · humidifier
  • Self-inflating and/or T-piece resuscitator for the disconnect-and-bag drill · manometer
  • Blood-gas examples (printed) · chest X-ray examples · the disease-settings table poster
  • Caffeine, surfactant (for cross-reference) · CPAP setup for post-extubation · copies of all checklists

Facilitator Script “This morning you learned everything you could do to keep a baby OFF a ventilator — CPAP, the whole NIV chapter. This session begins where that one ends: the baby for whom non-invasive support was not enough. Putting a baby on a ventilator is not a failure of the NIV chapter. It is the correct next step, made in time.”
The Decision Point — When NIV Is No Longer Enough The manual's indications for intubation and invasive ventilation, drawn from across the disease sections:

• Increased FiO₂ and CPAP inadequate to maintain gas exchange (RDS)
  • Infants who TIRE from the increased work of breathing
  • Worsening clinical distress; increased oxygen requirements
  • Worsening hypoxaemia / acidosis
  • Clinical instability and intolerance of CPAP
  • Apnoea severe enough to warrant ventilator support, even without lung disease

Cross-reference the NIV failure criteria: FiO₂ > 0.6, pH < 7.28 with PaCO₂ > 60, recurrent apnoea needing stimulation, worsening work of breathing, agitation not relieved. The baby who meets NIV failure is the baby who arrives in THIS session.
Case — The Baby CPAP Could Not Hold

A 28-week baby, day 1, on CPAP 6 cmH₂O and FiO₂ 0.55 for RDS. Over the last hour: rising oxygen requirement, now 0.65; a blood gas shows pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 64; two apnoeas needing stimulation; visibly tiring.
Ask:

• Has CPAP failed? Which criteria are met?
  • What is the next step — and what must happen before you set a single ventilator dial?
  • What surfactant decision runs alongside this?
ANSWER KEY
CPAP has failed. Three criteria met: FiO₂ now > 0.6; pH < 7.28 with PaCO₂ > 60; recurrent apnoea requiring stimulation. This is not a borderline call.

Next step: intubation and invasive ventilation. Before touching a dial — the intubation itself (taught in the Advance Airway session), confirmed tube position, and a plan. HFNC during intubation improves first-attempt success and stability (cross-reference NIV).
Surfactant: this RDS baby who is now intubated should receive surfactant — early rescue. The ventilator and the surfactant are one decision, not two (cross-reference Prematurity — RDS).

FACILITATOR HINT the teaching point is that ‘put him on the ventilator’ is the START of the work, not the end. The dangerous team relaxes once the tube is in. The next four sessions are everything that happens after that tube is secured.
Interactive teaching

Facilitator Script “The ventilator frightens people because of the acronyms. But there are only three questions any ventilator breath answers: who starts it, what limits it, and what stops it. Trigger, limit, cycle.
Learn those three and every mode on the machine becomes readable.”
The Three Breath Sequences (3.3)

SequenceWhat it means
CMV — Continuous Mandatory VentilationALL breaths are mandatory, AND spontaneous breaths do NOT occur between mandatory breaths
IMV — Intermittent Mandatory VentilationMandatory breaths, with spontaneous breaths allowed between them
CSV — Continuous Spontaneous VentilationAll breaths are spontaneous
The Three Phase Variables — The Spine of the Whole Session

VariableWhat it governs
TRIGGERRegulates the START of each breath — who begins it, the baby or the machine
LIMITSUSTAINS inspiration — what caps it (a pressure, or a volume)
CYCLEControls the TERMINATION of inspiration — what ends it
“Trigger, limit, cycle. Start, sustain, stop. Write it on the board and point at it every time a new mode comes up for the rest of the day.” The Four Control Variables (3.4)

Only ONE variable can be controlled and limited to a peak during inspiration — it becomes the independent variable, and the others vary with the baby's compliance and resistance. The controlled variable's waveform is fixed breath to breath.

ControlWhat is controlledWhere used
Pressure Control (PC)The pressure waveform — a square wave — and the pressure limit. Volume and flow varyCOMMONLY USED IN NEONATES
Volume Control (VC)The volume waveform and the volume limit. Pressure and flow varyCommonly used in PICU
Flow ControlThe flow waveform; volume and pressure varyPaediatric patients — NOT neonates
Time ControlFlow, volume and pressure during the set Ti depend on respiratory mechanicsHFOV is the example

In neonates, PRESSURE CONTROL is the common mode. The square pressure waveform is the one to recognise. When you set PIP and PEEP, you are setting a pressure and letting the delivered volume vary — which is why you watch the chest and the tidal volume, not just the dial.

FACILITATOR HINT draw the square wave. PIP is the top of the square, PEEP is the bottom. In pressure control you choose the height of the square; the baby's lung decides how much air fits inside it. On a stiff RDS lung, the same square delivers less volume — which is the whole reason the next session exists.

sections.title: How a Ventilator Breath Works: The Modes Used in Neonates

read.text: The Modes Used in Neonates

The Paediatric Mechanical Ventilation Consensus Conference could recommend NO specific mode over another. Mode choice is guided by clinician experience, patient pathophysiology, institutional protocol, and ventilator availability.

ModeIn one line
Assist Control (AC)Every breath — triggered by the baby or the machine — is fully supported to the set pressure/volume
SIMVSynchronized Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation — a set number of supported breaths, synchronized; the baby breathes spontaneously between them
Pressure Support (PS)The baby triggers; the ventilator supports each spontaneous breath with a set pressure
Dual / Targeted modesVolume-targeted — the ventilator adjusts pressure breath-to-breath to hit a set tidal volume

Do not let the group get lost choosing a favourite mode. The manual is explicit that none is proven superior. What matters is that they can read whatever mode their own unit's ventilator offers, using trigger-limit-cycle.
Teaching

Facilitator Script “Conventional ventilation gives big-ish breaths at a normal-ish rate. HFOV does the opposite — tiny breaths, smaller than the dead space, hundreds of times a minute, on top of one constant pressure that holds the lung open. It exists for one reason: to keep the lung open without the damaging pressures that conventional ventilation would need.”
What It Is

• Rapid ventilation rates with small tidal volumes (often LESS than anatomical dead space).
  • Active inspiratory AND expiratory phases.
  • A constant distending airway pressure (MAP) is applied to the alveoli, maximising functional residual capacity and V/Q matching, over which small tidal volumes are superimposed at high rate.
Indications

• 1. Alternative to conventional ventilation, as a PRIMARY mode.
  • 2. When adequate oxygenation and/or ventilation cannot be achieved on conventional ventilation — as a RESCUE mode.
  • 3. To minimise lung injury by avoiding high inspiratory pressures or FiO₂ on conventional ventilation.

Disease settings where HFOV may suit: RDS · chronic lung disease of prematurity · MAS · CDH · air-leak syndrome with pulmonary interstitial emphysema · pneumonia · pulmonary haemorrhage · hypoplastic lungs.

The One Danger to Teach Hard The disadvantage of high MAP is OVER-INFLATION of the lungs — which decreases cardiac output, reduces BP, raises pulmonary vascular resistance, decreases venous return, and causes pulmonary leaks. It must be identified in time by clinical assessment, BP and chest X-ray, and corrected by reducing the MAP. “HFOV holds the lung open with one steady pressure. Too little and the lung collapses; too much and you strangle the circulation. The chest X-ray and the blood pressure are how you tell the difference — not the saturation alone.” Weaning HFOV

• Primarily by reducing the MAP as compliance improves. Reduce FiO₂ as tolerated; once below ~30%, wean MAP in 1–2 cmH₂O increments (except when over-inflation is evident).
  • In air-leak syndromes, reducing MAP may take priority over weaning FiO₂.
  • Reduce ΔP (amplitude) in increments of 2–4 according to the PaCO₂; observe the chest wall for vibration.
  • Extubate from HFOV to CPAP, or transition to conventional ventilation first (set PEEP, then a PIP giving a MAP 1–2 cmH₂O below the HFOV setting).

Before You Set Anything — Define the Goal (3.6) The manual insists the goal is chosen before the dials. Assess the pathophysiology (RDS vs MAS, post-surfactant, lung hypoplasia), the clinical findings, the blood gas (oxygenation vs ventilation), and the imaging. Then define ONE goal:

• Improve V/Q mismatch — but avoid oxygen toxicity, OR
  • Recruit the lung — but avoid lung trauma, OR
  • Support respiration — and plan for extubation as soon as indicated.

“You cannot set a ventilator without a goal, any more than you can set off on a journey without a destination. ‘Improve the gas’ is not a goal. ‘Recruit this atelectatic lung while keeping the plateau under 30’ is a goal.” General Starting Point — Pressure Control (3.6)

ParameterUsual starting value
PEEP4–6 cmH₂O, usually 5
PIP14–25 cmH₂O, usually 16–20
Rate30–60/min
Ti0.30–0.40 s
I:E ratioAt least 1:2

These are the GENERAL starting numbers. The next table — the disease-specific one — is where they get adjusted to the actual lung in front of you. Teach the general set first so participants have an anchor, then show how each disease pulls the numbers in a particular direction. Initiation by Disease (3.7) — The Central Table This is the manual's disease comparison table. It is the single most useful page in the chapter. Walk each row, and after each ask: WHY does this disease pull the number that way?

DiseaseTiRatePIPPEEPStrategy / goal

Apnoea — complete dependenceProlonged Ti unnecessary30–40/min (physiologic )PIP/VT 10–18 (prevent hyperventilation)3–4 (moderate)Low gas flow
Apnoea — intermittent—12–15/min (low)Minimal—Minimal intervention approach

Quick Reference Ranges (3.7)
