0.3–0.8 s (disease dependent)12–40/min3–8 cmH₂O (lowest apnoea, highest BPD)10–30 cmH₂O (limited in MAS/CDH)

The logic to make them say back to you: STIFF lung (RDS, BPD) needs HIGHER pressure and PEEP. OBSTRUCTED / air-trapping lung (MAS) needs LONGER expiration, LOWER rate, capped pressure. HYPOPLASTIC / fragile lung (CDH) needs GENTLE everything and permissive targets. The disease dictates the direction; the table gives the number.

FACILITATOR HINT the commonest error at this table is treating it as numbers to memorise. It is not. It is five stories about five lungs. If a participant can tell you WHY MAS wants a rate of 30 and a capped PIP (ball-valve air-trapping, pneumothorax risk), they will reconstruct the numbers. If they only memorised '30', they will apply it to an RDS baby and do harm.
Demonstration + ward round

Facilitator Script “The ventilator does not care for the baby. You do. The machine delivers a breath; everything that keeps that breath safe — the oxygen you wean, the pressure you watch, the tube you secure — is nursing and medical work at the bedside. This session is that work.”

Oxygen — A Drug With a Deadline Inspired oxygen harms the lung parenchyma after prolonged exposure through toxic oxygen radicals. Reduce the FiO₂ to 0.5 (50%) or BELOW as soon as possible — ideally within the FIRST 24 HOURS. The primary determinants of oxygenation are FiO₂ and mean airway pressure. “The first 24 hours has a target: FiO₂ at or below 0.5. If you are still on 0.8 at hour 20, that is not the disease being stubborn — that is a baby who needs a plan, whether that is surfactant, recruitment, or a mode change.” The Pressures You Watch

• PIP reflects the pressure needed to overcome elastic recoil — the best estimate of peak alveolar pressure, an important indicator of alveolar distension.
  • Accurate peak pressure requires NO patient effort during inspiration or exhalation.
  • High inspiratory pressure risks barotrauma, volutrauma, and reduced cardiac output.

Inspiratory PLATEAU pressure should ideally be < 30 cmH₂O. Elevated Pplat may be reduced by decreasing PEEP (which may reduce oxygenation) or decreasing VT (which may reduce minute ventilation). Permissive hypercapnia and a controlled fall in pH may be accepted when a high Pplat must be reduced. I:E, Auto-PEEP and the Trap of Stacking Breaths

• Total cycle time = 60 ÷ respiratory rate. Inspiration and expiration share it; normal spontaneous I:E is ~1:2.
  • In obstruction (asthma, some chronic lung disease) expiration is prolonged — I:E becomes 1:2.5 or 1:3.
Reduce auto-PEEP by (in order of effectiveness):

• Decreasing the respiratory rate — the MOST effective way.
  • Shortening the inspiratory time — extends expiration for fuller exhalation.
Decreasing VT.

FACILITATOR HINT auto-PEEP is breath-stacking — the next breath arrives before the last one has fully left. The instinct is to breathe FASTER to fix a rising CO₂; here that makes it worse. Slowing down is the fix. This is counter-intuitive and worth a full minute.
Also Monitor

• Gas exchange, lung mechanics, work of breathing, neuromuscular capacity, metabolic status — assessed FREQUENTLY to guide changes.
  • Humidification of inspired gas.
  • Remember: adjusting one parameter is likely to affect the others — take care with every change.

• 3–4 ventilated babies (or simulated stations). For each: state the mode, the settings, the last gas, the FiO₂ trend, the Pplat, and the goal.
  • Each pair decides: is this baby over-ventilated, under-ventilated, or on track — and what ONE change (if any) they would make.
  • Enforce the rule: change one thing, then reassess. Never turn three dials at once.
Facilitator Script “Weaning and extubation are two different decisions. Weaning is turning the support down.
Extubation is taking the tube out. A baby can be weaned to low settings and still not be ready to have the tube out — and confusing the two is how babies get re-intubated.”
The manual is explicit: decisions about WEANING are separate and apart from decisions about EXTUBATION. Some babies wean easily to low settings but are not yet ready to breathe without the tube.
Weaning — The Factors That Say ‘Ready to Turn It Down’

• The circumstances that required ventilation must be RESOLVING.
  • Level of alertness; need for sedation.
  • Respiratory drive and adequate oxygenation — SpO₂ > 95% with FiO₂ < 40% and/or low PEEP requirement (< 7 cmH₂O).
  • Adequate ventilation — PaCO₂ < 45 (no chronic respiratory failure), or > 45 with acceptable pH.
  • Time since the most recent respiratory or haemodynamic decompensation.

Permissive hypercapnia helps weaning and reduces lung injury: target PaCO₂ 50–60 while keeping pH over 7.20 (limited by pH 7.20–7.25). Preterms on permissive hypercapnia for 10+ days showed improved respiratory drive, fewer days on the ventilator, and a trend to less BPD or death.

• 1. Have a written mechanical ventilation protocol — including weaning, extubation and re-intubation criteria — agreed by neonatologists, nurses and respiratory therapists.
  • 2. Use assist control with volume-targeted ventilation if a proximal flow sensor is available.
  • 3. Allow permissive hypercapnia (PaCO₂ 50–60) and set SpO₂ targets (91–95%).
  • 4. Give a LOADING DOSE OF CAFFEINE before extubation — ideally within 24 hours prior.
  • 5. Place the infant on CPAP or NIPPV IMMEDIATELY after extubation (PEEP ≥ 5) using short bi-nasal prongs or a nasal mask.
  • 6. Stop enteral feeds for 4 hours before extubation.
  • 7. Confirm acceptable weaning parameters: MAP ≤ 8 cmH₂O, FiO₂ < 30–40%, rate < 30/min with an acceptable gas.

Step 5 is not optional. A preterm has insufficient drive and muscle strength to hold his lung open after the tube comes out. The distending pressure goes on IMMEDIATELY — not after a wait-and-see. Have the CPAP set up and running before you pull the tube.
Why Caffeine

• A large multi-centre RCT showed caffeine before extubation gave less BPD, shorter oxygen duration, and intubation for almost a WEEK less.
  • Early caffeine (before day 3) may further reduce time on the ventilator.
  • Give within at least 24 hours of the projected extubation. (Cross-reference: caffeine prescribing and stopping, Module 2.)
“Caffeine buys you a week off the ventilator. There are not many single drugs on this course you can say that about. Load it before you extubate — every time.”
Post-Extubation, and When Weaning Fails
• After extubation, a distending pressure (CPAP or NIPPV) is necessary immediately to prevent post-extubation atelectasis.
Common reasons for FAILED weaning:
• Cardiac dysfunction · cognitive dysfunction · respiratory pump failure · respiratory muscle and diaphragmatic dysfunction · metabolic disorders

FACILITATOR HINT if a baby keeps failing extubation, the reasons above are the differential. It is rarely just ‘the lungs’ — check the heart, the metabolic state, the diaphragm, the sedation. A baby who fails twice needs the list, not just a higher PEEP.

Facilitator Script “A ventilated baby desaturates. The whole room wants to run to the machine and turn dials. The manual says the opposite: take the baby OFF the machine and bag by hand. Because your hands will tell you in three breaths what the ventilator cannot — whether the problem is the baby or the box.”
The Core Algorithm — Sudden Desaturation With High CO₂ (3.11)
DISCONNECT the patient from the ventilator and BAG by hand. This single action is the fork in the whole algorithm.

What happens when you bagWhat it means
The baby IMPROVES with hand baggingThe problem is the VENTILATOR or the tube. Check: O₂ source, increase FiO₂, mechanical or electrical failure. Check the tube for displacement, obstruction or leak
The baby does NOT improveThe problem is the BABY. Assess for pneumothorax, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, intraventricular haemorrhage, and sepsis

This is the neonatal DOPE, in the manual's own words. If bagging helps, the fault is in the circuit or tube (Displacement, Obstruction, Equipment). If it does not, the fault is in the baby (Pneumothorax and the rest). Teach the fork first; everything else hangs off it. The Other Three Troubleshooting Patterns

PatternLikely causeAction
Gradual desaturation with high CO₂Inappropriate ventilator settingsIncrease PIP / PEEP / I:E ratio;
repeat blood gas
Gradual rise in PCO₂ (PO₂ unchanged)Insufficient tidal volume or rate; increased dead spaceIncrease PIP by 2–5; and/or decrease PEEP by 1; and/or

PatternLikely causeAction
(long ETT, non-ventilated alveoli)increase rate by 5–10; and/or shorten a long ETT
Fall in PCO₂ (over- ventilation)Too much minute ventilationDecrease the rate; decrease PIP and/or increase PEEP

“Notice the pattern in the timing. SUDDEN means something broke — disconnect and bag. GRADUAL means the settings drifted from the lung — adjust and re-gas. The speed of the change tells you where to look before you look anywhere.” Complications of Mechanical Ventilation (3.10)

• Air leaks — pneumothorax, pulmonary interstitial emphysema (cross-reference: needle thoracotomy and chest tube, Prematurity — RDS).
  • Barotrauma and volutrauma from high pressure/volume.
  • Reduced cardiac output, reduced venous return, raised pulmonary vascular resistance from high mean airway pressure.
  • Ventilator-associated pneumonia (cross-reference: sepsis prevention bundles, Module 2 Section
  • 10) .
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia — the chronic price the whole chapter is trying to avoid.
  • Oxygen toxicity — ROP and lung injury.

Every complication above is a reason the goal was ‘support respiration and plan for extubation as soon as indicated.’ The safest ventilator is the one the baby comes off soonest. This session and the weaning session are the same argument from two ends.

read.text: Scenario — Run the Algorithm Live
A ventilated 27-week baby, day 2, suddenly desaturates to 78% with a rising CO₂ on the monitor.
Give the group 60 seconds.
Expected first action: DISCONNECT and BAG by hand — not reach for the ventilator.
If bagging is easy and the baby pinks up: ventilator or tube. Check O₂ source, FiO₂, circuit, and the tube for displacement/obstruction/leak.
If bagging is HARD and the baby stays blue: the baby. Think pneumothorax first — transilluminate, prepare to decompress — then hypoglycaemia, hypotension, IVH, sepsis.

The trap: someone will start increasing the ventilator FiO₂ and PIP while the baby is still connected. Let the debrief land it — you cannot diagnose a machine problem while still trusting the machine. Hands first.
